text: Tries: line piece stops on squares that block something else (e.g. f6 blocks a knight mate, g7 cuts a rook path)
Start with simple defences to explore; replace with heavier ones (pieces vacating squares) when refining
Not every idea is realisable: some are impossible by construction (e.g. a rook cannot block a pin by another rook on the same line) or there is not enough space.
Choose the thematic squares so that intermediate steps (tries, intermediate squares) can be differentiated later; poor square choice makes tries impossible to separate.
Pieces need not mate directly: the meaningful guard of a square prepares the mates.
Shift the whole setting (e.g. one file left) to gain space.
Force a choice by a line-blocking requirement: e.g. the key rook must stay on c2-c4 to stop ...Rc1; tries leaving that zone share the refutation, which is a mechanism, not the theme.
Tries by the key piece, each blocking a different White line piece (Rc4 cuts Ba2, Rc3 cuts Bb2); the mate that works in the solution fails in the try.
Defences that merely guard the threat square, answered by mates that merely exploit the unguard, are uninteresting; mates should impress.
If the key piece has no role in the mates, consider giving it a mating role, even though that makes the tries harder to keep working.
Change material to change the play: e.g. one queen instead of two bishops. Vacating a square near the king invites flight-giving tactics.

Replacing two bishops by one queen: the bishops used parallel diagonals (a2-g8 via c4, a1-h8 via c3) which no single queen square shares; the queen must use a rank + a diagonal (only b3 works: diag to d5 via c4, rank to d3 via c3), so the guarded squares change (d4 guard lost).
source: Claude exploration s3, for E. Bourd review

text: A queen near an exposed king brings direct cooks (Qc2#, Qd3#); closing them cost two Black guards (Bb1 for c2, Sf2 for d3), and Bb1 turned the key into a Black line-cut (Rc2 cuts b1-d3).

Random search again failed without a constructed skeleton (dropped the queen, drifted). Reasoning about line geometry first, then solver-checking single changes, found the working mechanism in 3 steps.

Without the solver Claude found key, threat and 3/4 variations of the 2002 half-pin #2, missed the subtle unpin defence 1...Qd6 2.Qd3#, and made a geometric slip (thought Bc4 checks a king on d4: c4-d4 is a rank, not a diagonal). All claims must go through the solver.
A device (e.g. the pin of d5) should play in all thematic variations; in yacpdb 2753 the d5 pin decides only 2.Qc4# (the unpin is a defence motive in Qd6/Sxd7 but not a mate factor).

A capture key that removes the only guard of the threat square AND supports it is obvious. A quiet key needs a new mechanism that guards the threat square in the diagram and is switched off by the key (e.g. key cuts a Black line).
source: Claude analysis s3 (reviewed with E. Bourd)

text: Multi-functional units (e.g. bPf5: guards e4 against Qe4# and stops Se6+) make a setting tight but hard to improve locally; tool test: removing f5 gives 8 keys.

Searching for the key: fix the post-key play first, then look for first moves that produce it (a piece arriving at the same square from several origins, a piece leaving a line, a knight leaving d6 to open a pin). Do not commit to a key early; collect candidates that allow more play, then check what each try spoils. Refutations should be thematic, not incidental.

If the refutations of the tries are unthematic the tries are much less interesting; the try mechanism has to be related to the theme (here the half-pin), and the thematic mates may be changed if that fits better.

Hard scheme: dual avoidance for the mates is not easy to find, and adding thematic tries is rough even after the theme is clean. Order of work: get a clean dual-avoidance scheme first, then add tries.
A shared refutation is acceptable in itself, but it is worse when the refuting move is a random//unthematic move.
A dual in a thematic variation is unacceptable: the thematic purity is gone. Also the thematic defences should USE the theme (1...Sxd7 did not use the half-pin).

Post-key scheme search: a sound post-key position is just 'White mates in 1 after every Black reply'. Testing that costs ~1ms instead of ~300ms for a full #2 analysis, so 4000 candidates/second and exhaustive enumeration of small cores become possible. Tolerate unanswered replies as 'holes' during the prototype stage, then close them.

Content must be measured per PIECE, not per move: eight moves of one piece answered by the same mate is not content. For a half-pin: each half-pinned unit should provoke its own mate, disjoint from the other unit's (true dual avoidance).

A mate that CAPTURES the pinned unit, or that merely needs the half-pinner as a guard for the mating piece, does not use the pin (2.Qxe5# protected by Bh8 is not thematic). The pin is exploited only when the pinned unit, were it free, could capture the mating unit or interpose on the check line.

Dual avoidance needs an additional effect: there must be a concrete reason why the other mate fails after the other defence (the freed unit guards or captures the mating square, blocks the line, occupies it). "The king simply escapes" is a weak reason.

Aim for unity in the defences: here both thematic defences go to the SAME square (g3) and neither captures. Compare the motivation too - if one defence works by line opening and the other by giving a flight, that is a drawback.

Make the defences easy to generate (almost any threat is met by them), so they force one of the two queen mates; then choose the key square as the only one commanding BOTH mating squares. The other approach squares (b3, d2) each command only one and fail to the corresponding thematic defence.
A structure where the queen holds many squares in the mates is fragile.
Choose a threat that also attacks the half-pinned unit (f5), so that "not guarded any more by the knight" becomes a defence.

The underlying motive of a dual-avoidance problem is WHY the other mate fails in each variation; mark it explicitly when giving the solution, e.g. 1...Rg3 2.Qxd4# (2.Qxe6? Rxe6!) / 1...Sg3 2.Qxe6# (2.Qxd4? Kf5!). The KIND of reason should be unified across the defences - a capture by the freed unit in one and a king flight in the other is the missing second layer of unity. Compose with this motive in mind.

Purer motivations, in rising order of unity: (a) a sibling mate refuted by a unit that never moved (incidental); (b) the king simply escaping (weak); (c) the defender itself keeping hold of the line it held before it moved; (d) each defence opening a line for another Black unit. (c) and (d) are unified motives worth composing around.
The point of composing is exploring new exploits: inventing mechanisms, testing them and iterating - not only satisfying known themes.

A half-battery of two black PAWNS is impossible on a diagonal: the rear pawn guards a square that lies ON the pin line (e.g. pawn f6 with pinner Bh8 and bKd4 guards e5, which is on h8-d4), so a White unit mating there interposes on its own pin line and the pin is never exploited. Only pawns on the same ROW or COLUMN work: there both guard squares lie off the line, and a mate on one of them uses the half-pin.

Derived structure for a black pawn half-battery on a FILE (pinner Rd8, pawns d6/d5, bKd4): the rear pawn cannot advance (blocked by its partner) and the front pawn cannot advance (the king is there), so BOTH defences must be captures - a unity for free. The four squares c4/e4/c5/e5 serve double duty: each is both a possible bait (to be captured) and a possible mating square, so bait and mate must be assigned crosswise (d5xe4 -> mate c5; d6xe5 -> mate c4).

Two further constraints found by search: (1) a pawn capture only counts as a defence if the captured unit was essential to the threat; (2) the thematic mates land next to the black king, so the mating unit must be guarded - this is the main construction cost and the reason small cores fail.
score_core must reject dual threats and holes outright rather than merely penalising them: a core with a dual threat (Sc6#/Sf3#) still topped the ranking through other bonuses.

On a RANK the pawns can advance, so the defences need not be captures - and the mate can capture the advanced pawn itself (1...e4 2.Qxe4#). My earlier conclusion that pawn defences must be captures applies to the FILE only.

Method: describe a thematic variation by three independent choices - how the unit leaves the line (advance/capture/piece move), how the pin is exploited (capture prevention/interposition prevention), and why the sibling mate fails (defender retains control/line opening/another unit/king flight/no check). Known problems fill cells of that grid; empty cells are candidate mechanisms to build. compose/motif_space.py keeps the map in knowledge/motifs.json.
source: Claude s9, for E. Bourd review

text: Bug found by E. Bourd: when several Black moves refute a sibling mate, reporting the FIRST legal one hides the motive (2.Qe5? was reported as refuted by Kd3, when the thematic refutation is Bxe5). Classify every escape and keep the most thematic.

Necessity must be judged on CONTENT, not soundness: removing bBc7 from the completed problem leaves it sound and dual-free, but the dual-avoidance motive degrades from line opening to a king flight. The tool now reports that as "needed for the content".
dual_avoidance_after must exclude Black moves that are answered by the threat itself, otherwise non-defences pollute the unity verdict.

Extra (non-thematic) variations are usually unavoidable and are a necessary evil; they merely add extra play. They stop being a cost when they carry something of their own - here the extra variation ends in a switchback mate.
A key by a piece that is out of play is somewhat weaker than usual. It can be redeemed by what it does: this key unpins a Black unit, and that unpin creates an extra variation.

Tries that prove the half-pin are worth a heavier position; dual avoidance can be simple and still be fine if it is unified. Verdict on b2R4/b6p/8/N2pPQ2/2Npp2R/1pPk3P/1Pp5/2n2KB1: not too complex but decent.

Only defences BY the half-pinned units are thematic. A variation from another unit is extra play even when it is pretty (switchback) or caused by the key (unpin); unity of dual avoidance must be measured over the thematic defences only.

Design for a White-king key: the king stands on a line of a White piece and blocks it; every king move opens that line, so the choice of destination is free. Tries = destinations that CLOSE another White line; the key = the destination that closes nothing. Unified concept for the try refutations.

Why my searches failed: with little Black material every try is refuted by a king flight, so the key ends up merely guarding a flight rather than opening the line. For the interference to BE the refutation, the cut line must be essential to the mate that answers one specific defence. The real spec is three-way: defences d1,d2 with distinct mates m1,m2; m1 needs White line L1 and m2 needs L2; king destination t1 cuts L1 (refuted by d1), t2 cuts L2 (refuted by d2), and the key square cuts neither.

Negative result: ~150,000 positions searched across six geometries (wK blocking a rook on c8/c1/d8/e8/b8, queen + bishop + 1-2 black pawns). None gave two king tries whose refutation exploits the line the king closed. Reason: with only two added White pieces the lines are not load-bearing - the king has about five usable destinations and the lines through them rarely matter for any mate. The mating net has to be built first (more White force and Black defences); only then does closing a line cost something.

Order used by E. Bourd for the king-key task: (1) set up the lines and the possible king moves, (2) set up the mates, (3) THEN extend so that the defences themselves open the White lines - which turns the tries into anticipatory closings (a double paradox). Content is added by deepening the motivation, not by adding variations.

Evgeni built the king-key problem in stages: first the lines and the possible king moves, then simple mates (2N5/4p3/1R6/npk5/b5P1/2P1NK2/2P4B/5B1Q, where the tries are ORDINARY shut-offs of lines that are already open), and only later DISCOVERED that the defences could be made to open those same lines - which turns the tries into anticipatory closings. The deepening was a discovery while working, not something searched for.

A third interfering line only earns a thematic try if the square it guards is not already guarded by another White unit. Adding Rh4 pointing at c4 fails because Bf1 guards c4 anyway, so 1.Kg4? costs nothing and is refuted incidentally. The third defence would first have to block Bf1 (on e2 or d3) - and every Black unit that can reach those squares either guards d5 (killing the threat Qd5#) or refutes the key some other way. Verified by search.
Rotating/reflecting the whole setting can create room for an extra defence (here a third one, unguarding the rook mate). A cheap structural move before adding material.

To stop slow alternatives from also solving, give Black a strong universal resource: here bSh3 attacks g5, and 1...Sxg5 unguards f6, so every slow White move fails to it. That forces the intended threat without extra White material.

Necessity must also count TRIES as content: wPb6 takes part in no mate and leaves the problem sound when removed, but without it two of the three thematic tries disappear. The tool now reports lost tries and treats such a unit as thematic, not as a cook-stopper.

Geometric requirement, from the planner: for each try destination t there must be a Black line piece P and a White piece W with P, W, t collinear in that order, and W must be the mating unit for the defence that refutes that try. The key destination must complete no such pin. With W placed on several squares around the king, almost EVERY destination becomes pin-completing for some pinner - so the scarce resource is a clean destination for the key, not the pins.

Searches that failed: 102k rigid positions (Q + 2 knights vs R + B) produced no unique king key at all - the Black pinners are strong defenders, so the position rarely mates in 2; a hill climb drifted to two queens. The pins and the mate have to be built together, starting from the pin geometry.

Order for self-pin tries: first construct the LINES and work out which White pieces could be self-pinned; decide which units those are (here two knights); only then find the mates, and choose defences that make exactly those mates necessary. The pinnable units are chosen before the play.

For changed-mate problems the post-key search is useless: the mechanism lives in the relation between two first moves, so the whole diagram must be judged at once. Changes can run set/try, try/try or try/solution; the reasons range from simple geometry (the same piece mating from a different square) to flight changes, changed guards and battery changes.

Structural trap found in 2Rn1N2/7K/3P4/3k4/pB1p1P2/3n1P2/1p1Q1p2/8: the try threat Qe4# and the key duals come from the SAME resource - the c2-d3-e4 diagonal that the d3 knight opens when it defends. Blocking d3 to kill the duals also kills the try (a black blocker on d3 simply captures the queen on c2/e2; a white one destroys the defences or cooks). When two first-move squares are linked by a line through the defending unit square, the change mechanism and the duals are the same mechanism.

Set+solution is the easier form and can succeed where try+solution fails: in the set version the queen never needs the e4 square, so guarding e4 with a Black unit removes BOTH the immediate-mate cook and the Qe4 duals at once. In the try version Qe4 had to stay available as the try threat, which is why the duals could not be removed there.
source: Claude s16, after E. Bourd suggestion

text: Construction pattern Evgeni used twice: one thematic defence unguards a FLIGHT (which forces White's reply), the second is a DIRECT defence, and extra pawns block Black's other moves so only the thematic defences remain. Rotating the setting helps enforce a single thematic defence.

Set play is content too: a unit can exist only to provide an answer to one Black move. wPg6 leaves the problem sound, the key, all variations and both changes intact - but without it 1...g6 becomes unprovided. Reported now as a set-play filler rather than a cook-stopper.

E. Bourd's construction order for changed mates (session 18): (1) choose the squares and the Black EFFECT that creates several possible mates at once - a self-block is the usual one; closing a line, opening a line, or unguarding several squares do the same job; (2) find the DIFFERENTIATION between the phases - here the mating squares are controlled by Black pawns and each first move (try or key) removes one control, so each phase allows one pair of mates; (3) only then look for a threat and clean the setting. He tried set+solution as well; the try+solution form is what came out.

Same-piece changed mates need a Black move whose effect is exploitable by several mates, plus a second effect that selects among them within a phase. In 8/4p2K/Q2B4/1N1Np3/1pP1k1P1/6P1/2n1P3/8 each self-block (Sd4, Se3) lets either White knight mate, the flight the knight unguards (e3 or d4) picks WHICH knight (dual avoidance by king flight, unified), and the phase picks the SQUARE (c3 after 1.Bxb4?, d6/f6 after 1.Bxe7!). Two selectors, two changed mates, no duals.

A try refuted by a line closing that the key itself makes impossible is a strong pairing: 1.Bxb4? 2.Qg6# fails to 1...e6! (the pawn closes the queen's 6th rank); 1.Bxe7! captures that pawn, so the refutation disappears and the same threat works. The key piece's two captures are the whole differentiation.

Claude's attempt at same-piece changed mates by search (session 18): four skeleton families, ~5M positions, with a whole-diagram evaluator (set play + quiet key + changed mates, holes tolerated) and a beam hole-closer. It found geometries (bKd5 bSc6 guarding d4+e5, wRe4: set mates on d4, solution mates on e5; a reciprocal Q/R change after Se5/Sd4) but nothing sound: the key square attacked by the defending knight, knight checks on the White king, and a complete block cooked by every waiting move. Two hand completions were cooked by queen mates in one that Claude did not see. Missing was the composer's first step: a Black effect that yields SEVERAL mates, then a selector - the search only looked for one mate per phase and hoped relocation would change it.

A set+solution changed-mates diagram must not be a complete block: if every Black move has a set mate, any White waiting move cooks it. Either leave a Black tempo move unprovided (the key's threat then answers it) or make every waiting move spoil a set mate. The search must reject a diagram with a White mate in 1 outright.

Twice in session 18 Claude built a position by hand and asserted it had no mate in 1; the solver found three each time (Qf7/Qc5/Qa2, then Qd6/Qb5/Qb3): long queen lines to check squares are what the unaided reading misses. Nothing about a position is settled until mates_after() on the diagram says so.

Mating squares and the lines that serve them should be close to the Black king; a Grimshaw square in particular must lie near the king, with the two lines intersecting there. Far-off lines are hard to hold structurally (every guard costs a unit).

Fast start for "two pieces defend on the same square": let them CAPTURE a White unit there (e.g. 8/3n4/8/3kP3/8/4r3/8/8: Sd7 and Re3 both take e5). Then arrange the different mates around it, then find the differentiation between phases, then a threat that these captures defend against. A Grimshaw is also a fast start.

Two units defending on the same square (Rd4/Sd4 in 1K3b2/1P1p1B2/3r2p1/Q3P1RN/R1n1k2p/3p1p2/4nP2/4Nb2): the common effect is the self-block; the phase selector is the QUEEN'S POST - on a5 it guards d5/e5 (so Bxg6# and Rg4# work), on d2 it guards e3/f4 (so Sf6# and Qf4#). Each first move supplies the guards its own pair of mates needs; the try 1.e6? does it with the pawn (d5/f5) and fails to 1...Bg7! guarding the threat square.

Necessity must count changed-mate relations lost by a removal, whoever plays the try: wPe5 plays 1.e6? and bPg6 keeps the try phase dual-free; both were reported as cook-stopper / not needed. Fixed: lost changed relations mark a unit as content, and a unit that plays a try inside a changed-mate relation is a thematic unit.

Two pawns that each look removable on their own can be jointly necessary: bPg6 guards f5 (else 2.Qf5 duals in the try after 1...Rd4) and bPh4 guards g3 (else 2.Sg3 duals in the key after 1...Sd4). Test removals in pairs before calling a unit superfluous.

One-knight change from 8/8/8/5n2/3Pk3/8/8/8 (E. Bourd's start): the knight's departure opens the 5th rank for a queen on g5 (2.Qe5#), 1...Sxd4 self-blocks d4 and removes the pawn's guard of e5. Set 2.Re3# needs d5/f5/f4 held by the queen; after the key the queen must PROTECT d4 (2.Rxd4#) and abandon one of d5/f4/f5 so that Re3 fails - that abandonment IS the change. From g5 only f6 (abandons d5) does it.

Why the diagram flight cannot be removed: the queen must reach e5 only after the knight leaves f5, so it stands on g5/h5; from d6/f6/h2 2.Qe5 is mate at once. With d5 covered by any other unit the position has Qg4# in 1 (or Re3 becomes a dual after the key). So in this scheme d5 is a bare flight by construction; the price of a small setting.

The evaluator + beam closer reached a sound 10-unit setting in one pass once the start was the composer's three-unit scheme and the criterion was ONE specific changed defence (Sxd4), not 'any change': 85 raw hits, ranked by whether the changed move gets a mate no other knight move gets, then closed with units that answer the remaining holes (Rg8 for Kf4, Sf8 for e6, Se1 for f3, a Black tempo pawn to forbid waiting keys).

Providing the diagram flight d5 in 5NR1/8/8/5nQ1/3Pk3/3R1p2/3K4/4N3: 18 single White units give a set mate after 1...Kd5, but no pair of added units keeps the Sxd4 change, a unique key and dual-free play (full pair enumeration, 0 hits). The flight stays; a different scheme is needed to remove it.

Do not build around a Black king with a flight: positions with king escapes are structurally hard (every escape must be answered in every phase). Control the king without escapes first; it is much easier.
Simplest form of a one-defence change: the key piece that moved just gives the other mate itself (set 1...Sxd4 2.Qe3#, after 1.Qf6 1...Sxd4 2.Qxd4#). No second mating unit needed.

Reuse general ideas and the search process, not the same structures. The same solutions appear in various directions: manipulate the pieces, rotate or reflect the board, work from the constraints of the position.

Bishop version of the one-defence change: with the king boxed (no flights) the search found a 6-unit setting at once: 7b/8/3K4/8/3Pk3/2Q5/8/5R2 - set 1...Bxd4 2.Qf3#, 1.Kc5! (2.Qf3#) 1...Bxd4+ 2.Qxd4#. The change is motivated by the key alone: the king's arrival protects d4, so the queen no longer needs f3 and captures instead. Compare the knight version, where the queen post did the same job.

The no-flights constraint (E. Bourd) changed everything: the same enumeration that needed a beam closer and 10 units for the knight version gave sound 6-unit hits directly, because every hole it used to fight was a king escape.

An unprovided CHECK in the set play is a fatal flaw (worse than an ordinary unprovided move): a Black check with no set answer must be avoided, not merely noted. The evaluator now rejects any diagram whose set-play holes include a checking move; the critique should rate it major.

The closer's cook check was capped at 'more than one key' so a position with 12 keys scored the same as one with 2, and the greedy search could not tell it was digging deeper into a cooked hole (8/b1PR4/N4Q2/8/3Pk3/8/2RK4/8). Count cooks exactly and weight them; and prefer pawns and Black units as additions, since every added White line piece brings new keys.

Rook-key version of the one-defence change: 7n/6b1/1Np5/R7/3Pk1K1/2Q5/8/8 - the rook on a5 covers d5/e5 from the side; 1.Ra4 gives that up to protect d4 along the 4th rank, so the queen captures on d4 instead of mating on f3. Same idea as the king key (Kc5) and E. Bourd's queen key (Qf6): the key piece hands d4 a protector. Three keys, three pieces, one mechanism.

Self-pin by capture with changed mates (E. Bourd's 3rN2b/1p5b/8/2Q5/1R1Pk1P1/4P3/4K3/8): the SET mates come from the key piece itself (Se8: Sd6/Sf6, each capturable only by the unit that is now pinned), so the key switches them off simply by moving, and its arrival square protects one new mating square (c7 -> d5 for Qd5#). The second new mate needs no protection at all: 2.Qe7# is a distance mate whose only interposition square e5 is 'covered' by the pinned bishop. Pin exploitation by interposition prevention, not only by capture prevention.

Why the search missed it although the evaluator accepts the position (verified: it passes every filter): the enumeration budget, not the rules. His setting needs two White pawns (e3 for f4, g4 for f5) and two Black plugs (b7, h7); my families allowed one pawn. And my hand reasoning assumed the new mates had to be adjacent queen mates needing protection, so 'no key square protects both d5 and e5' looked like a proof. Rigid in the hand analysis, too thin in material.

Pinner on the rank + a White pawn on the pin square + queen nearby = a discovered-check cook: the pawn steps forward with check from the pinner, and the pinner protects the vacated square for the queen (1.d5+ Bd4 2.Qxd4#). Any self-pin-by-capture scheme with this shape must give Black a refutation of the pawn advance before anything else.

To stop a cook, give Black a resource that lives in the cook's line: 1.d5+ (discovered check) is met by a knight that can block on c4. If that resource also refutes the intended key, do not throw it away: INVERT the phases - the intended key becomes the try (1.Sc7? Sc4!) and the other first move becomes the key (1.Qh5!). The changed mates survive the inversion.

I found the c4 blocker (bSa5) and rejected it because 1...Sc4 also refuted 1.Sc7, calling the cook structural. A composer reads the same fact as a try refutation. Rule: when a repair refutes both the cook and the key, ask which first move should be the key, before declaring the shape broken.

A try whose play equals the set play (1.Qh5? here in the try-less reading) still 'adds the main play without the set': the changed mates are shown between try and solution, so the problem does not lean on set play at all.

Two free Black rooks reach every rank and file in one move, so no White king square is check-proof by distance. Shield the king with thematic blockers (a knight on b4 closes rank 4, c3 closes rank 3, h3 the h-file) and plug the rook's own file with a Black pawn that cannot move (a6 behind Ra5). A plug must never cut the rook's THEMATIC line (b5 killed the rook's guard of e5 and made Qe5 mate in one).

Every White line piece near the king's field adds its own checks and hence cooks (Be2 gave Bd3#/Bf3#, a knight on g1 gave six knight checks). Protect a mating square with a unit that has no line to the king, and that cannot itself capture on the square with mate (the g2 pawn duals with gxf3).

With a knight-bishop battery aimed at the king (Bh7, Sf5), every knight move is a discovered check; the threat is the battery mate and a Black pawn guarding the knight's square does nothing (cxd6 is illegal against double check). If the key square also covers a square the front knight protects, a second queen threat appears (Qe3): single threat needs that square guarded by Black or unreachable from the key square.

A unit that protects a thematic mating square along a line can mate along a parallel line for the same pin reason (Rd7 protects d5 for Qd5# and mates by Rxe7# because the pinned rook cannot interpose on e5): a thematic dual born of the pin itself. Move the protector back along its line so its second line is blocked (Rd8: e8-e7 is closed by the pawn) - the protection survives, the dual dies.

The hardest step (E. Bourd, in his words) is a REASON why the thematic moves defend. A capture defends when the captured square lies on a line from the capturer through a White piece to the White king: the capturer pins the piece that carries the threat (Rxe4/Qxe4 pin Qe2 against Ke1, so 2.Qd3 is illegal). The same capture can self-pin the capturer against a White rook on the rank (Rh4), so one move both defends and creates the weakness the new mate uses.

Two Black line pieces aimed at one square from different directions (Qa8 diagonal, Re8 file) give two thematic captures on it; putting the White queen and king on the extension of ONE of those lines (e-file: e4-e2-e1) makes both captures pin the queen because the queen sits on the file and the diagonal piece, once on e4, is on the file too. A rook was changed into a queen so it could reach the square along the diagonal while the other reached it along the file.

The key piece gives the set mates and switches them off by moving, again: Qh5 mates Qe5#/Qd5# on the pinned captures, then 1.Qxe2 replaces them with Se6#/Sc6#. A set-play queen on the diagonal that leads to the key square (h5-e2) is the cheapest way to get changed mates from one piece.

A White king that takes part in no mate is thematic, not passive, when a defence pins a White piece against it - that pin IS the defence. The critique now reports 'thematic king' with the pinning defences instead of 'passive king'.

Two keys with the same threat from the same piece (Qf3 and Qxe2, both 2.Qd3#): give Black a capture on the unwanted key square (Bh1 -> 1.Qf3? Bxf3!) and the cook becomes a try that shows the threat without the pin mechanism. A dual mate after a non-thematic defence (1...Sf2 2.Qxf2/Qe3) is killed by a Black pawn that guards the dual square (g3).

From the bench journal (383 steps, 3 sittings, 90 solves): session 2 spent 45 minutes and six rotations/shifts on the first scheme without ever producing a key, including a 16-minute stretch of placements with no solve; the problem was finished 33 minutes after CLEARING the board and rebuilding from the idea (king d4, pawn e4, two Black line pieces on e4, a rank pinner). When a scheme has no reason for its defences after a few solves, restart from the idea instead of rotating the structure.

Solve after every structural change: in session 3 the breakthrough (Qe2 giving threat Qd3 with the pin reason) was seen in a post-key solve one minute after the piece was placed, and the last three flaws (cook Qf3, dual Qxf2, then the missing try) were each fixed within a minute of a pre-key solve. Remove pieces in pairs at the end: the solver's necessity check found bRh4 and the Rf4 shift unnecessary (17 units keep everything).

Two Black units capturing the same White unit get DIFFERENT mates when the capture square sits on two White battery lines at once: the departing unit opens one line (Bd4 leaving d4 opens Rc4-f4 with Se4 as front piece), the arriving unit self-blocks on the other (Qxe5 lets the Bf5/Rf8 battery fire). Each defence closes the line the other opens, so dual avoidance is unified by 'no check'.

With batteries doing the mating, the White queen's post selects WHICH departure mates: Qh3 guards g4 so every Bf5 move mates (six duals in the tries), Qg2 behind its own g3 pawn guards nothing there so only Bh3 mates; Qh1 gives Qf1# instead of a knight departure. Moving one queen between three squares gave three phases for one defence and two for the other.

Fourth sitting on the two-captures idea: 21 minutes, 43 solves, finished. The two previous sittings (33 and 33 minutes, Sept 13 evening) ended in zugzwang positions with 20-27 holes and no threat. What differed: the sitting started with the batteries already in place (Rf8 behind Bf5, Rc4 behind Bd4/Se4) and looked only for the queen post that gives a threat; the first sound key came after 15 minutes, then four cook fixes and a rotation to bring the key square onto the board.

A sibling mate that gives NO check is refuted by nothing Black plays. The dual-avoidance classifier reported 'another unit captures the mating unit' for 2.Sxg3? after 1...Qxe5 because a capture happened to be Black's first legal move; the real reason is that Bd4 still closes the c4-f4 battery. Fixed in both solvers: no-check is tested first and the closed battery and its blocker are named.

A corner key needs a reason the corner is the ONLY square. The Bristol supplies it twice over: the line piece must vacate every square the queen will pass (so it goes to the end of the line) and must keep protecting the mating square from that line (so it cannot leave the line: 1.Ba6? clears the diagonal too, but Qg2 is then unprotected and 1...Kg1! escapes). The kernel Q7/KB6/6N1/8/8/8/7k/8 shows the whole logic in 5 units.

When the queen's mate square is protected by the key piece from the far end of a diagonal, every interposition on that diagonal also cuts the queen's protection of the corner square: the key bishop on h1 is then en prise to the king. Mates after interpositions must therefore protect h1 themselves (a knight on f2), x-ray it (a rook checking on the h-file), or be the one line-opening the interposer cannot undo.

Only a pawn can open a White line by interposing on another line without being able to close it again: a knight or rook that interposes on the a8-h1 diagonal from the b8-h2 diagonal can step back onto it against Qb8+ (Se4-d6, Rd5-d6), a bishop cannot reach a diagonal of the other colour at all. So the line-opening interposition is a pawn move (f4-f3), and the pieces interpose for other reasons (unguard, self-block).

A queen in a corner has three long lines; block each with a unit that already has a job. Here the white king on c8 blocks the whole 8th rank (Qc8-h3, Qg8-g2, Qh8 in one unit), the e1 knight that mates on f3 also blocks the first rank against Qa1-g1/h1, and the black knight on d4 that interposes also blocks the long diagonal against Qa1-h8. Two pure blocking pawns (a3, g5) fell away once those units were in.

Order that worked: (1) mechanism and its reason for the key, tested as a 5-unit kernel; (2) box the king in the diagram with the fewest units, checking cooks by hand after each addition (the first-rank rook that protected h1 also mated on h1 in one); (3) enumerate only the LAST layer, Black defenders plus at most one White unit around the fixed kernel, with a cheap prefilter (key still forces mate) before the full solve - 60k positions in four minutes; (4) trim: remove each unit and re-solve. Hand reasoning found the two pawn defences; the enumerator found the d4 knight and the e1 knight that made four variations from ten units.

A third knight, a third rook, a second queen, or two bishops on one colour is a PROMOTED piece and a fatal flaw unless the idea cannot exist without it (E. Bourd). Check the force count before showing a position; the enumerator now rejects obtrusive force in its prefilter.

The third knight's two jobs (mate on f3 after an unguard; block the first rank against Qa1) were done by a rook on a3 that both blocks the a-file and mates on h3 when the black knight on c3 leaves the rank to interpose: same four variations, ten units, no promoted force. When a unit is illegal, list its jobs and find one legal unit that does them from a different line.

An underpromotion key needs the other three promotions to fail for stated reasons. The cheapest uniform reason is stalemate: the queen pins or covers the last black move; each minor piece fails for its own reason (a bishop cannot pin on a file, a rook cannot pin on a diagonal, a knight pins nothing but must then produce the mate). The cost is structural: to be stalemated after the wrong promotion, Black must have almost no mobile units, so such problems stay thin - all three settings have at most one mating move, and 150,000 enumerated additions of one or two units found no version with a second variation.

With the pinned piece a bishop on the promotion file and knight mates on d6/f6, the bishop's own guard of d6/f6 gives dual avoidance (Bc7 keeps d6, so only Sf6#; Bg7 keeps f6, so only Sd6#), but its self-blocks on d6/f6 give duals (Sxd6#/Sf6#), and its captures of boxing pawns (Bxg3) refute. A knight pinned there interposes on both bishop lines with dual avoidance by interference (Sd7/Sf7) but self-blocks on the mating squares c6/g6 and lands on non-interfering squares for duals. Neither yields a clean two-mate setting without heavy pawn blocks (16+ units).

When the black king is fully boxed, every White check is a mate in one: a first-rank rook protecting h1 mates on h1, a bishop covering g6 through f5 also mates from e2, rooks reaching a square adjacent to the king with protection mate at once (Rd4#, Re3#). Box with units that cannot reach a protected adjacent square, or leave the hole the intended mate is meant to fill.

Promotion problems: the black king on the promotion file makes the queen/rook promotions checks that the king answers by escaping to the hole the knight mate would fill, but then the flight must also be answered after the quiet key, which the promoted knight cannot do; this route failed three times (e4 king, h4 king). The stalemate route worked first time for each piece once the pinned unit could not capture the promoted piece (a bishop on the pin diagonal takes it) and could not block the mating line (a knight on g6 cannot reach the h-file; on f7 it reaches h6).

Underpromotion motivated by a FLIGHT instead of a pin: the king's only square lies on the promotion file (e6 for e8), so queen and rook cover it and stalemate; the bishop leaves it and then mates from the diagonal-adjacent square f7, covering the king's old square d5 by x-ray through e6. Geometry: promotion square P, flight F on P's file, mate square M diagonal-adjacent to P with M-F-old king square collinear. The knight must fail after the forced king move: block its checking squares (the white king on c7) or leave d5 uncovered for it.

With a forced king move to the promotion file, any White check that also covers the vacated king square is followed by e8=Q# (Rc4+, Rd7+, e4+): every unit near the king must be unable to check d5 while covering it. Cover the box with a rook along a rank blocked from the king's rank by a protected pawn (e5), a knight that covers c5 and e5 without touching d5 (d3), the white king for c6/d7, a rook on the f-file for f5/f6/f7.

Flaws are weighed against content, not counted: when the theme is tripled (four promotions of one pawn, each failing for its own reason), flaws that would be fatal in a simple problem - diagram flights, a flight-taking key, tries refuted by king moves, a king-flight variation - can be accepted as the price of the complexity. Clean and simple is usually judged below complex with some flaws. Partly subjective; E. Bourd's call on 5K2/3P4/1N2p3/1P2k1NP/1P4P1/3p4/3B4/8. Corollary for composing: doubling or tripling the theme buys tolerance; economy buys little.

Both solvers dropped zugzwang tries (the JavaScript one required a threat) and stalemating first moves (no refuting move to report), so the wrong promotions of an underpromotion key were invisible on the bench. Now zugzwang tries count their refutations and a stalemating first move is a try refuted by the stalemate.

Shrink to the minimal form. E. Bourd took a 12-unit bishop-promotion setting, tried stripping it (rooks d6/f6, 4 solves), abandoned it, and rebuilt from the mate picture with the fewest units: a pawn on the 7th, one queen, two kings, moving the queen and the white king one square per solve. Nine solves, three minutes, four units: 7K/3P1k2/3Q4/8/8/8/8/8. The minimal form shows the essence: the promotion itself gives the flight (the pawn's attack on e8 disappears), Q/R re-cover it along the rank and stalemate, S checks and cannot protect e7, B protects e7 for Qe7#. Building UP from a kernel (my 8-unit version) never reaches this because each added guard hides which units the idea really needs.

A promotion gives a flight by itself: the pawn on d7 attacks e8; any promotion removes that attack, and the promoted piece either re-covers e8 (Q, R along the rank) or not (B, S). So the flight-giving promotion key needs no other unit to open anything. The promoted piece's job after the flight is to PROTECT the mating square for another piece (Bd8 protects e7 for Qe7#), which a knight on d8 cannot do; my version made the promoted bishop the mating piece instead, at twice the units.

When two promotions both solve (18:36: d8=B and d8=R both keys), E. Bourd did not remove one; he chose which should be the key and made the others fail for their own reasons, arriving at all four promotions as try/key (5K2/3P4/1N2p3/1P2k1NP/1P4P1/3p4/3B4/8). A cook between two thematic moves is a tripling opportunity, not only a flaw.

His sittings on the promotion theme: 18:25 load my setting and strip (abandoned in 3 minutes); 18:28 new scheme with a queen on g4 (solved in 7 moves, double threat, abandoned); 18:32 pawn d7 with knights and bishop, cook between B and R promotions turned into the four-promotion problem by 18:42 (19 solves); 18:48 the minimal four-unit form in 9 solves. Four restarts in 27 minutes, each from a smaller idea than the last; no restart kept more than the pawn and the black king.

The promoted piece is chosen by ONE geometric fact: from the promotion square it must reach (protect or cover) the square the mate needs and the other pieces must not. Bishop: the needed square is diagonal-adjacent to the promotion square (d8 protects e7). Knight: a knight's move away (c8 protects e7). Rook: on the file or rank. Queen: reaches everything, so she fails only by covering too much (stalemate). One position, shifted one file, changes which minor piece is right. That is the rule; the counts of how many such positions exist are not knowledge.

Facts are infinite; record the rule that predicts, the dead end that prevents work, or the process step that saves time. An enumeration's output is a check on a claim, not a lesson; what enters the lessons is the mechanism it confirmed, in one sentence with one example. Everything else stays in the problem collection as data for lookup.

A key that vacates a square to unmask a line (Sc5-e4 opening the c-file for Qc4/Qc6) is not yet a key: every other departure of that unit unmasks the same line. The key must be the one departure whose ARRIVAL does something the others do not - here closing the g6-d3 diagonal so that ...Bd3 refutes Sd7?/Sa6? but not Se4. Decide what the arrival square does before solving; the solver only lists the cooks.

When one other arrival square of the key piece also works (Se6 covered d4, so Qc6 became a second threat and Kxe6 walked into the same Qc6#), occupy it with a white unit the black king can capture: the cook-stopper becomes a second flight (wPe6, protected only by the knight, given up by the key).

Two flights mated by the same queen: the mate after each flight must fail as the threat. Against a king on e4, Qc4 (rank check) x-rays f4 and needs e3, f3, f5; Qd3 (diagonal check) x-rays f5 and needs f4 plus protection. Leave e3 or f3 uncovered and the threat Qc4 fails after Kxe4 while Qd3 mates. A rook on the third rank or a knight on e1 covers f3 and kills the distinction.

With a queen on c3, a black king on d5 and c4 empty, 1.Qb3+ Kd4 followed by Qd3# is a cook whenever d3 is protected (the queen covers c3 and e3 from d3). No white unit can block b3 without either protecting c4 (Qc4# in one), covering d4 (Sb3, so Qc6 mates everywhere) or covering the third rank (Rb3). A black pawn on a4 answers the check by capture and costs one unit.

The two-flight search in the abstract (bK e4, a bishop or queen leaving the a7-g1 diagonal, up to three added units, about 10M positions) found nothing; Evgeni's three-unit scheme with the key named (bK d5, bP e5, wS c5, 1.Se4) reached a sound position in one sitting. Start from a scheme with the key move named, not from a theme statement.

A knight cannot re-guard a square it guarded from its origin (its origin and destination are on opposite colours, all guards of one square on the same colour). So a knight correction re-guards nothing: it captures, interposes, or lands on a square whose loss the mate exploits. Here the correction captures the rook whose rank cover of e4 the random mate needed, and is itself captured with mate.

The random move's error must be something the key-side does not already own: an unguard, or a white line opened through the origin square, whose beneficiary is a piece that could not move before (the queen's file to c7 through c6). If the opened line only duplicates a cover the diagram already has, no mate is created. And the threat must not use the piece the correction removes, or the correction refutes the key instead of correcting.

A queen on the c-file behind a rook on d4 (Qc3, Rd4, bKe5) is a battery: every rook move is a discovered check and cooks. A queen on c4 next to the rook makes Qd5 and Rd5 both mates (double threat) unless d5 is attacked by a black pawn on e6. A rook on h6 with a knight on g7 gives Re6# in one. Each of these cost a solve; check adjacency and lines to the king before placing the queen.

E. Bourd's order for a correction problem: threat, then the random defence (a line opening makes every move of the piece a defence), then the correction with its own plus and minus. Three abstract mechanism searches (about 8M positions) found nothing because they fixed the wrong mate; the hand sequence threat -> defence -> error -> correction, with the solver checking each step's set play, reached a sound position in about fourteen solves.

Adjacent knight (bK e5, bS d6): a knight always attacks its origin, so a mating line through the origin square is interposed by every knight move; and every far destination interposes on some line to e5 (e3 from c4/f5, c5 from b7/e4, g5 from e4/f5/f7). The only mating line no far move touches is h2-e5 (Qh2/Qg3/Bg3/Bh2), which the adjacent squares e4 and f5 parry by guarding g3. So a self-block correction on e4 pairs naturally with a random mate on that diagonal.

A rook on the d-file behind the knight (d7/d8) that covers d4/d5 once the knight leaves gives free duals: Bd4# for a bishop on f2 (the rook protects d4) and Rd5# whenever anything else guards d5. A rook on a6/b6 that covers e6/f6 after the knight leaves gives Re6#, and e6 must be guarded for the d4# mate anyway. So the knight's departure cannot open a white ROOK line as the enabling error in this cell.

When the random mate's pre-move failure is a cover the mating bishop itself removes (Bf2 leaves d4 when it mates on g3), every flight is covered in the diagram, and then any queen check is mate. The queen must have no check at all, which costs a blocking unit per line (a-file, a7-g1, h-file, e-file, 1st rank). Budget for it before choosing the queen's square, or use a rook as the threat piece.

The threat parried by a bishop line opened through the knight (Ba3, threat Qe7#) cannot share a diagonal with the random mate: a queen mating on c5 through f8-e7-d6 is captured by that bishop. A random mate on f6 along the 6th rank is parried by Se8 as well as Se4, so it forces a second correction with its own mate. Random-mate line and defence line must be different lines through the origin square.

Two small ones from this cell: a black pawn on d7 jumps to d5 once d6 is emptied and interposes on any 5th-rank check, so bPd7 kills a c5/b5/a5 mate; and a queen anywhere on the 8th rank reaches d5# through the emptied file as soon as d5 is protected (block e8/g8 or leave d5 unprotected). A key rook moving to d7 stands between an a7 queen and e7: the 7th-rank threat and the d7 key exclude each other.

Start small and keep the mechanism light, so it can be extended with more content later: a random move and one mate on three units, then the threat, then one correction, then a second. A structure that is heavy, rigid, or dependent on very specific flights cannot take an extension; a cell where every flight is covered by exactly one unit has no slack. Judge a kernel by what can still be added to it, not only by whether it is sound.

Doubling the theme from both sides is exponential in chess content: a black knight correction (random move, two self-block corrections) mirrored by a white correction of the key piece, whose 'random move' fails, whose aggressive corrections are each refuted by the corresponding black correction, and whose true correction (the key) has no negative effect. Each correction play could stand alone; the combination is the problem. Look for the mirror whenever the key piece has several posts.

A knight standing next to its king defends by DEPARTURE: it gives the king the square it stood on, so every knight move defends against a threat that needed that square covered. No black line and no white line through the knight is required; the error is the line it leaves (the b-file for Qb3#). This is the light form of the 'any move defends' mechanism, lighter than a line opening.

Knight correction by line play: the queen ambushes behind the knight (Qh5 behind Sf5). The knight's departure unmasks a black line (Qh3-e6, so Qe6 parries Qf7#: every knight move defends) and a white line (h5-d5, the random mate Qd5#); its arrivals close other black lines (Se7 cuts f8-c5, Qc5#; Se3 cuts h3-d3, Qe2#). Departure opens, arrival closes: one motive for the random move, one for each correction, and the queen plays every white move.

A knight has two arrival squares on any diagonal it can reach (from f5: d6 and e7 on a3-f8). An interference correction on that diagonal therefore comes with a twin that cuts the same line; the twin is a random move with a dual unless its extra effect (Sd6 guards b5 and f7, Se7 guards d5) is made to matter. A strict one- and two-unit search (about 4,000 solves) found no repair on this scheme; the dual is structural, not a plug problem.

Two plugs worth naming: a black pawn on a6 guards b5 so the ambushing queen does not get Qb5# as a second mate along the opened rank; a black knight on b1 stops a second key (1.Be3 c2 2.Qxc2+) by interposing on c3. Every cook-stopper has one job; say it in the log so the next reader knows which unit may not move.

Kill a twin-square dual by occupying the twin: with the black bishop on e7 instead of f8, the knight has one interference square (d6) on the e7-c5 line. And let the correction close a WHITE line too: rook d8 guards d5, Sd6 cuts it, so the random mate Qd5 fails for a reason and Qxc5 is the only mate. The rook's price was a Rxd4 dual after Sxd4, paid with a black pawn that recaptures (c5, its square covered by Ba3).

In a symmetrical theme (corrections, pairs of self-blocks, reciprocal play) the thematic variations should carry roughly the same weight of effect. One correction with a double motive next to one with a single motive is a drawback even though the double one is nicer on its own: balance the pair (both double, or both single) rather than admire the odd one.

A fully boxed king turns every protected check into a mate in one, so a Dombrovskis kernel cannot be built by covering every flight with pieces. Slesarenko's trick: the queen on a file is the SOLE guard of two king-adjacent squares, so any queen move off the file opens them; the try piece closes one, the mate square covers the other, and the pawn that interposes on the file also self-blocks. Five hand kernels died to mates in one (Qb5# along the check rank, Rd2# down an open file, c4# protected by the queen's diagonal, Qxe5# because the try piece protected the self-block square); the search over two added units found the sound form in seven minutes once the kernel had only the mechanism in it.

Single Dombrovskis, minimal reasons: try piece T covers square S that the mate A needs and the queen's origin O covers; the defence d vacates square F next to the king (a pawn's own square) so A fails to K-F; the key covers F and threatens a capture along the queen's line that d interposes on while self-blocking S, so A now mates without T. Qx(S) after d in the try phase must fail: leave one flight (c4) covered only from O, so the queen cannot both capture on S and hold it.

source: Claude s28, on E. Bourd's sketch
text: Capture form of the single Dombrovskis (his sketch: bKd5, wPe5, bPd6, defence dxe5). The threat the capture parries: a rook mate Rxd6# whose only protector is the e5 pawn, so the capture removes the protector; the key rook arrives on the 6th rank and by the same move controls d6, which is what makes the play after the key pure (his note). Requirements found the hard way: e6 empty for the rook's path and covered by something that cannot mate on e4 (a pawn f5, not a bishop); the knight that protects e5 must not also protect d6 (c4 does both, then dxe5 parries nothing); its mate square must not be attacked by the pawn arriving on e5 (f4) or by the d4 pawn (e3) and must not lie on the 6th rank (f6 blocks the rook); the d-file above d6 blocked by a protected black pawn, or Rd8 is a second key; the 5th rank blocked (f5) or exd6 and Rh5 cook.

A try that must add a guard of a square next to the king without touching another one is often impossible by geometry: any knight that can reach c6 already attacks c6 from where it stands (knight moves are symmetric), a light bishop covering c6 or e6 also covers d5, a rook on the 6th rank covers d6 too. Then the only try left is a capture (Rxc8 covering c6 through c7). Check this before building: list the pieces that can newly cover the square in one move.

How to double a Dombrovskis on captures: two white units each the SOLE guard of one square beside the black king (a knight guarding d4, a pawn guarding d6); two black captures, each removing one guard, each refuting a try whose threat needs that square; one quiet key by a piece that covers both squares at once (a bishop on c5 next to the king, protected) and threatens a mate that both captures parry for their own reasons (one captures the threatening piece, the other guards the mating square through the vacated line). The key piece's other moves can serve as the tries. Black self-blocks (d3, e3) can be thematic even when a necessity check calls them idle: they carry a try.

A black pawn on d7 guards e6 and c6: a white piece landing there is captured (dxe6), so a mate on e6 becomes possible exactly when the pawn steps. Both steps of one pawn give the same freedoms (d7 vacated: a flight, the a4-e8 and c8-h3 lines through d7, the e6/c6 squares no longer guarded); the difference between them is only what the landing square closes and guards. To get two different mates, give each mate a white line through the OTHER landing square: here 2.Qe6# runs a2-d5-e6 (cut by d5) and 2.Ba4# needs Ba3 guarding e7 through d6 (cut by d6).

A reciprocal change on one pawn's two steps is very hard: each step switches off the white lines through its landing square, and with the king next to d6/d5 the squares those lines guard overlap, so a doubly guarded square cannot switch. Twenty minutes of guided search found none on five king squares; the archive (7,912 problems) has none either. Worth asking the mentor before spending a day on it.

The evolutionary search finds what its score rewards: rewarding two different mates returned five-unit miniatures with diagram flights; rewarding hits without a threat count returned triple threats and capture keys (it plants a black unit for the key to take). Put the whole publishable shape into the score and the hit test (one threat, quiet key), and give it the exact target mates once the mechanism is known; then finish with kernel_search on the fixed key, which killed the last cook in two seconds.

Read a line piece's random squares as a set: when every random move lands on one line through a mating square, that square stays guarded after any random move, and the correction that leaves the line is the one that allows the mate there. A bishop between the king and an open file is a clean random error for a bishop: any move opens the file (here Rd8 guarding d3-d5), so the queen may leave its rank.

evolve with CORR=<square> from a blank core (king + correcting piece + queen) finds rich random/correction sets but no key in twenty minutes; seeded with a hand sketch of the mechanism (the line the random move opens, the queen's rank) it found a sound eight-unit setting in two minutes. Sketch the mechanism by hand, let the search finish the box and the key.
Always show a problem in chat with its diagram: send the card image (tools/card_png.py) with the solution and the questions, never the solution text alone.
example: cards for daily No. 1 and No. 2

text: A key made by a piece out of play (a knight on the edge, far from the king, guarding nothing near it) makes the solution obvious and is a fatal flaw. The key piece must be in play before it moves.

Corrections must be strong and their errors subtle. Two weak corrections are worse than one good one: remove the weaker. If the random move almost allows the correction's mate and a pawn exists only to block that, the blocker is fake and the mechanism is not clean.
example: 3R4/8/6K1/4P3/3bk3/N1p3Q1/8/8: Bxe5 Qe3 / Be3 Qxe3, c3 pawn

text: A known mechanism reproduced with no added value, especially in a reduced form of a published problem (a single where the original shows it doubled), is almost a non-problem. Do not publish what the post itself has to call 'not new as a mechanism'.
A White unit that takes no part in the solution and is there only to make a thematic try is a fatal flaw: far too high a price. Tries must come from units that also work in the solution.
example: 6K1/1N6/4p3/1PBk3p/8/8/4Q3/6N1: Sg1 plays only 1.Sf3?/1.Sh3? (gate rule try-only unit)

text: The key piece must have a role in the diagram: guarding, delivering a set mate, or blocking a piece. His words: 'the key piece is always in play; the issue is that on the initial diagram it has no role - not guarding, not delivering mates, not blocking pieces. So its only role is to come out of thin air and place itself obviously on the key square' (1.Rf1 from h1). Critique rule 'idle key piece' checks exactly these three in the diagram; softer when the key piece also plays thematic tries.

Set-play mates that the key changes are never a small addition to a finished mechanism: a complete mechanism has to be thought for the change from the start, especially when the play is rigid (here each pawn step allows exactly one mate for a line reason). Do not offer 'two or three more units' for a change; design the change first.

He liked the dual avoidance in the pawn-step problem: after either step both mates (2.Qe6 and 2.Ba4) seem possible, and each landing square kills exactly one of them for a line reason. Mates that both look available after every thematic move, separated by one precise effect, are the good kind of play.

His method for changed mates (session 29): first get each thematic defence answered by two mates at once, then separate. Separation is the hard part. Find the white piece that selects each mate (the one whose square or line decides it); when the selectors are two different pieces, no single key can switch both, so change the geometry (he shifted the scheme one file) until one white move carries both switches.

Double-function phase moves: in his pawn-step problem 1.Be6 vacates c8 (Sc8#) and closes the queen's 6th rank (no Qh6), 1.Ke4 vacates f5 (Sf5#) and closes the queen's e-file (no Qxe5). Each phase move does one square vacation for the knight and one line closing for the queen, so the two changed pairs come from one idea.

In his pawn-step problem both steps are self-blocks, each on a square guarded by a different white piece: c6 releases the knight that guarded c6, c5 releases the queen that guarded c5, so the mates split between knight and queen. That is what the choice achieved here, not proof that it was the right choice: other defensive effects could have worked as well (his correction, session 29).

He builds the post-key position first and then retracts the key (king e4 to f5). Look-up and journal show long dual-killing by adding blockers (about 70 solves) before the selector idea; a separator tool (chesscomp/compose/separate.py) now lists which single white moves split the duals and which pairs give changed mates.

Pawn move themes are limiting by nature: the board cannot be rotated or moved up or down (a double step ties the pawn to its home rank), only shifted by files or mirrored left-right. The mechanism is more rigid and less open to enhancement, so design changes into it from the start; geometry will not rescue it later.

The no-rotation limit applies to themes made of pawn moves. Incidental pawns (cook-stoppers, blocks) can be rearranged after a rotation; only when a pawn move is thematically critical is the board really fixed.
The edge is very limiting: far fewer mates and freedoms to play with. Keep the black king and the thematic pawn central (c-f files) unless the edge itself is the idea.
Set-play duals that are not part of the intended thematic play are not important (E. Bourd). Do not count them as flaws; show them only as information.
A threat makes the problem richer; a zugzwang is limited and a bit less interesting by nature (E. Bourd). Prefer a threat when the mechanism allows it.

To keep one wanted mate among rivals, add a unit that kills the rivals for a reason (his bPe5 removed the queen's other mates and kept Qh6). Search for it with keepkill instead of hoping; if no unit works, the split needs a different reason. Putting two effects into each phase move is the hard part.

Do not call a composer's choice 'right' after the fact because it worked. Say what it achieved and what else could have been tried. 'It worked. Not that it was right, many other things could be right as well. And if not, I'll change so it was wrong?!'

Reuse pieces for guarding, threat and mates. The threatening piece should be in play in the diagram (in his knight self-block sketch the threat bishop guards c6 and d7), not brought from far away. Each self-block square guarded by the unit that then mates.

A key that leaves every set mate unchanged and only adds the threat generates no new play; it lowers the complexity a bit. Not that bad in a single-phase problem, where set play is not even mentioned, but a more dynamic key that changes or introduces play is more interesting for the solver.

'Must / can't' changes: one mate pair must have a flight guarded (it does not cover it), the other pair can't mate because the mating square cuts a guard line. A single key that takes over the cut guard and gives up the flight guard switches both pairs; the flight it gives becomes a variation.

Adding a black piece that stops a lot of White's play is fine, even when it is the same type as the thematic piece (a second black knight next to the thematic knight). Do not count it as a blemish for that reason.

Construction limits: improvements could be infinite (extending, cleaning). Accept a known weakness (here d1 promotions repeating the self-block's mate) when it pays for soundness against a strong cook (1.Qc3), and stop. When judging, name such a flaw together with what it buys.

E. Bourd, Problemesis 2005 (2B1R3/8/3Q2n1/2Ppn3/3k2N1/3P4/8/2R2K2): 1.Ba6? / 1.Bf5! each protect the d3 pawn through one of the rook mating squares (a6-c4-d3, f5-e4-d3). After a random knight move the d3 pawn must stay protected, so the rook mate on the bishop's line is impossible (it cuts the protection: 'can't'); after 1...Sxd3 the pawn is gone and the mate must land where the bishop protects it ('must'). One line, two opposite roles depending on the defence: the same square flips from can't to must, so the mates swap between phases.

J. Kovalic, Sachova skladba 2001-02, 1st Prize (3Q4/4p3/K1p1p2R/2k1pP2/4p3/2pP4/P7/B6B), Lacny split over three phases: three gates d4/d5/d6 next to Kc5. Each phase move closes one gate (Rxe6 d6, Bxc3 d4, Bxe4 d5), each defence closes one by opening a white line (c2 opens Ba1 to d4, e3 opens Bh1 to d5, exf5 opens Rh6 to d6), each queen mate closes one by x-ray through the king (Qb6 d4, Qa5 d5, Qxe7 d6). In every phase+defence the mate must close the one gate left: a Latin square of requirements, so the mates cycle.

Reading changed-mate problems: for each phase and defence, write what is still required (which flight must be covered, which line must not be cut) and which mate meets it. Reciprocal and cyclic changes are arrangements of these requirements; design the requirement table first, then the units (session 29, after his must/can't problem).

L. Lacny, Przepiorka Memorial 1950, 1st Prize (8/3pK3/b2p4/3Q3B/qRp2Nn1/r3kNB1/rRp5/n5b1), the theme's namesake. Set: c1=Q Sg2#, c3 Qe4#, Sh2 Qd4#; 1.Sd2! (2.Sf1#) c1=Q Qe4#, c3 Qd4#, Sh2 Sg2#. Each defence opens one white line (c1=Q opens Rb2 along the 2nd rank, c3 opens Rb4 along the 4th, Sh2 opens Bh5 towards f3/e2). The hinge is the white knight next to the king (f3 in the set, d2 after the key): the king can take it, so every mate needs it protected, and each opened line either protects the knight or covers a flight depending on where the knight stands (Rb2 reaches e2 past an empty d2 but stops at the knight on d2; Bh5 stops at the knight on f3 but reaches e2 once f3 is empty). One knight move re-routes all three lines, so all three mates rotate.

Recipe from the two Lacnys studied: let each black defence open one white line (a guard appears), and let the phase change move one white unit that sits on or beside those lines, so each opened line now serves a different requirement (cover a flight, or protect a capturable white unit next to the king). The mates rotate because the requirements rotate, not because three separate effects were added.

V. Markovtsy, Die Schwalbe 2001, 2nd Prize (2K2BB1/8/5P2/8/2pkP1R1/Q3p3/6b1/2r1N3): 1.f7? (2.Bg7#) c3 Qc5#, Ke5 Qd6# but Bxe4!; 1.Bg7! (2.f7#) c3 Qd6#, Ke5 Qc5#, plus threat reversal. Requirement table: in the try Bf8 still protects c5 and d6 but the f7 pawn blocks Bg8, so the queen must mate next to the king (protected, covering the new flight herself: Qc5 after c3 frees c4, Qd6 after Ke5). In the solution Bf8 has left, so a queen next to the king is taken, but Bg8 now sees c4 and e6 and Bg7 covers f6, so the queen mates from a distance (Qd6 after c3, Qc5 after Ke5). The king's square (d4 or e5) decides which of c5/d6 is adjacent; the phase decides whether adjacent mates are protected. Two requirements, each phase meets one, the defences swap.

'Maybe we jumped to Lacny a bit too fast, from reciprocal or weaker forms of paradox transfers.' Learn changed-mate forms as a ladder: changed mate, transferred mate, reciprocal change, threat/variation paradoxes (Le Grand family, threat reversal), then Lacny. Each rung adds one requirement switch.

Two black units that capture the threat's only guard on one square give a natural changed-mate pair: in the set play each capture is answered along the white line its departure opens; after the key one mate uses a departure (an unguard) and the other the arrival (a self-block). The key piece can be the selector by leaving the line of one set mate.

evolve with CHANGED=1 from bare cores (king + the defending pieces + a queen) found nothing sound in four 15-minute runs; seeded with the reference's two-captures core (8/3n4/8/3kP3/8/4r3/8/8) it returned sound two-change settings in under ten minutes. Its hits then need hand work on the White king (unprovided checks) and on units that serve only the set play.

A shift can supply the reason a scheme lacks: moving the whole board down one rank put the capture square e4 on the White queen's rank, so both captures there became self-pins and the set mates became pin-mates (the pinned unit cannot go back to block the opened line). Look for a shift that puts the capture square on a line of a piece already present before adding units.

One Black error per phase, one dual-avoidance reason per phase: set play, captures on e4 self-pin and open the d-file (rook mates; the other pair fails to Kd5); after a key that leaves the pin line and guards d5, the same captures unguard b5 and c3 by departure (the rook mates fail because the unpinned unit blocks again). His aim: more cohesion than unguard + self-block.

source: Claude, on E. Bourd's e4 self-pin problem
text: A flight that the key gives onto the square the king just left the neighbourhood of: every square guarded through the king's own square gives check in the diagram, so after 1...Kxe4 the mating move must cover d4 itself. Only 2.Qg4+ (rank x-ray through e4 covers d4 and f4) and 2.Qxe5+ came close; Qg4 leaves exactly d5, the square that selects the phases, and protecting e5 for Qxe5 makes 2.Qxe5# a dual after 1...Sxe4. When a flight is wanted, check first that its mate does not need the phase selector square.

The bench's JS solver tested every candidate mate by playing it again, although chess.js already writes '#' into the SAN of a mating move; filtering on the SAN made solves 3.5x faster with identical reports. Remaining cost is chess.js writing SAN for every generated move.

A white unit tied to a single thematic mate feels like an outsider; give it a second job, ideally one that repeats the theme's motive. His knight a3 -> a7 plus a black knight d8: the key Qe6 became a queen offer, 1...Sxe6 2.Sc6# (d8 leaves c6), so all three post-key mates are captures whose departure unguards the mating square. 'All the pieces seem to have a more active role, and the solution is the one switching, so the play changes.'

source: Claude, theme '3 defences on the same square' (E. Bourd's request)
text: Three black captures of a white pawn on e5 (Sd7, Re3, Ba1) next to Kd5, threat Qd6# (the pawn is d6's guard): evolve from No. 3's kernel found 8/3n4/8/1K1kPB2/1P6/1NQ1r3/8/b7, 1.Qc7! Sxe5 Qc5#, Bxe5 Qc6#, Rxe5 Qxd7#/Qc6# (dual). Qc6 fails after Sxe5 (Sxc6) and Qxd7 after Bxe5 (Bd6 interposes), but nothing separates Rxe5 from Bxe5 for Qc6: the rook and the bishop on e5 change nothing around c6, and the rook's departure from e3 opens no line that matters. keepkill: no single unit; a 3rd-rank pin line (wKa3, bRh3/g3/f3, pinning Sb3 once Rxe5 opens e3) broke the threat. Lesson: with three capturers, each pair must differ in what its departure or arrival does to the OTHER mates' squares; check the 3x3 table (defence x mate) on paper before searching.

The archive's form: a sacrificial key onto the square, captured three ways (Strebkovs, Problemesis 2003, 8/1R1N4/1p1kp1n1/Rn1P2Q1/2Pb4/1K6/1B6/8: 1.Sc5! Bxc5/bxc5/Kxc5; E. Bourd, Problemesis 2003, r2R1R2/B2pnbN1/1q6/1N2p3/1pB1k2n/4P3/3P4/1K3Q2: 1.Se6! Bxe6/dxe6/Qxe6 with all mates on d3). Search on 'Défenses sur la même case'.

A mate that relies only on what all the defences do in common (here the self-block of e5 by every capture) cannot be told apart by the defences: after the rook's self-block the mate Qc6 also works after the bishop's, unless the bishop does something more. The dual is in the logic, not in the placement. Each mate must depend on an effect that only its own defence has (a departure from a specific line or guard, an arrival that interferes with a specific line); the common effect gives the reason the moves DEFEND, the distinct effects give the MATES. Write the effects of each defence first, then pick each mate from an effect no other defence shares.

His construction order for defences on one square: threat -> pieces that can capture on the square -> arrange one mate per capture (each from what that capture's departure gives up) -> find the key, which is most of the work. Making the captured unit the key piece that supplies the threat (1.Be4 guarding d5 for Qd5#) gives every capture the same reason to defend for free; the mates then come from three different departures (three knights' squares unguarded). My failed attempt started from a fixed white unit on the square and searched for mates, the opposite order.

Do not read the journal's timestamps literally: he takes many breaks for life (food, caring for his father, shopping), so gaps are not thinking over steps. Measure a sitting by its steps and solves, not by its minutes.

A Black move that does not stop the threat is not a variation, so extra mates after it are no dual, even when the threat mate is then played as a capture (1...f4 2.Qxf4# is still the threat Qf4#). Compare the threat by move (piece, from, to), never by notation. The bench's post-key view compared notation and called it a dual; fixed.

source: Claude, keyfind on E. Bourd's four schemes
text: Why the key is the hard part: a post-key position built for its play usually lets White mate in two in many other ways (his schemes: 23, 14, 12, 1 besides the threat). Taking back one unit only breaks the solutions that need that unit on its square, so a key exists only if one white unit is needed by every one of them (his 1.Be4: all seven other solutions need the bishop on e4). Check this while the post-key position is still soft: count White's other mates in two and see which unit they all share; quiet extra solutions (Kg8, Bg6) mean the post-key position is a complete block and any waiting move cooks.

A key by a queen (or rook) standing idle on the edge or in a corner is as bad as an out-of-play knight: 'very bad key, queen completely out of play' (1.Qb1 from h1). The out-of-play rule now covers all pieces.

In a post-key position (White to move) every move that leaves the threat standing must solve, or the solution has a refutation; listing such waiting moves (Kg8) as cooks is noise. Only moves after which the threat no longer mates but White still forces mate (checks, captures, new threats) constrain the key.

A constructional gap (a hole such as 1...Se4 with no mate) is filled by finding an ERROR of that move that no other defence shares, then building the mate for it; a one-unit search cannot supply a missing error and expecting it to is naive. In scheme C the only own errors of Se4 are the self-block of e4 and two line closures that help Black; the unguard it shares with Sb5 (Qb4-e1 opened). Tool: chesscomp.compose.effects lists errors and marks the shared ones.

When no unit of a finished post-key position can be taken back as a key, try a NEW unit as the key piece: place a white unit on an empty square of the post-key position (play unchanged) and take it back one move. A unit blocking the threat line gives a clearance key (1.Rb6-a6! opening b4-b8). Also: be assertive when he asks for a fix; he expects his co-helper to carry it through, not to hand the decision back.

A clearance key by a unit placed only to be moved off the threat line, and doing nothing afterwards, is unacceptable (1.Rb6-a6!). A natural blocker is acceptable even if simple: his pawn d6 blocks the threat's line b8-e5 AND occupies d6, the square of a mate after the key, so 1.d7 clears both and adds a variation. Critique fix: a key piece standing on the line or square of the threat or of a post-key mate is not idle.

The difference between 1.Ra6 and 1.d7 is material: a pawn that only plays the key (or only stops a cook) is cheap; a completely useless rook, bishop, knight or queen is usually fatal. Critique: 'useless key piece' (major) for an officer in no mate after the key; a pawn stays a minor 'passive piece'.

His way to a key from a finished post-key scheme: take the key piece from the units that already play, never a new one. Rearrange so that a unit with an existing role stands on the threat's line (or a mating square) and blocks it, and give it a job on that square that it must keep after moving (the rook d6 guards e6/f6 along the 6th rank), so only one clearance square works; then clean cooks one by one. The clearance squares that fail become tries (1.Rxc6? Rxc6!, 1.Rxh6? Sxh6!).

Trim recursively: some units are artifacts of others (bPh6 only stopped the checks of bRh5; once the rook went, the pawn could go). After every removal, test all removals again, or explore removal sets: chesscomp.compose.trim.

source: Claude, theme 'two defences on one square, no capture, not next to the king'
text: Grimshaw on c3 (bRa3, bBa1, bKe4): the split works on paper and in every search (1...Rc3 cuts the bishop's guard of d4: 2.Rd4#; 1...Bc3 cuts the rook's guard of f3: 2.Bf3#; each wrong mate fails because the arriving unit still guards its square). What failed is the threat: it must run through c3 and reach the king, and the 3rd-rank rook interposes on e3 against any e-file check (2.Qe1), while 2.Rc4 needs d5 protected without blocking c4. Decide the threat line and its interpositions BEFORE the mates; bare-core searches (8 runs) and seeded ones (12 runs) did not supply it.

Hand construction goes wrong on board sight (a white pawn on e6 'protecting' d5; 'Rc4 mates'). Check every coverage claim with chesscomp.compose.matecheck FEN MOVE: it lists each square of the king's field with its white guards or FREE, every interposition and every capture of the checker.

Threat first (E. Bourd): for a Grimshaw on c3 (bRa3, bBa1, bKe4) the threat must cross c3 and reach the king: 2.Qc6# from c1 (no interposition on d5); Qb4-e1 is the other line. Then a post-key local search (chesscomp.compose.postsearch, threat fixed, defences named) found clean post-key positions in minutes, e.g. 3R4/8/8/7R/4k3/r2p4/3PP1KB/b1Q5: Rc3 2.Rhe5# (bishop's e5 guard cut), Bc3 2.exd3# (rook's d3 guard cut). Remaining: the queen on c1 is far too strong for a key (Qxa3, Qxa1, Qc4+, Re8+ and c-file moves also solve).

Order that worked for a theme from scratch: (1) threat that makes the thematic moves defend (his rule; here 2.Qc6# crossing c3), (2) post-key local search with the threat and the defences fixed (postsearch), (3) the same search with READY=1, minimising White's other real mates in two until one unit is shared, (4) keyfind, (5) recursive trim, (6) gate. Diagram-level searches without a fixed threat found nothing in 20 runs.

After a flight-giving key the square the king just left can be covered only by the mating move itself: a line piece aimed at it already checks the diagram king, and no knight guards it without checking. Choose the flight's mate first (2.Sc3# from b5 covers the vacated d5 and checks e4), then build the box around that mate.

Flight-giving key from scratch: bare-core evolve (4 x 15 min), seeded evolve with batteries/CORR (4 runs) and post-key searches with a fixed threat all failed to give a sound diagram in 110 minutes. Post-key positions with the flight mated were easy; keys were not: a rook sacrifice 1.Rc4! (n3r3/8/4p3/3kp3/R3N3/3p4/KB6/3Q1B2) needed a diagram flight c6 that was the only square stopping two mates in one. A zugzwang self-interference key (1.Bd4 cutting Ra4 from e4) worked but the diagram was a complete block, cooked by waiting moves.

Order the work by how much each problem constrains the geometry: first what may force a change of scheme or board (threat with two flights, the guard of a square next to the king, how to get two phases), then the mates, then construction (each unit with a stated purpose: set mates for flights, cook-stoppers), last the non-thematic duals. Late changes to an early decision undo everything after it. A level switch (threat to zugzwang) can reframe the same Black moves (defences become corrections).

A key that moves a White piece Black attacks is a flaw (it reads as an escape). Weigh it against the alternative: an attacked piece is milder than a piece out of play, but neither is a real improvement.
