A threat on a square next to the black king (2.Qe6# against Ke5) turns every Black guard of that square into a move into the king's field: self-block-shaped defences for free (Rd6, Sd4, Sf4 in 3r1r2/4p3/5pR1/3PkNBp/2R4P/5B1Q/4n2K/8). Whether each is a real self-block must be checked move by move (evolve SELFBLOCK mode, motives 'self-block on'): here one of three was. When a diagram flight cannot be covered without making another mate a threat (a d6 guard made 2.Qf5 a second threat), let the key give the flight, with a unit that closes the threat line and guards the flight square at once (Sf5: 1.Sg7!).

Self-blocks from bare or lightly seeded cores (8 evolve jobs, 5-18 min each, SELFBLOCK=2/3) ended on checking keys every time: a boxed king plus a queen makes every check a candidate. A brute force of three guards around a rook-knight battery (Ke5, pawns d7/f7) produced only complete blocks where White also mates in one. What worked: the threat first (Qe6#), a post-key search with the three guard-of-e6 defences named, then a unit that blocks the threat line in the diagram as the key piece.

Variety and cook handling from a random start (bench demonstration, NOT his recommended way to construct a problem: E. Bourd, 10 Oct 2026, 'not the best mechanism to construct a problem, but shows the general idea of handling cooks and creating some variety'). Put up a position where many mates are visible at once; pick as the threat the mate easiest to defend; add Black units whose moves each stop the threat and let one of the other mates through, so the mates become variations; kill the remaining White solutions one by one; find the key last by taking a White move back. It yields varied play quickly (sound six-defence version in 70 steps) but no idea: the mechanism-first order of the compose skill stays the way to build a problem worth publishing.

List each thematic piece's OTHER defending squares before construction (E. Bourd: the rooks do not only close the line, they have other defences - address that early). A rook reaches everything on both its lines: squares on the threat line, squares on the mating square's rank or file with a clear view, captures of the threat piece or its protectors. Also follow every planned line to the edge: the threat line a8-d5 ran on to the king (a check, not a threat). And in an open position cooks are not a verdict: iterate them, name each one's cause, block it with one unit (here three black pawns did it).

Order: (1) the post-key position works (threat, every defence with its mate, no holes) - verify with the post-key table; (2) a features pass by reasoning: every line to the edge, every White unit Black can capture (fxg4 on a knight placed on g4), every unit's check squares, both kings present; (3) only then the key. Do not jump to the key with an unverified post-key position.

Key types to consider first: a piece arriving to guard a square (the threat's mating square), a line opening, a queen arriving from a better square. Give every unit an extra job (reuse) - each extra job makes the problem more efficient; a queen that only sits on a diagonal with a set mate is weak.

A knight leaving a square still guards it from wherever it lands (knight moves are symmetric): 'vacate e5 and guard it' gives eight tries, each needing its own refutation. And a cook by a pawn check + recapture (1.d3+ Rxd3 2.exd3#) exists when the recapturing unit gives check and the pre-key position covers the recapture square: choose the key piece's start square so it does not cover that square.
example: knight on f4 guarded d3 -> 1.d3+ Rxd3 2.exd3#; from e7 it does not

text: Two rooks capturing one white knight: let the knight be the THREATENING piece (a guard-knight gave no reason for distinct mates). Each rook captures along one of its lines and keeps it, losing the other: a rook capturing down its file loses its rank, along its rank loses its file. Put the two mating squares of ONE second knight on the two lost lines (f6 on the 6th rank of the b6 rook, g3 on the g-file of the g1 rook): the mates are unguards, and dual avoidance is built in because the rook that did not move still guards the other square.

When the key piece must only clear the threat square, give it a second and third job on arrival: on d4 the bishop blocks the pawn push d5-d4 (which would capture on c3) and protects e3, which turns the pawn check d2-d3 into a mate against the knight that leaves d3 (1...Sd1 2.d3#). But the same protection makes d2-d3 a SECOND THREAT unless a black unit attacks d3: a black knight on f2 did it and added the variation.
example: 1.Bd4! (2.Sc3#, not d3# because of Sf2xd3) Sd1 2.d3#

text: Claims the solver corrected in one problem: (1) a queen threat from d1 left f3 uncovered once the queen moved; (2) 'e5 covered by the bishop through d4' was redundant, f4 covered it all along, so the key's real jobs were different from the ones I reasoned; (3) protecting e3 with the key created a pawn-check double threat. Each was visible from a guard list of the king's field (matecheck) and from the threat list after the key; do both before the next placement, not after the solve.

Two free black rooks reach almost every square with check, so the white king needs every line to it blocked by units that have jobs (here Ph3, the black pawn g4 and Pc4), or the rook checks refute. Choose the king square from the blockers you already need, not first.
example: Kh4 behind h3/h5 and g4, with the 4th rank shut by c4

text: A capture-mate on a cut square (Bxd5#) re-blocks the very line the cut closed: the rook behind d5 no longer guards d4, so a second guard of d4 that outlives the capture is needed. Here the key knight supplies it: Sf3 covers d4 and e5, the threat Sg5 leaves f3, and that is exactly why the d-file cuts defend only the threat and not the mates.

In a bare post-key position every move that makes a threat is a key, because the mates are static. The cure is Black counterplay against the wrong threats only: a black pawn e5 guarding d4 killed 2.Rd4# and blocked 2.Re8#, so 1.c3/1.e3 (guard d4 with a pawn) no longer threaten anything; the pawn then also gives a third variation (exf4 2.Rd4#).

A bishop guarding a square next to the king from a diagonal has, on every square of that diagonal, a checking move along its other diagonal; when the king's other flights are covered that check is a mate in one (Bb1#, Bf5#). Block the checking line with a unit that cannot step aside with a threat (a pawn can: 1.c3 cooked); the white king on the line (Kc2) works because its moves abandon d4 or walk into a knight check.

Cap every search at five minutes, one solve per command, and write a progress line before each; thirty silent minutes is a process failure. The hour-long 'hang' of 10 Oct was a chained 3x5-minute command plus an output-token cutoff, not a search.

A unit that serves only the set play is a big flaw if it is completely redundant after the key (its guards duplicated, nothing else needs it). Critique rule `set-play-only unit`: major when nothing else needs it, minor when it also holds soundness or the tries.
A passive White king is acceptable: it is usually the hardest piece to give a role when Black has many pieces. Critique: `passive king` is a note, not a flaw.
example: Daily No. 3 alt: Kh4 with Sa5

text: Two changed mates on one effect with no tries is enough content for a changed-mates problem, but always look to extend the content (a try phase, a third pair) at the cost of pieces.
A complete-block matrix where many White moves keep the set play is hard to finish: stopping every waiting move is probably not worth it. Drop it or change the scheme rather than piling on blockers.
When a daily run fails, he wants to see the failed attempt too, with diagrams and its cook named, not only a study post.
A try refuted by a king move is a big flaw even when the flight is the theme (each try gives a flight with no mate). The rule stands with no exception.
A unified defence (all defences guard the same square) is better than a set of self-blocks with one real one; always look to unify the scheme: the squares of the defences, the tries and so on.
example: Daily No. 5: Rd6/Sd4/Sf4 all guard e6

text: A key piece attacked by the king but protected, whose key gives a flight, opens a line and guards the threat square, is a good key: the escape look is no flaw when the key has several jobs.
Cook-stopper pawns are acceptable at ordinary content level: much more material is usually added to stop cooks and to move things around.

A rook or bishop mate along a line to the king can be interposed by the defending knight: after Sd6 the knight reaches c4 and f5, so Rb4+ and Bg6+ fail. Choose the mating line so that its squares are not knight moves from the cut square, or mate from an adjacent square.

A pinned bishop guards nothing off the pin line: a bishop on e7 pinned by Re8 does not stop Sc5#, so the interference Sd6 has nothing to interfere with. Interference mates need an unpinned black line piece, and that piece can usually close the thematic line itself (Bd6, Rd6), which then needs its own mate.

Every square a knight reaches from e5 attacks e5 (knight moves are symmetric), so a key knight leaving e5 always protects e5 afterwards: a rook mate on e5 becomes available after every departure. A rook adjacent to the king on its file or rank gives check; a line-blocker next to the king must be a knight, bishop or pawn.

In a position where Black has only one mobile piece, every waiting move that keeps all mates is a key (zugzwang cooks 1.Bg3/1.Bh2 along the thematic line). One free black pawn (h7-h6) kills them all; a pawn whose move changes something (d5-d4 opening Bb7#) does not.

The Grimshaw square must lie on the threat piece's PATH to a square next to the king (Qd8-f6 through e7 against Ke5), not on the line of a checking mate: with a check through the crossing (2.Qe8# down the e-file) the rook and bishop interpose after the check and nothing defends. Then check the rook's squares just before and beyond the crossing: none may guard the threat square (Rf7 guarded f6), or that move needs a mate of its own.

When keyfind finds no key because the post-key position already mates by checks, give the key piece exactly one free square: a rook on the threat square with its own king on the file behind (f6 -> f3 with Kf2: f4 is next to the black king, f5 checks, f7/f8 are captures). Then cure the checking cooks one unit per solve.

A white line piece on the same line as a black guard it faces (Bb3 vs Bg8 on a2-g8) gives capture and block cooks (1.Bxg8, 1.Bf7). Cover the same squares from other lines (a knight on c7 covered e6 and d5 and also blocked the b8-e5 check line of 1.Qb8+).

source: Claude, theme 'bishop opens a white line twice' (E. Bourd's request)
text: A black line piece that defends by leaving a white line can always step back to the square it left, which lies on both of its own lines. So a CHECK along the opened line (a battery or a rook check through the vacated square) is interposed by the return move. The opened line must be a guard line or the mating piece's path (the queen travels through the vacated square to its mating square), never the check line itself, unless the mate is a double check or the arrival square pins the defender.
example: Ke5, Bc5 between Ra5 and Sd5: every knight move gives check and Bd4/Bd6-c5 interposes

text: The white line piece behind a black blocker always attacks it. With a lone black blocker, 1.Qx(blocker) or 1.Sx(blocker) is a cook. Put the blocker next to its own king, which protects it (Bd4 next to Ke5 in front of Qd1), or give it a black protector at scheme time.

A departing bishop guards its origin square from every square it can reach, so a mate on the vacated square never works, and only the mating squares beyond it are selectable. The selection by arrival comes from the arrival guarding one of them (Bc5xd6) or cutting a guard the other one needs (Be3 cuts Bc1-f4, and only the mate whose x-ray through the king covers f4 survives).

Flight-giving key by the threat piece: put it, before the key, on a line where it guards the square that only the diagram needs guarded (every mate covers e6 itself); the key moves it to the threat line and gives the flight. It replaced a cook-stopper bishop (Bg8 for e6) and an out-of-play key (Rh2-h7) at once. The given flight must be answered: here the threat itself mates after it, with Pf6 protecting e7.

A bare black king plus the thematic bishop against Q+R+B+S: every White waiting move works (all bishop moves already have set mates) and every free queen move has its own mate threat (Qd3 f4#, Qd2 Qg5#/Qf4#, Qb3, Qc2, Qh1, Qe1+/Qe2+). Cook-chasing one unit at a time went in circles for about 25 solves. What converged was Black pawns that each close one White line at scheme time (e2 the e-file, g5+h6 the c1-h6 diagonal squares, f7 the e6 square), plus a lighter key.

A clearance key along the bishop's own diagonal (Bf7-g8, keeping e6/d5) is cooked by the retreats on the other side of the guarded squares (Bc4/Bb3/Ba2). A white blocker on c4 that is a pawn or a piece guards d5, which made 1.f4+ Kxe4 2.Bd5# a cook. Only a rook on c4 would not guard d5, and it would be a cook-stopper.

He dislikes a cook-stopper that attacks a White piece in the diagram (a black e2 pawn hitting the queen on d1). Prefer a white unit or another setting. Here the plug's jobs were split: a far black a2 pawn for Black's spare force (a1=Q also guards d4), and the white king on g2 for the 2nd rank. A king on e2 instead boxed d3/e3 and made 1.Qxd4+ Kxd4 2.Bb2# work.

source: Claude, theme 'a bishop and a knight defend by unpinning a black piece' (E. Bourd)
text: Two interpositions on the same square, chosen by departure: Bb2 pins Sd4 against Ke5. Bb4-c3 and Sd5-c3 (or Se2-c3) both unpin it against the threat Sf3#. Each departure unguards one mating square (d6 by the bishop, f4 or f6 by the knight), so each sibling mate fails to the defender that stayed: one dual-avoidance motive for both. The post-key position is easy to make sound (postsearch READY found many); the key is the hard part.

Pinning key 1.Bb2 (White pins, Black unpins twice): from a3 the bishop is blocked by Bb4 (idle, attacked); from c1 it either guards f4 (then 1.f4+ Sxf4 2.Bxf4# or 1.Bf4+ cooks) or is shut in by a pawn on d2/e3 (idle, fatal). Threat-knight keys: from e2 the knight attacks the pinned d4 knight (1.Bxd4# in one); from h3, with a pawn mate on f4, 1.f4+ Sxf4 opens d5 for Qxd4#. With the queen mating on both squares (h6: Qd6/Qf6), the free queen gives ten keys. A diagram search scored by the solver (pinkey_search, key fixed) finds sound diagrams quickly but cannot see 'idle key piece': add that test to the score before the next run.
example: 3Q4/8/2R5/3nkp2/1b1n4/3P2P1/3P1P2/2B3NK (sound, 1.Bb2!, bishop shut in by d2: fatal)

source: E. Bourd, bench mv3ukaxu (read by Claude)
text: Where my searches found only idle keys, he gave Black an officer (a rook on a4) and made the key an anticipatory interference: the bishop leaves f5 (where only the threat knight protected it, so 1.Sf3+? Kxf5) for d3, keeping e4/f5 and closing the rook's 3rd rank before 1...Ra3 can guard f3. The key piece's diagram square has a job (it blocks f5 next to the king) and its new square has two. Black force that restrains White beats more White guards.

Clean thematic play first: an extra defence by a thematic unit for another reason (1...Bd6 self-block) is 'not clean'; prefer one White piece giving both mates (the queen along the 6th rank) to a pawn kept only for one mate (f2 for f4#).

source: Claude, theme 'two black knights capture the same white pawn' (E. Bourd)
text: Two knights capturing on one square have identical arrivals, so the mates must come from the departures: Sf3xe5 gives up d4 (2.Rd4#), Sd3xe5 gives up c5, so the d3 knight can no longer interpose on the rook's line (2.Ra5#, with c4 now covered by Bf1 through the vacated d3). The king's own capture Kxe5 adds a third mate (2.Qe6#). Post-key 7K/8/1Q6/3kP1N1/R7/3n1n2/8/5B2 (9 units) came from postsearch READY. Key 1.Qe3-b6 gives the flight Kxe5 but leaves c6 as a diagram flight; covering c6 lets White take the unprotected knights (Bxd3, Qxd3+) or play Qe4+. As in his unpin problem, Black needs force, which here means protecting the knights.

I read 'two knights uping a pawn' as capturing; he meant unpinning (it followed his unpin problem). When a theme word is garbled, read it against the previous request and ask or state the reading before building. The capture scheme was recorded as a side result.
example: two black knights unpin a black pawn on the same square: Sb5-c3 / Se2-c3 unpin Pd4 (Bb2 pin) against Re3#

text: Two knights unpinning a pawn on one square: Bb2 pins Pd4 (Ke5), threat Re3# (the pawn would take on e3 once unpinned), Sb5-c3 gives up d6 (2.Qd6#), Se2-c3 gives up f4 (2.f4#), each sibling mate failing to the knight that stayed. postsearch gives sound post-keys, but each knight has a second defence (Sd6 self-block, Sg3 blocking the rook's path), which is 'not clean' by his standard. Diagram search: 1.Ra6-f6 is the only key but takes a diagram flight. keysearch must reject White-in-check diagrams (it returned king escapes as keys).

source: Claude, giving up on 'two knights unpin a pawn on one square' (for now)
text: Clean post-key found quickly (Ra5 pins Pd5 at Ke5, threat Bc3#, S7c5 Qh8#, S3c5 Qf4#, no other defences), but about 12 searches and solves gave no fatal-free key. Unique keys came only with a diagram flight (Bg6, Rf6, Ke7, e8=S taking it), as captures (Bxd2, cxd6 opening the pin line, which also gave a double threat), or cooked (Bg5-d2 by Qh8+, Qg3+, Bxd3, e7). A white blocker on the pin line moved away by the key is the thematic idea, but the blocker squares (b5, c5, c3) each attack the black knights or need a capture. Next try: give Black an officer whose defence the key closes in advance (his Bd3 in bourd-bench-unpin-c3-bd3).

chesscomp/compose/diagsearch.py scores whole diagrams by solver and critique. Put the theme's carriers (pinner, pinned unit, thematic defenders) in CORE, or it optimises the theme away. Pass solver SAN for the defences (S for knights). It favours diagrams with a flight, so read the major findings, not the score.

source: E. Bourd ('you are pretty weak at transforming, or finding softening of a position')
text: Before searching for a key, soften the post-key position by transformations. (1) Move a mate next to where its piece naturally stands: Qh8# became Qf6# with the queen on g5, beside both mating squares. (2) Give a free White officer a second duty it must keep (the queen protects the f5 pawn), so its loose checks disappear. (3) Replace White guards by Black self-blocks (black pawns d6, e4 instead of Rc6, Bg6, Pe6). (4) Protect the mating squares with short-range units (Sh5 covers f4 and f6, Pe3 covers f4). Then the key falls out: the pinner arriving (Ra6-a5). I gave up after adding White guards and running key searches on an unsoftened position.

Do not give up while transformations remain untried. Before declaring a dead end, try in this order: move each mate to a square adjacent to its piece's post; give each free White officer a duty it must keep; turn White guards into Black self-blocks; retract the piece that carries the theme (the pinner) as the key. He finished in 39 bench steps what I abandoned after about a dozen searches.

When a position resists, restructure a whole side by reasoning from what the mechanism needs, not by one-unit steps; one change per solve applies to cleaning an already sound position. Keep the thematic core and rebuild the rest (mating squares, double-duty pieces, Black self-blocks for White guards, the key piece) as one change, then solve.

Two black interpositions on one square that unpin a piece: let the pinner be a queen and put the interposers on the squares that block her two diagonals next to the pin square (Qa5 pins Sc5 to Ke5, rooks b6/b4 interpose on b5). Each departure opens one queen diagonal, so the pinner herself mates (Qc7#, Qc3#) and the other rook keeps the dual shut. The unpinned knight must not reach the mating lines (from c5 it cannot reach d6 or d4).

A pinning queen that must arrive along the edge file is out of play in the diagram: from a2 or a8 her diagonal into the king's field always reaches the knight's capture square next to the king, which is the threat square, so the threat check is cooked (Re6+ Sxe6 Qxe6#). An unmasking key is the way out: a unit standing on the pin line next to the king leaves it. A knight cannot do it well: every knight move from d5 still guards d5, so its new square must guard another flight, which is then open in the diagram. A bishop can: Bd5-f7 keeps no diagram guard; its new job (protecting the threat rook on e6) does not exist before the key.

Searching by unit roles worked: a free-threat post-key search (exactly one threat, the named defences each with their mate) gave the queen-pinner post-key in four minutes; the key came from reading why each search failed (the flight a knight key leaves, the capture Rxc4 a d3 bishop invites) and changing the key piece, not from more search time. New tool chesscomp/compose/unmask_search.py scores the post-key, idle White units, diagram flights and checks, the key piece being in play, and key uniqueness.

A static key is acceptable when the key carries the theme (it pins); the way to enrich it is tries by the key piece that block the thematic mates, so that each is refuted by one of the thematic defences.

Mask the pin on the interposition square itself, not next to the king. A white knight on b5 (between Qa5 and Sc5) stops 1.Qxc5 and is not a flight, while a mask on d5 is either a flight (Kxd5) or, once protected, lets 1.Qxc5 cook. From b5 every knight move blocks a queen mate (c7, d6 / c3, d4) except the edge squares; a guard duty on the edge (Sa3 protects c4, so ...Rxc4 Sxc4#) picks the key.

A theme is a request for a good problem around it, not the simplest one showing it. After the theme works, look for what to add (tries by the key piece, changes, a cleaner position) and try it in steps before showing; do not ask him whether it is worth it. Symmetry by design is a flaw; publish tries as a pair, one per thematic refutation.

Two different black bishops cutting white lines: let them cut the queen's two lines (rank at c4, diagonal at c5 from Qb4) and let the queen mate along the uncut line (Qd6 / Qf4). Each cut then also stops the other mate, the strongest dual avoidance. Enable each mate by the bishop's departure (opening a rook line to protect d6; stopping a guard of f4). Knight threats near a dark king square stand on light squares, which a light bishop can always reach: block its diagonals before choosing the threat square.

The errors of the thematic defences should share one motivation (both unguards, or both line openings), not one of each. A by-play that repeats a thematic mate is a big flaw. The threatening unit should take part in the play, not stand out of play in the set and the solution.

Same white line for both bishops: the threat itself is the line (Qc1-c7+ along the c-file); the light bishop d5 cuts at c4 or c6, the dark bishop e3 at c5. Each defence is an unguard error: Bd5 guarded e4 and e6, Be3 guarded f4; the mates land on those squares (Re4#, Re6#, Bf4#), and the square the bishop still guards from its new post kills the other mate (c4 still sees e6, c6 still sees e4). Open problem: the white pieces this needs give the diagram deflection sacrifices on the mating squares and long-diagonal checks, so no key yet.

Pick a dynamic, local threat (a mate around the king's squares, e.g. something that needs the guard of d6 or e6), not one that runs along long lines with pieces outside the play. With a dynamic base the bishops are free along their diagonals (dark e5/d4/c3, light e4/d3/c2) and each spot gives a variation; there is more freedom from the start. A defence that also guards a square (Bc5 guarding d6) is impure next to a pure line closing.

On his bench scheme (Kd5, Rh6 guarding the 6th rank, bishops cutting at f6/g6): choose the origins for unguard errors - dark Be5 guards f4 (1...Bf6 2.Sf4#), light Bd3 guards c4 (1...Bg6 2.Qc4#); black pd4 keeps the dark bishop off d4 (where it would guard c5); threat 2.Qc5# needs Rh6 for e6. Post-key 8/1NQ5/3B3R/3kb3/3p4/1P1b1P1N/8/K7 is sound with no other White solution; the queen key 1.Qg7-c7 is unique but leaves c6 as a diagram flight, and covering c6 otherwise turns Qf7+/Qg8+ into mates.

Pick the scheme's placement spread, with the mechanism's parts apart: the guarding line long, its cut squares away from the king, the cutting pieces at a distance with free paths. A unit inside the king's field (my bishop on e5) interferes with too much and takes the freedom away; every later change ripples through it. It is not always possible, but starting from a softer scheme is a skill.
example: his scheme 8/8/3P3R/3k4/8/2bb4/8/8 (Rh6, cuts on f6/g6) vs my 8/1NQ5/3B3R/3kb3/3p4/1P1b1P1N/8/K7 (Be5 guarding d4, d6, f4, f6, on the e-file and the 5th rank)

text: Shifts and rotations of the whole board do not ruin the base of the theme: the line pieces keep their geometry (both bishops change colour together under a quarter turn). What changes is the pawns (direction, captures, promotion), and the edges (room for the White king). Use one when the stuck point is a pawn or the White king's room, not the mechanism. Tool: python3 -m chesscomp.compose.transform FEN --all --post.
example: 2n5/2Np4/1p1p4/3B3R/1Qpk4/1Kpb1R2/2pb3B/8 (the c4 pawn checks Kb3, c2 promotes) -> quarter turn -> 8/2KQ1p2/1ppp2Nn/1bbkBpp1/8/2R5/8/1B2R3 (b6/c6/d6 static, the mates' targets)

text: Two bishops cut one rook line far from the king (Re1 on e2/e3) so that the king can take the guarded unit at the line's end (Kxe5 after the threat Se7+ removes the knight's guard). The errors are unified unguards of pawns next to the king that the queen captures (Bb5 held c6, Bc5 held d6); the other bishop's guard stops the dual. Pawns as mating targets make pure unguard errors.

When findkey gives several unique keys, choose the origin that also gives a try: from f8 the knight has 1.Sh7? (2.Sf6#) Be2!, a changed threat refuted by a thematic defence; from h4 it has none, from h8 only 1.Sxf7? Sxf5! (a capture, unthematic).

His sitting order: scheme (5 units) -> post-key with a knight threat, solved after every few placements (double threats, then holes, each fixed by a unit) -> findkey on the post-key -> when the only key was a check (1.Rh4+) and a pawn then killed it, no more one-unit steps: White king and queen moved, three Black units removed, the board turned a quarter -> three changes to a hole-free post-key -> findkey -> the key with a try. 103 bench steps, about 20 solves.

Leave freedom in the geometry around the threat: decide the line, not the square. The square the threat needs guarded can move along the guarded line (he switched from d6 to e6 on the 6th rank) when the construction asks for it.
example: mv4dvvuh threat square d6 -> mv4gmdxo e6, same Rh6 line, same f6/g6 cuts

text: Put the bishops' error mates away from the line they cut (Bc3 holds b4, Bc2 holds b3; the cuts are on f6/g6). Mates on the far side interfere less with the rest of the play and need little patching; mates near the cut squares tangle with everything there.

Among keys, take the origin that gives the key a thematic job, even at a cook-stopper's cost: 1.Qf1-b5 was the only key with 10+4 and no set play; 1.Qe2-b5 gives up the queen's e-file guard of the threat square e6 (the bishops' cuts become defences only after the key), brings set play and the change Bg6 Qa2# -> Qb3#, and costs the pawn g5 against 1.Rh5+.

A cook-stopper can often be re-placed so that it also plays: remove it and test every single unit in its place (chesscomp.compose.restop). The a8 knight that only stopped Sc7# works from e8 too, and there 1...Sf6 cuts the same line with an unguard error, 2.Sc7#.

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: Le Grand / mate exchange with a flight: pick two mate squares A, B with A next to king square K1 and two away from K2, B the reverse. Key: one unit protects A and B together (a diagonal through both, a knight forking both); try: a unit takes the one square the distant mate leaves free.
example: Bourd 8/2K5/B7/8/4k3/7Q/6P1/6B1 (Bc8 protects f5,e6; Be3? takes f4); Labai 8/1R5n/2p5/2k3N1/4Q3/K7/8/8 (Sf3 protects d4,e5; Kb3? takes c4)

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: Build a key with two jobs. The try does the first job only; its refutation is the defence that the second job answers.
example: Kazimov 2R5/8/2N5/1N1kpP2/KR5b/8/8/6B1: Rg4? and Rc4! both vacate b4 for Sb4#; only c4 also reaches c5 against 1...e4

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: Dombrovskis via side effects: the same Black move refutes the try by a side effect (it vacates a flight) and defends in the solution by its main effect (cuts the threat line); the key guards the vacated square, killing the side effect.
example: Slesarenko & Gvozdjak 3n1KB1/3p1n2/2p1k3/8/5P1B/2PQ4/8/8: d6/d5 vacate d7 (refute Be7?/c4?); 1.Ke8! guards d7, d6/d5 cut Qxd7 and self-block

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: A defence that lands on a White line piece's line to the king self-pins and cannot interpose against the mate; the pinner needs no other job. A king that walks onto a pin line re-pins its own unit, so such a flight costs nothing.
example: Milewski Boros 1k1b4/1r1P4/Q7/4R2K/5Rp1/8/7B/8 (Bh2 pins Bc7/Rc7); Rice R7/4N3/4p3/1k1nR3/3B3Q/1PP5/8/5K2 (Kxc5 re-pins Sd5)

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: A black unit on the crossing point of two white lines gives focal play: whichever White piece it captures, the other's line opens. A masked bishop behind each mating knight covers the square the defender vacated.
example: Marin 2BkNK2/N2p4/3n4/8/8/4p3/4QB2/4b3 (pe3 on Qd2-g5 x Bf2-b6); Velikÿ 1R4bB/8/1R3N1K/2k4p/2Br4/8/1N6/B7 (Ba1/Sb2, Bh8/Sf6 aimed at d4)

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: To read how a #2 works, run chesscomp.anatomy: guard field per mate, essential pins, why each try's threat fails, role table. A guard map alone misses pins (Bh2 in the Boros problem looked idle).

source: Claude, studies of published #2 (E. Bourd's request, 11 Oct)
text: Published #2s (1998-2006) often carry a White unit used only for a try or as a plug: Pg2 (Bourd), Ka3 (Labai), Pc3 (Slesarenko), Pd6 plug (Milewski). E. Bourd's 7 Oct rule calls a try-only unit fatal; asked him whether it is weighed against the try's content.
example: Slesarenko without Pc3: 1.Ke8! still sound, only 1.c4? lost

text: A PDB LaTeX export (pdb.dieschwalbe.de, he logs in and downloads) goes in with tools/pdb_tex.py SRC knowledge/<name>.json --skip-known, then register it in db.COLLECTIONS and run db.run('check', collection=...). Long algebraic must become SAN from the diagram for the key: dropping the origin square loses a needed disambiguation (Sb1-c3 is Sbc3 when two knights reach c3) and the check reports a false mismatch. Fairy pieces are '*N' prefixes in the FEN: such records are not orthodox and cannot be drawn by show.py as they stand.

His Gmail answers questions about his record (WCCT, WCCI, FIDE Album, Variantim) in Hebrew and English; the Israeli team captain's threads carry the selections. Search results are too large for the context (50 threads ~100k chars): delegate the reading to read-only agents split by period, with a tool-call cap, and ask for thread ids as evidence. Attachments (diagrams, team PDFs) cannot be opened, and mail before mid-2010 is missing. What was found is in knowledge/bourd_record.md.

text: A White unit there only for a try is a drawback weighed against the try's content, not fatal (E. Bourd, 11 Oct 2026, replacing his 7 Oct verdict).
Miniatures are too simple to publish or to learn from as an advanced composer, even with changes; study and aim for complex #2s (E. Bourd, 11 Oct 2026).

Reuse the mating pieces: let the two mating units share a guard square, so that in each mate the other mating unit holds it. Each unit then has a job in the other variation and the play is connected, not two distant variations. The key can create the link by adding the second guard (1.Qb5 makes c5 guarded twice; in the set Sb4 fails because only Sa6 holds c5). chesscomp.anatomy prints it under LINKS.
example: nK6/3B4/N2PP2R/2Bk2P1/5P2/2b2P2/2b1Q3/8, 1.Qb5! Bf6 Sb4# (Qb5 holds c5), Bg6 Qb3# (Sa6 holds c5)

text: For 'one unit, several defences, each closing a different line', enumerate the geometry first: python3 -m chesscomp.compose.line_skeletons K lists threat square, knight square, two arrival squares that both guard the threat square, and the black lines through each arrival that guard a king-field square. Dual avoidance comes free: the other line still guards its square.
example: d5: T e3, Se1 -> c2 (Rc1 file) / g2 (Bh1 diagonal)

text: A key that only adds a guard of a king-field square cannot create a check threat: in the diagram that square is either a flight (fatal) or already covered, and then the threat mates at once. Create the threat by bringing the threat piece, clearing its square, or opening its line.
example: queen h8/e2/e3 -> e8 over 4Q3/2K5/8/3k4/2R5/1Pp5/8/1Nr1nN1b: Ke6 flight, or Se3# in the diagram

text: A pawn protecting a mating square diagonally next to the king recaptures with check: Qe4+ Bxe4 dxe4# and Qc4+ Rxc4 dxc4# cook the diagram. Protect such squares with a rook or knight, whose recapture does not check.

A try by the threat piece that blocks one mating line is refuted exactly by the defence that needs that mate (1.Sc4? Sc2! when Sc2 is answered on c4). For a pair, the two mates must run on different lines: one queen line through both mating squares makes every block kill both.

Waiting on background searches: pgrep -f 'name' matches the waiting command itself (its text contains the name) and never ends; use a bracket pattern, ps -eo args | grep '[c]hesscomp.compose.unmask_search'.
