text: Everything is ours: every tool, skill and file belongs to all sessions; improve any of them; work reaches main so long chats see current knowledge (CLAUDE.md).

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 2003, judge P. Robert)
text: A try that captures a black unit is a serious flaw: Robert refused three otherwise ambitious #2s for it (D57, D58, D59). Name it as a flaw, like a capturing key.

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 2003, judge P. Robert)
text: Do not let ambition buy a fatal flaw: a twin cycle with a major dual in one part and an idle rook in two was refused; we had given it 2nd Prize against our own judge's named flaws.

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 2003, judge P. Robert)
text: A clear, economical change mechanism with a good key can take 1st Prize without secondary play (7+7, no white pawn); do not mark it down for thin play. Real informal awards place about 1 in 4 entries.

source: Claude, studies of E. Bourd's complex #2s (12 Oct)
text: Give each queen mate its own supporting line piece and let each Black defence cut the OTHER mate's support line: the defence prevents the dual itself.
example: Bourd StrateGems 2007 2HM B4R2/2K5/1N2pP2/4k3/2Pr3p/2P2Q2/1b1N4/2B5: Rd5 cuts Ba8 (Qf4#), Rd2 cuts Bc1 (Qe4#)

source: Claude, studies of E. Bourd's complex #2s (12 Oct)
text: Le Grand without flights: a Black plug at the crossing of two Black lines (rook rank and rook file); a capture key removes one rook, the plug shields the other's mate square (threat), the plug's move opens the other line (other mate).
example: Bourd Sredba 2003-05 1HM 2n5/1KNp1r2/3p1Q2/pN3br1/1Pp1k1p1/qR4P1/3P1b2/B3nB2 (Bf5 plugs Rg5-d5 and Rf7-f4)

source: Claude, studies of E. Bourd's complex #2s (12 Oct)
text: Masked battery with a black mask: while the mask stands, the front piece's departure pins it (it cannot capture the mating piece); once the mask moves, the departure gives double check. Two such batteries choose the mating knight.

source: Claude, studies of E. Bourd's complex #2s (12 Oct)
text: The anatomy's removal test (remove a White unit from the mate position; still mate?) finds plugs on Black lines, protectors and pins that a guard map misses; a unit standing on a flight is credited with 'on <sq>'.

His complex #2s start from a geometric scheme (the lines and the mating units: two masked batteries, two knights mating on one square); the paradox (here reciprocal change between two tries) evolves from what the scheme can carry.

Count phases, not variations: a 2x2 change across tries and key, a doubled Le Grand on one defence, or Mäkihovi + Zagoruiko is full content with few variations; we marked such problems 'thin' and real judges placed them high (MK2-14 3rd Prize, MSK-16 top of the 2011 problems).

Before scoring, tabulate every phase (set, each try, key) against each thematic defence; MSK-12 (Mäkihovi + Zagoruiko, 1st Prize ECSC 2011) lost half its content in our blind report because one changing try was missed.

With a rich phase complex, real judges tolerate a diagram flight, a king-refuted try and a capturing try (MSK-27, 2nd place in the Moscow Ch. 2012 thematic section); our 'fatal' list is the standard for our own compositions, not a prediction of awards.

For a half-pin, list for each of the two units the squares it covers and the lines it can block. The mate for one unit's defence goes on a square or line of the OTHER unit, which the defence has just pinned (Qd6 on a knight square, Qd3 on the rook's rank). Then use what the moving unit itself changes (the knight frees e4: Qd3 covers it, Qd6 does not) for the dual avoidance.

postsearch with three named defences converged on one mate for all three (Qd6#): its score cannot invent a split. Name each defence's error first (compose 3c'), then search; the split came by hand in four solves.

A wait loop `until ! pgrep -f compose.postsearch` never ends: pgrep matches the waiting shell's own command line. Wait on the output files, or on PIDs from ps -eo pid,comm,args filtered on comm=python.

A flight-giving key came from keyfind on a post-key position that had a flight answered by the threat: the queen retracted to the square guarding the flight (Qa6 <- a7, guarding d4). The cooks it left (Rc4, Bxf3) took one black unit each.

Flaw tolerance grows with content: a one-variation problem pays for nothing, a reciprocal change can carry plugs, try-only units, heavy force. Cooks, thematic duals and double threats stay fatal. Place the problem on the light/medium/rich scale before weighing.
example: 5Rq1/2p2b2/2Pp1Npn/2nQ2RP/4Pk1P/4N3/3rPPBK/2Brb3 (rich, 25 units, plugs) vs 6K1/1N6/4p3/1PBk3p/8/8/4Q3/6N1 (light, sunk by one try-only knight)

text: Bring the White pieces close to the play and take the key from a central square: knights and queen on the edge (Qe8, Sb1, Sd2-f1) are 'somewhat off'.

A key that clears the threat square creates the threat without adding a guard: the knight on d4 blocks the queen's mate on d4 and leaves. If the mates are knight checks on two squares, the key square is the one knight square reaching both (e2 for c3 and f4); the other departures reaching only one are tries refuted by the defence that needs the other (1.Sb5? Sf5!, 1.Se6? Sc2!).

A black line piece whose OTHER line reaches the threat square defends by going there and gives the same mate as the knight's closing of its first line (Rc1-d1 guards d4 down the d-file and leaves the c-file: 1...Rd1 2.Sc3#). Choose line pieces whose other lines miss the threat square; a White plug on the d-file stops it but the gate rejects a unit that is in no mate and not needed for soundness.

line_skeletons --knights --central lists skeletons whose closed lines unguard knight-check squares (knight mates close to the king) and sorts by how central the knight and its arrivals are; unmask_search now penalises a by-play that repeats a wanted mate.
example: python3 -m chesscomp.compose.line_skeletons d5 --knights --central -> T d4 Se3 -> c2,f5

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 2004, judge M. Mladenovic)
text: Real judges filter 'rude refutations' first: checks and captures as refutations, flight-taking tries and keys (M. Mladenovic, Problemesis 2004: our two top-rated problems were unplaced for exactly this). Weigh the refutations before the content.

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 2004, judge M. Mladenovic)
text: A capturing try is not a fixed flaw: Robert (2003) refused three problems for it, Mladenovic (2004) gave 1st HM to an Albino whose two tries capture. Judge whether the capture is the theme.

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 2004, judge M. Mladenovic)
text: In a mutate (block, waiting key) the tries are not the point: judge the key and the change; plugs and shared try refutations weigh little (Problemesis 2004, 1st Comm).

A by-play that repeats a thematic mate is fatal when it also refutes the partner try: 1...Rd1 (guarding d4 down the d-file, leaving the c-file) refutes 1.Se6? as well as giving 2.Sc3#, so the pair 1.Sb5? Sf5! / 1.Se6? Sc2! cannot exist. One try of a natural pair 'gives bad taste': once 1.Sb5? is there, 1.Se6? is almost a must.

Escapes of the line pieces (moves that reach the threat square) come in two kinds: along their own line onto or past the target, stopped by a black self-block on the king's field (Rf6-f4 by e4) or by a White unit that also covers a flight (Re6 cuts Re7, Bf5 cuts Rh5); and along their other line (Rc1-d1 down the d-file), which only a plug stops. Choose skeletons with the first kind only: python3 -m chesscomp.compose.knight_pair_skeletons d5.

For a try pair by the key piece, the try squares must be free of black attack: Sd3 failed to the c4/e4 pawns and Sc6 to a rook on the c-file; the rook moved from c7 to b7 (same rank line through d7) and the search found the exact pair.

Two black units self-blocking one square next to the king: no threat may check through that square, and no White line may guard it. A check through it is met by the blockers interposing at once (they can reach it before the threat); a White line through it guards the square, so the block is not needed. What works: a White line masked by the threat piece runs through the square to the next field square (Rc1-Sc5 through c7 to c8); the threat unmasks it, the block cuts it.

When the key gives the self-block square as a flight, the diagram guards it, and then every thematic mate is a mate in one unless the key adds something that mate needs or Black can parry it there. Here 2.Re8/Qe8 needed the e8 protection the key brings, 2.Rb8 was parried by Bg3xb8 through the empty c7, and the threat lost d7 (left by Sc5) to the key. The cook that remains, 1.Sb7+ Kd7 2.Qc6#/Qc7#, is killed by a rook (not a queen) behind the masked line.
example: 1.Sd5-f6 cooked by 1.Sb7+ Kd7 2.Qc6#; with Rc1 and the key from e8: sound

text: A king in the centre needs seven static guards when each mate covers two squares; the same mechanism on the edge (Kd8, square c7) needs three. When the post-key search keeps returning heavy positions with many other White solutions, move the king to the edge before adding units.
example: Kd5/c4 versions: 'others=7-8' in every post-key; Kd8/c7: sound in four runs

text: A sacrifice on the square captured by king, knight and bishop is Strebkovs, Vratnica-64 2003 (8/1n1p2p1/1Q4R1/p2Nk2n/2P3P1/5P2/5K2/2b5, 1.Sf4! Sxf4/Bxf4/Kxf4) and Muralidharan, Problemesis 2002 (six captures on f4). Self-blocks on an empty square need another defence motive.

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 1999-2002, judge J. Morice)
text: Judges have schools: Morice (Problemesis 1999-2002) paid for line strategy (bivalent effects, masked lines, anti-Lewmann, Franco-Latvian, equipollent moves) and put a mechanical four-phase queen scheme last; Moscow judges paid for phases. Name both kinds of content before weighing.

source: Blind tourney experiment (Problemesis 1999-2002, judge J. Morice)
text: When all tries are refuted by the same black unit, check whether its refuting moves mirror the white tries (equipollent moves, theme A): that unity is the theme, not 'distinct refutations' (Problemesis 1999-2002, 2nd and 3rd HM).

White correction is a theme, not a mechanical try set: a white piece's random move fails to one refutation, its corrections make their own errors and change the threat (tertiary threat correction took 1st Prize, The Problemist 2014). Read the tries of one white piece as random / corrections before calling a shared refutation a flaw.

Multiple threats are legitimate when the theme separates them (English Novotny, Fleck, Brogi); judge from the author's solution and theme, never from the FEN alone (The Problemist 2014-15 blind experiment).

source: Blind tourney experiment (StrateGems 2015, judge H. Gockel)
text: Rude moves (capturing key or tries, an open flight) do not sink a correctly shown modern theme: Gockel placed threat-correction problems with them (StrateGems 2015, 1st HM and 1st Comm). The 'refutations first' filter is one judge's taste (Mladenovic); weigh, do not filter.

source: Blind tourney experiment (StrateGems 2015, judge H. Gockel)
text: Changed play can be a role exchange with no common defence: a white king battery in the try against a black king battery in the solution (StrateGems 2015, 2nd Prize; our judge called it 'two batteries that never meet').

source: Blind tourney experiment (The Problemist 2010, judge C. Wiedenhoff)
text: Before weighing a heavy, rude-looking problem, find the line mechanism: rook moves in a half-battery (try, try, key), each phase with its own mates, took 3rd HM while our judge ranked it last as 'mixed changes, heavy, rude'.

A White officer that mates in only one variation is a weakness he names even in a position he calls impressive ('the b2 rook only being active in 1 variation'). The flight-giving key onto the self-block square was the part he liked: 'the key is nice giving flight ... using the flight mechanism of self-block.' Very hard constructions are not the goal: he will show easier ones around the same idea.

His order for 'two units self-block one square': (1) which mates can come on a self-block: a bishop, a rook or a queen gives one mate each, so the other mate needs an interference; (2) the separation: why one mate works after one block and not after the other; (3) why Black defends on that square. 'They cannot block a line of a white piece, as that would imply that c5 is guarded, and it cannot be guarded additionally, thats part of our theme.'

Six defence motives for two units self-blocking one square, all built in one sitting: capture of a White unit on the square (separated by line opening, by a guard, by a pin), cutting a line masked by the threat piece (my 1.Sf6!, 'very complicated'), stopping a double check (the threat unmasks a line through the square at the king; a double check cannot be interposed, so the block has to come first), and zugzwang ('the least soft, and least freedom given'). The capture is 'probably the simplest' and he tried it first.
example: Qd6, Bf4, Bf6, Qd3, Re8 schemes; bourd-bench-sb-*

text: I dropped the capture motive because Strebkovs 2003 has a sacrifice key captured by K, S and B on one square. That anticipates the sacrifice key, not capture defences on a square where a White unit already stands: his Qd6/Bf4/Bf6 schemes capture a unit the threat needs, after a quiet key. Check what a published problem actually shows before ruling out a whole motive.

My blockers interposed against a single check through the square; his double check through it cannot be interposed. When the threat must pass through the self-block square, make it a double check (front piece mating, rear line through the square): Black can only block the rear line before the threat.

freethreat.self_block_needed accepted a mate that fails without the blocker only because the blocker also cut a black line (1...Sxc4 cutting Ra4-d4 against 2.Qd3+). A self-block means the king itself could step to the emptied square; the check now requires a legal king move there.
example: 5B2/8/1P6/1P1knK2/r1N5/2Q5/8/8 b: Nxc4 Qd3# is interference, Rxc4 Qe5# is a self-block

text: Rook and knight on the same square separate themselves: the rook on it interposes or captures along its lines (d5 against Qc6+), the knight guards its own squares (e5 against Qe5). With his capture motive and the queen as protector and mater, the post-key came in one search round; the key was a clearance of the threat square by a bishop that keeps its diagonal guard through it.

Capture motive, lightest form found: the captured White unit protects the threat's mating square (Pd4 protects e5 for 2.Re5#), the queen protects the unit and mates elsewhere in both lines. Orthogonal square: the rook-blocker interposes on the diagonals (d3, d5), the bishop-blocker on the file (e3, e5), so diagonal and file queen checks separate them. A free-threat search with SELFBLOCK and loose patterns (Q*) found it in one round.

To extend a problem whose thematic mates are all by one queen, the phases have to come from the queen's square, so the threat must come from the queen's move; a threat by another unit that is ready in the diagram is already a mate in one. Changing the key piece's start square (f8 -> f6) made it a flight-giving sacrifice, a third variation and removed a cook-stopper: the cheapest extension was in the key, not in tries.

'the composing entity should push for a bit more now than the basic requested theme. your problem is actually nice, but its too simple thematic wise, lets try to go forward.' A requested theme is the floor: add a second layer (tries refuted by the thematic defences, changed mates, a correction, a cycle) before showing.
example: 8/8/1Q3R2/3N4/r2PkN2/8/5bK1/8 (1.Rf5!, two self-blocks on d4): nice, too simple

text: Two black units unpinning on one square add a second theme for free when that square is where their own lines cross: each interposition unpins (the defence) and cuts the other unit's line beyond the square (the error): a Grimshaw on the unpinning square. Put the rook's guarded square and the bishop's guarded square beyond the crossing next to the king (c6 for a knight check, d4 for a pawn check) and keep the threat off both lines.

source: Blind tourney experiments (Problemesis 1999-2002, Variantim 2019, The Problemist 2011)
text: A cleanly rendered task or named scheme (a battery task with nine mates, a Burmistrov combination, a doubled Fleck/Brogi, one black unit refuting all tries) is placed by real judges at Comm to HM level; our judges score such entries 4-5 as 'mechanical' and leave them out. Score the task's completeness and cleanliness, not its novelty alone.

source: Blind experiment: WCCI 8 section A winners (scored)
text: At world level content decides and our flaw list barely matters: the only 10/10 in WCCI 8 #2 (a Burmistrov combination with a Zagoruiko on two defences on e4) was our 13th of 15 for an unprovided flight and a try-only pawn, while the cleanest, most economical entry was our 2nd and scored lowest. Apply 'tolerance grows with content' at full strength: with rich multi-phase content, an unprovided flight or a try-only pawn costs fractions, not ranks.

'Try to add tries ... you need the pin in the initial position and consider how to make multiple tries. Usually by the same piece that moves away to open a line or to guard a square.' Plan the try piece first: one White unit whose every move creates the threat, and whose landing squares each spoil one thematic mate.

A knight standing on the threat square is a natural try piece: every move vacates the square (opens the threat line) and guards it. Its landing squares separate the mates only through what they guard or block. A knight mate (Sc6#) has no line to block, so its try lever is the flight its mating knight gives up (f5 for Se7): only the landing squares guarding that flight keep the mate, and every other knight move fails to the same defence. A line mate (Bg1-d4#) gives a pure try by blocking its path (Sf2). A pure pair needs the flight lever on a line through a landing square (f6 from Rf8/Qf8 or Rh6), a third heavy piece.
example: 8/b3N2p/3ppP1K/R2pk1P1/3pN2R/8/7P/2r1n1B1: only Sg3 guards f5; 1.Sf2? fails to Bc5 and Rc5

text: After 1...Bc5 on the pin line a check through d6 (2.Bc7) fails: the bishop on c5 interposes on d6. The Bc5-mate on the c-file must be a knight check (Sc6#). With a queen on the threat rank, 2.Qd4 doubles 2.Bd4# (the bishop protects the queen); a rook threat on rank 4 protects d4 without mating there.

On the full WCCT 11 section A field (79 scored entries, theme given) our blind panel agreed with the total at Spearman 0.63, and with each country at 0.47-0.56, while the countries agreed among themselves at 0.34-0.72: we judge like a sixth country. Misses: double threats in every phase of a record content (3rd-4th place, our 21st; 8th-11th, our 54th) and a new task arrangement (five occupiers of d4 refuting five bishop tries, 6th, our 46th). Over-generous where originality (anticipation) or a flight-taking key decided.
example: A01 8/3p1Qpr/8/p2N2R1/1B1kb3/N1n1R3/n3PP2/K3b3: 1.Sf6! (2.Bc5,Qc4#), Zagoruiko 3x3 in four phases, 9 points

text: 'without a pure pair, its almost not worth having 1 pair. showing the other try with both refutations is not a thing. the effect of guarding f5 looks too limiting.' And: 'with only 1 real try it just seems unfinished problem of 2 tries ... its always worth going further, and then look back.' A try counts only with exactly one refutation; two thematic defences need two pure tries, one each. A lever that only one landing square satisfies (the key guards f5) makes every other move fail the same way: not a try system.

For a pure try pair each thematic mate needs a line a try can cut. With the pin on the king's rank (Ke5, Pd5, Grimshaw on c5) the bishop's mate can only be a knight check (every line from c6/c7/c3 passes a square next to c5, where the bishop interposes). Pin on the diagonal instead (Ke5, Pd4 pinned by Bb2, Grimshaw on c3): Bc3 cuts Rc1's file (Rc5# along rank 5 through d5), Rc3 cuts Bb4's diagonal (Qe1# along the e-file through e2): two lines, two blocking squares for one try piece (Bf3: Be2?, Bd5?).

Pure white-interference try pair with a knight mate on one side: the knight mate (Sd8-c6#) has no line, so give its flight lever a line through a landing square. A white pawn on the flight (e6) protected twice, by the mating knight and by a rook along the rank (Rh6 via g6, f6): after Sd8-c6 only the rook protects it, and the landing square f6 cuts the rook (1.Sf6? Bc5! 2.Sc6+ Kxe6). The line mate's path gives the other try (1.Sf2? closes Bg1-d4: Rc5!). Choose the key square with no onward checks (Sg3) and block the others (d2 occupied, d7 occupied, d3 guarded).

Geometry of a Grimshaw on an unpinning square: with the pin on the king's rank or file the bishop's mate can only be a knight check (every line from a freed rook square passes a square next to the interposition square, where the bishop interposes); with a diagonal pin both mates can be line mates, but a threat square next to the bishop's diagonal (e3 beside d2) gives the bishop a parry (Bd2) that needs its own mate.
example: Ke5, Pd4 pinned by Bb2, Grimshaw on c3: 1...Bd2 guards e3

text: Random-walk searches (unmask_search) find try pairs only inside clutter (22 units, junk stoppers); use them to find the levers, then rebuild by hand one stopper per solve, or enumerate one or two stoppers around a clean kernel with compose.trypair (key, tries with their single refutations, wanted mates, threat). A black check that refutes every try hides cooks: block it and re-solve.

On a 22-unit pure try pair with a Grimshaw unpin: 'its ok imo, pretty complex. it does feel a bit heavy and probably can improved, but its decent.' A complex mechanism (pure white-interference pair, four knight tries) carries 22 units and six stoppers; weight is a flaw to weigh, not a veto. The lever (a pawn protected by the mating knight and by a rook along a line the try cuts): 'a good mechanism achieving the goal'.

Bishop + rook half-pin on a diagonal (Bh7-Rg6-Bf5-Ke4): the pinned bishop can be used only on g4 (capture or interposition against a check from h4); knight checks never use a pinned bishop, since no knight checking square is a bishop square. So the rook's variation needs a line mate through g4, and the bishop's variation a knight check the pinned rook would take (Sf6, Sd6, Sg5, Sg3). Two blocks on e6 against an e-file threat separate themselves: the rook on e6 covers f6, the bishop on e6 covers g4 through f5.

Choose the try piece from the lines of both thematic mates before choosing the mask. With an e7 knight as mask and key, no landing square touches the rook's mate line (g1-g4), so no try can fail to the rook's defence and a pure pair is impossible; only the knight's own mate changes (Sc8? Sd6# vs Sg8! Sf6#).

A mask knight that attacks a half-pinned unit gives a capture cook (1.Sexf5 with a double threat) that no single unit stopped (compose.trypair, 340 placements). Cure: a black rook on the unit's rank (h5) that retakes and then guards the threat square. Cost: every move of the half-pinned bishop opens that rook's line, so the bishop's defence becomes B~, and a block on g4 brought a dual, removed by a black pawn on g4 (also the target of Rxg4#).

A white pawn on e2 covers d3 and f3 next to a king on e4: it replaced a black pawn on f3, the white pawn on f2 that stopped it running, and the king's d3 duty (18 -> 17 units). A white pawn d4 can replace a bishop whose only jobs are guarding e5 and standing on d4.

Pure try pair by one knight in a B+R half-pin needs both thematic mates to be knight checks the pinned unit would capture. A bishop pinned on a diagonal never covers a knight checking square of its king (parity), so this works only on a file or rank pin with the bishop next to the king: Ke4, Be5, Re6, pinner on e8 (rook mate Sc3/Sg3, bishop mate Sd6/Sf6; key square b5, d5, f5 or h5). Kapros, Problemesis 2002 (psis-0dd597ba62) already shows it: 1.Sxb5! Rc6 Sc3#, Bd4 Sd6#; 1.Se2? Bd4!, 1.Sf5? Rc6!; the key opens Rb4-d4 (pinning Qc4) and Bd4 closes it again, a motive that is close to forced for the d4 origin.

On 1...Be6/Bd7/Bc8 2.Sf6# (every bishop move defending because it opened bRh5-e5): 'this is not good, means again that we cannot make a try, as all of these will refute. and the motivation of defense is not pure.' Also: 'way too many impurances, and lack of extension is sad'; heavy positions and cook-stoppers are fine when no major flaw remains. Each half-pinned unit should have one defence, so that a try can fail to exactly it.

A self-pinned black piece is dead as a defender but still controls squares against the white king. With a royal battery (Ra4-Kb4) closed by a black knight, the knight's captures that check the king and pin themselves choose the king's mating square: the knight cannot interpose on the battery line, and the square it still attacks is the one the king cannot use.

A self-pinning capture only helps White by what it vacates: the removed White unit and the occupied square hurt White, so a mate available after the capture is already a threat before it, unless it runs through the capturer's old square (a battery the capturer closed, Avner & Retter 2000) or the capture is a check that forces the white king to move (royal battery).
example: Avner & Retter 2000: Be5 closes Bh8-d4; daily No. 8: Sd4 closes Ra4-Kb4

text: Two white knights in front of two pinners (Ba8, Re8 against Ke4) as the units a black knight captures: two loaded batteries, every evolve run found checking keys only, and the zugzwang post-key was mate in two by thirty white moves. The captured blockers must be units that cannot discover check.

postsearch run with the same RNG and seed but different THREAT ids converged to the same zugzwang (the threat term is a penalty, not a filter): vary the RNG per job, and treat a TOP line with an empty threat as a zugzwang, not a threat hit.

Pure try pair in a diagonal half-pin with both units blocking one square: the try piece is not the mating knight but the unit that masks the threat piece (wBf4 masking Rf1, threat Rf4# with Pe5 pinned by the e-file piece; Re6/Be6 both unpin Pe5). Its landing squares spoil the two mates by different means: Bg3 closes Rg1-g4 (refuted by Re6), Bxe3 makes a capture flight once Sd5 leaves for f6 (refuted by Be6). I had assumed the knight that mates had to make the tries; any unit whose every move creates the threat can, if its squares touch both mates.

Several tries by one piece refuted by the same thematic defence are not a 'same refutation' flaw when they are the random stage of a white correction: 1.B~? (the bishop stops guarding d3) Bd6!; 1.Bf5!? (keeps d3 through e4, but closes Rf8-f4) Rd6!; 1.Bc2!. Read the try set as random error, correction with a new error, key before cutting tries down to a pair (I proposed wPf3 to remove the random tries: it would have deleted the correction).

A pure try pair needs a threat that several first moves create. A knight-jump threat (Sg5#) has one creating move, the knight's arrival on f7, so no try can share it, whatever the freedom of mates. Plan the threat as an unmasking or unblocking (a unit on the threat line or on the threat square) so that every move of that unit threatens, then let the landing squares spoil one mate each.

Zagoruiko 2x2 by one knight on a file half-pin (Ke4, Be5, Re6, Re8; Se7-d5 gives Sc3#/Sf6#, Se7-f5 gives Sg3#/Sd6#): the same rook defence and bishop defence must work in both phases, but every line-cut motive is phase-bound. The d-file guard of d5 fits the d5 phase (both its mates re-cover d5) and fails the f5 phase (Sg3 and Sd6 do not cover d5); the f-file guard of f5 is the mirror. Also: whenever White guards e5 for the bishop's mates, Rxe5+ by the pinner is a rival mate after the rook's defence unless Black can retake (bPd6).

On the full WCCT 10 section A field (93 entries, theme 'anticipatory unpin of a white piece' in try and/or solution) our blind panel, with the checklist calibrated after WCCT 11, agreed with the points at Spearman 0.73 (countries with each other 0.62-0.78). Misses: a theme shown only in a try was marked down though the theme admits tries (2nd-3rd place, our 41st); the logical progression of a multistage try sequence (1st place, our 14th) was read as a list of changes; white units idle after the key were noted but not punished as the countries did (two bishops without post-key function: 50th).
example: A040 n7/1Q1R4/4p3/4k1P1/1K1N2P1/pn1p4/bBP2Rpq/4r3: 1.Qf3!; Hannelius + Zagoruiko over four phases, theme in the try 1.Kxa3?

text: On a rank half-pin (Qa4: Rb4, Bc4, Kd4) the white correction of claude-halfpin-file-sf7's scheme works: the key bishop unmasks a rook guard of d5 and must cover e4 for Sb3#, which only c2 and b1 do through d3 (Bd3 itself closes d3 for Rd3#). Two equal key squares mean a capture key or a unit on b1. The ugliness is a cascade from one guard: Bd6 protects Sc5 and gives 2.Be5#, the e5 stopper bPf6 attacks the 5th-rank rook, and the cures of fxg5/f5 bring the promotion pawn and four more stoppers. Fix the source (who protects c5) rather than the cascade.

Rank half-pin Qa4: Rb4, Bc4 to Kd4 with the threat Sc6#: the black bishop guards c6 from b5 (thematic) and from d5, so d5 decides the construction. Free d5 needs a mate after 1...Bd5 that is neither Rd3# (that repeats the rook's mate, and needs c4 guarded by a second unit, which brings 1.Rd3+ Bxd3 2.Sb3# as a cook) nor Sb3# (Bxb3). A white pawn on d5 needs a capture mate after Bxd5 (E. Bourd's Rg5, whose 5th rank also guards e5 and makes Bd6-e5# a dual, the f6/g7/h8 cascade). With the key bishop starting on c6 (its departure frees the threat square; from g2 it guards d5 and e4 along the long diagonal) Rg5 and the cascade go, 1.Be4? Bb5! stays pure, and only the d5 question is left (E. Bourd: 'the resolving using d5 pawn is a bit chaotic').

To find a dual's cause, list the guards of the king's field in the unwanted mate: after 1...Bxd5 2.Rd3 in bourd-halfpin-diagonal-bb1 c4 is guarded only by Sd2, which the thematic Rd3# (after Rb6, the pinned bishop still on c4) never needs. The cure is a b3-mating knight that does not see c4 (Sa1/Sc1; Sc5 sees e4 and b3 but not c4), and every other job of Sd2 (e4, the by-play mate Sf3#) must move with it.

"I think you are too harsh with capturing of white or black pawns, these are minor flaws." A key, try, mate or refutation that captures a pawn is a minor flaw; I had put 1.Bxc2! (capturing a black pawn) first among the flaws of bourd-halfpin-rank-bxc2. Weigh it with the other minor flaws, after duals and stoppers.

"It's not even the pieces, it's incomparable for me. The additional content is almost always worth it, elevating the problem. You can see by your tries how hard it is to construct additional content." A light problem and its version with a second layer are not compared unit by unit: the layer wins unless it brings a fatal flaw. How the layer came here: he moved the knight off c5 (it blocked every manoeuvre) and put every try and the key on one diagonal of the key bishop, so random move, two corrections and key tell one story; my fixed-mate searches (Zagoruiko by one knight, knight wheel, halfpin_tries) found nothing.

"i think start simple, and then maybe consider the enhancement. look how easy it is to construct imo, before pushing into a much harder theme. a basic scheme is needed to play around... once you see that you are easily implementing the basic scheme, consider the addition. if the basic scheme turns to be very limited already, we need to somewhat limit expectation of the content. its not always the case, sometimes when we look for alphabetical changes (reciprocal, lacny, shedey, le-grand), we look for a paradoxical scheme before deciding how even pieces look on the board." On the rook-and-knight half-pin I planned the second layer (white correction) before a sound base existed and lost an hour in two sketches.

"such general themes (self-block, unguard, bishop and knight play to same square) are almost never anticipated, those are simple motives. unless they push to some limit (unguard 14234 times, self-block 7 times etc). otherwise those are just unifying effects over some other complex addition usually (tries, changes, and so on)." I had treated Barnes 2002 (both half-pinned units defend on e6) as an anticipation of the rook-and-knight half-pin: it is not; only a specific multi-phase layer (Dyachuk 2002: pure pair with reversal of first move and mate) would be.

Rook-and-knight half-pin on a diagonal (Ke4, Sd3, Rc2, Bb1): build by colour. The knight on d3 covers dark squares only, so its pin mate is a line mate through a dark square it covers (4th rank from the east via f4: Qg4#), and its own arrival must spoil the rook's mate (Sf4 blocks the 4th rank). The rook's pin mate is a line mate through a square on its own line (Qc4#), spoiled after its defence because it keeps that file (Rc5 still holds c4). Four blind searches from near-empty seeds found nothing in 280 s; hand placement with one solve per change reached a sound post-key in nine solves. Trap: any static guard of the knight's square plus a guard of every flight lets the pinner take the pinned knight with mate after the rook's defence (Bxd3#); leave one flight (d4) that only the mating moves cover, and let the key give it. Result claude-halfpin-rs-qg8: 7Q/3NN3/3p3B/8/1p2k3/3n2K1/2rP4/1B6, 1.Qg8! Sf4 2.Qc4#, Rc5 2.Qg4#.

Once a basic half-pin scheme is sound, seed compose.halfpin_tries with the diagram whose key piece can reach several squares (queen on g7: g8, f7, g5) and fix only the king and the half-pin core: it finds the pure pair by moving the guards. It gave the thematic defence a second effect (1...Rc5 also cuts Ra5 from e5) so that one queen square loses its mate after Rc5 and another keeps one (Qf4 covers e5 itself). Hand cook-stoppers for the same job (a black pawn on h5 against Qg4) brought new black checks.

A try refuted by a thematic defence can come from a closed line instead of a cut one: in bourd-halfpin-rs-qf7 the knight g6 that guards e5/f4 also closes the g-file, so 1.Qg8? has no Qg4 after 1...Rc5, while 1.Qd7? reaches g4 by the diagonal (a changed mate Qg4 -> Qf4 against the key). Choose the try squares so each threat is single (his Qd7 instead of my Qg5, which also threatened Qe3). A knight on a field square (Se3, protected by two pawns) can replace three distant guards (Se7, Bh6, Ra5) and protect the mating squares c4/g4.

"naaah, i like that you try. you are my co-author. always welcome to try more." On his bench positions too: do not stop at the verdict with 'it's your position'; try improvements (lighter cook-stoppers, a unit with a second job, more content), verify each with the solver, and show what worked and what did not.

A half-pin scheme whose mates use only line interpositions and captures carries over between unit pairs: the rook-and-knight problem became a two-knight one by Rc2 -> Sc2 in one solve, because the knight on c2 also covers d4 (the rank mate's interposition square) and its defence Se3 guards both c4 and d5. Each knight reaches the threat square from two squares, so a 'both to one square' version needs the second squares blocked; blocking them with pawns takes the mating squares (f4) and, with every flight guarded, the queen's checks all mate. Keep one flight that only the mating moves cover.

"nice, you could reuse the same thing. lets find another mechanism, something without king flight, its a bit limiting in general." A scheme that needs a free flight in the post-key (so that the pinner's capture of the pinned unit, or the queen's checks, fail) forces a flight-giving key and leaves little room: prefer mechanisms where every flight is covered and the stray checks fail for another reason (a black unit protecting the pinned unit's square, mates by several pieces instead of one queen).

"its not bad adding that rook behind, for the dual avoidance, but what i meant by flight here, is that the dual avoidance is made by the flight on d3. lets find some other mechanism. maybe lets change to orthogonal pin." In the half-pin schemes the second mate failed because the adjacent knight's departure left d3 free: a dual avoidance by a vacated flight, the same in every version. Look for separation by what the arrival does (blocking the other mate's line, guarding its square) or by a line the departure opens (the black rook behind, which he accepts).

Two knights half-pinned on a file or rank stand on opposite colours, and each knight's arrival covers the colour its partner covered: so the arrival can spoil the partner's pin-mate only by blocking its line or occupying its square, never by guarding a square of that line. Plan the two mates as line mates whose lines pass the other knight's arrival square (Se3-g4 shuts the 4th rank east, Se2-d4 the 4th rank west). Rank and file mates cover few field squares, so the static guards multiply and every white check mates; prefer mates by pieces that cover many field squares, or a king on the edge.

For a half-pin with a try pair, make the threat a line opening: a white piece standing on the threat piece's line (Bf5 masking Qd7-f5) is the key piece, and each of its landing squares is a try; place the two pin mates so that one landing square spoils each (Bxg4 occupies the mating square g4, Be4 cuts the mating line d4-f4), and each try then falls to the matching thematic defence. He found this after five threat designs in one sitting; my designs started from the knights' guard squares and never got a key. When the masking piece has too many squares (cooks Bg7, Bh8), a shift towards the edge shortens its diagonal.

Two-knight half-pin with the dual avoidance by black line opening, doubled: each knight's departure unblocks a black line that refutes the OTHER knight's pin mate (Sd5 leaves: bRa5 reaches e5 against Bf6+; Sd6 leaves: bBf8 reaches b4 against Rb4+). This is the 'rook behind' he accepted, used for both knights, and it replaces the vacated-flight separation he rejected. Put the black line pieces behind the knights on lines that cross the other mate's interposition or mating square.

For an underpromotion key with a threat, list the squares only the promoted piece reaches from the promotion square (a knight on e8: d6, f6, c7, g7; no queen on e8 reaches them) and make one of them the guard a white line piece needs once the promotion unmasks it (Bd8-e7-f6, threat 2.Bxf6#). Q and R then fail for a reason in the position, not by stalemate, and Black can be fully mobile.

Evolve on a bare promotion core ran at about one evaluation a second and found only a thin zugzwang in 10 minutes; postsearch on the post-key position (promoted piece already on e8, threat fixed) placed the whole defence and mate system in under five minutes. When the key is a promotion, compose the post-key position with the promoted piece in place, then put the pawn back.

In a half-pin post-key where every flight is guarded, White's checks that force a knight move (Bf6+ Sxf6, Rb4+ Sxb4) reach the same pin mates, so they cook every diagram that differs from the post-key only by an idle key. A key that kills them must give the pin mates something they all need; a square that is no flight in the diagram because a black unit stands on it and leaves in the defences (the knight's square) is the natural one, and the threat must need it too (or be created by the same move). His bench answer for the 5th-rank version: the key guards f6, which the threat knight itself leaves (1.Bd8, threat Sxh6).

On the 27 best entries of WCCT 9 section A the five judging countries agreed with each other at a mean Spearman of 0.08 (-0.50 to 0.37); our blind panel agreed with the total at 0.16 and found the 1st place. Among good problems only the outstanding one is a shared verdict. Content: effects the set theme produces by itself (Dombrovskis and Hannelius when try threats must return as mates) were scored as the floor; the textbook versions placed 20th-27th, while different refutations for every try and genuine five-phase play were paid for.
example: 1st place 1Q5b/8/3PBp1N/3R3K/r3kp2/2n1P1p1/3P2P1/8: 1.d7! fxe3 2.d3#, Sxd5 2.Bf5#; tries Qb6?/Sg4? (2.d3#), Qb7?/Qg8? (2.Bf5#)

text: An attacked key piece is a milder flaw when its diagram square has a set-play job: "key is slightly less flawed here, as we have a set mate, and the bishop seems to guard e5 as well" (1.Bc7-d8! in bourd-halfpin-ss-bd8, where Bc7 is the only guard of e5 in the set 1...R~ 2.Rxe5#). Before calling a key an escape, ask whether the piece is needed where it stands in the set play and whether that square is the only one that does the set job and reaches the key square (c7 is); the attack is then a by-product and the key gives up a set mate. What remains of the flaw is the capture left without a set mate (1...Sxc7). The critique now names both (key_piece_set_roles, key_piece_captures_unprovided).

His three types of 2x2 changed mates: (1) the same White piece mates in both phases on a different line (Qh7 with knights d4/c3: Qf5/Qe4 -> Qe6/Qd5; or Qh4 -> Qh6 with knights b5/c5: 'the mating piece changes line'); what matters is the arrivals and that each Black piece guards two of them, one per line, not symmetry; it 'requires something that guards/allows both'. (2) Different White pieces mate (Rf6/Rd4 with knights c7/d6: Re6/Rf5 vs Re4/Rd5, separated e.g. by a bishop moving f5-e4). (3) The same piece has two mates, one excluded per phase for some reason, then doubled; king flights extend the geometry at the cost of rigid play.

Type 1 with two black knights next to the king (Sd4, Sc3 for Ke5): the knights interpose on every rank or file check (Qe8+ Se6, Qc5+ Sd5), so a threat by distant check must come along a diagonal whose interposition squares no knight reaches (Qb8+ through c7/d6). Knights on different colours (b5/c5) can never guard a common threat square, so their defences can only differ in motive. Give each knight's pair of mating squares ONE White protector: Sf6 for e4/d5 (it also blocks the queen's 6th rank, killing the other line's mate in the set), Bd7 for f5/e6. Result claude-changed-type1-qg8, 8/3BB3/5NQ1/4k1Pp/2pn4/2n1P3/8/7K, 1.Qg8!.

A changed-mates set phase in which only the knights can move is a complete block, and every waiting move cooks it (1.Be7, 1.Bf3, 1.Kh6 ...). Leave a Black move without a set mate: a tempo pawn that also stops a cook (bPh5 guards g4 against a Sg4 dual and its h4 refutes the waiting tries), or a knight move whose arrival cuts a protector (Se6 cuts Bd7-f5). A white pawn added to double a guard (Pd3 on e4) can free the guarding piece and create threats: the second guard is not free.

WCCT 8 section A (28 entries printed with a diagram, theme black correction + change of function of white moves): Spearman 0.30 against the place, while the five countries agree with each other at 0.22. The WCCT 9 calibration ('effects the theme produces are the floor') overcorrected: our judges discounted a Zagoruiko + Dombrovskis + Hannelius that this theme does not force, and the 1st place fell to our 9th. Rule: only what the theme's wording logically entails is the floor. Also: a black correction must commit a new error; a move that only avoids the random move's error (a Grimshaw piece staying on its line) is not full-value correction (GB on the 26th place).
example: 1st place 3Q4/3pP3/8/2nP1R2/2Nkp2r/3P2Bp/BP6/2N1R1bK: 1.Qa5! S~ 2.Be5#, Sxd3 2.Se2#; tries 1.Sa5? (2.Be5#) Bh2!, 1.Rd1? (2.Se2#) exd3!

text: "I wouldn't call it 6 changed mates. Realistically all knight moves are the same." A knight whose every move unguards the same squares gives ONE change, however many of its moves are listed; count changes per defending unit and effect, not per move. He then asked for the knight defence to be unique: one move of each knight defends, the others let the threat mate.

Unique knight defences for a knight-pair change (claude-changed-type1-unique-qg8): knights on dark squares guard only dark squares from their arrivals, so a threat that is a white knight check (always from a light square) cannot be guarded; make each knight's only defence the CLOSING of a White guard line through one of its arrival squares. The threat knight f6 itself guards e4/d5, so its move 2.Sg4 needs d5 from the queen's new line (the key creates the threat) and f5 from Bd3 alone: Se6 cuts g8-d5, Se4 cuts d3-f5. A guard square has two knight posts (f5+e6: d4 or g7); the post g7 also shut the queen's 7th rank and g-file and removed the twin key 1.Qf7. The bishop's own move to the cut square (1.Be4, also guarding d5) must fail: here it unshields the king on d7 from a rook (1...Rd2+).

evolve UNIQUE=1 (chesscomp/compose/unique_defence.py): every DEF must be the only defence of its unit in the key phase; it found the sound unique-defence version from the hand mechanism in under five minutes, where TARGET/CHANGED alone returned zugzwang keys with random knight defences.

WCCT 7 section A (single-phase blends of at least three thematic groups; 27 entries from the scanned book; out of sample): Spearman 0.22 against the place, the five countries 0.00 among themselves. The countries judged each blend by its weakest group ('last system inferior', 'artificially added variations', 'first three groups one system'); our judges added groups up, and our top three placed 8th, 21st and 19th. In a single-phase problem the key weighs most: 'the best and most thematic key of the tourney - double sacrifice, unpin, flight-giving, change of 4 mates' took 2nd place.

Replacing a knight defender by a bishop or rook in the queen-changes-line scheme (claude-changed-type1-unique-qg8). A bishop can guard a knight's pair (e4+d5 or f5+e6) only along ONE diagonal (the pair lies on it), so it can step along that diagonal while still guarding both: from the long diagonal its own squares attack every knight-check square around e5 (f3 guards g4, c6 guards d7, e4 guards d3/g6, d5 guards c4/f7), so against a knight-check threat it always has an on-line defence with no thematic mate; its unique defence must leave the line against a threat on DARK squares (pawn check, b8/h2/h8 diagonal), where the remaining knight gets several defences. A rook guards a pair only from d4 or f6, and every rook move keeps one of the two guards, so its only defences are stepping onto its own squares (Re4/Rd5, Re6/Rf5), and on d4 it checks a king on d7. Best searched near-miss: bishop c8 switching to b7 to guard f3 against 2.Sg5-f3# (2.Qe6#), but Bg4 also guards f3 and the black rook that held it gave a capture key and an unprovided check.

His answer to 'a bishop always keeps an on-line defence': block the bishop's own diagonal with a black pawn on the far side (bPf3 stops 1...Bf3 guarding g4), so the bishop's only defence is to LEAVE the line (Bb7-c8 guards g4 along c8-h3, through the other defender's squares). The king leaves d7 and Sd4 protects e6/f5 instead, so the bishop's new line gives no check. A white bishop on b1-h7 can switch to a2-g8 like the queen (1.Ba2 covering d5): cut a2-d5 (wPb3), or replace the bishop by a blocked pawn (wPd3 behind Sd4). 'A knight is probably easy to replace with a bishop (a rook from d4 seems logical too, or a queen with more freedom for defending, maybe too strong)'.

source: Claude, on E. Bourd's bench sitting mv8ffb5c
text: His diagonal->orthogonal type-1 scheme (bK d4, bRe1 guards e4/e5, bSb4 guards d3/d5; wQ g6 with Bh7 behind on b1-h7: Qe4/Qxd3; 1.Qg5 with Rh5 behind on rank 5: Qe5/Qd5; threat 2.Bc3# because the queen now guards e3). Built to: key 1.Qg5 unique, set R~ Qe4, S~ Qxd3; after the key Rc1 Qe5, Re5 Qxe5, Sa2 Qd5, Sd5 Qxd5. Two structural limits: (1) the rook's departure 1...Rc1 always allows 2.Qf4# too, because once the e-file is open the queen checks from f4 along the rank, and Rh5 re-covers d5/c5 as soon as the queen leaves g5; f4 cannot be controlled since the key's guard of e3 runs through f4. (2) With 2.Bc3 as threat each defender has two defences (Sa2 and Sd5 both guard c3; Re5 cuts the queen's rank), so no unique defence. Cure needs a different threat (one the key creates without the g5-f4-e3 line) or a different B-square.

source: Claude, comparing with E. Bourd (bench mv8ffb5c)
text: When a scheme's flaw comes from the THREAT's own line (his 2.Bc3 needed the key's g5-f4-e3 guard, so 1...Rc1 always allowed 2.Qf4), proving it 'inherent' and stopping is the wrong move: change the threat and the orientation together. He turned the board a quarter and rebuilt the white side around a new threat whose key-guard line (c7-d6-e5) crosses nothing the defenders open, in 16 minutes and 104 piece moves: B1RK3b/1Q1Pp3/1P6/7r/2pkpB2/8/3nP3/3N4, 1.Qc7!. I had the transform tool (compose.transform --all) and the constitution's 'restructure a whole side' and used neither; I kept his threat fixed and searched units around it.

"The defences only guard the threat square. I don't think it's a flaw, it's somewhat pure single moves." With changed mates the change is the content; a defence that only guards the threat square is a pure single-purpose move (his 1.Qc7!: Rh3 and Sf1 both guard e3). The session-2 rule (guard + unguard is uninteresting) stays for single-phase problems.

"I didn't like the recapture of the queen on the defense squares. That's why I looked for defenses not on the thematic squares." A defence that lands on a mating square and is captured there by the mate (claude-changed-type1-unique-qg8: 1...Se6 2.Qxe6#, set 1...Se4 2.Qxe4#) is a flaw of construction: choose defences away from the thematic squares. The critique flags it (mate captures defender).

Type 1 with a rook and a bishop as the two defenders (E. Bourd: 'maybe other pieces doing the defences'): if the queen switches between two whole lines, it is impossible for any king square (chesscomp.compose.type1_geometry.line_pairs(K, 'RB') is empty). A bishop's pair is two light edge squares of the field, a rook's pair needs a corner square on a rank or file; they never split one-and-one over two queen lines, and two bishops would share a colour. A defender at the corner of its two squares (Rd4 for Ke5) keeps one guard on every move. It works only with queen POSTS whose reach differs (post_pairs): for Kd4 one-step Qc7-b7 and Qg3-g2, longer Qa3-a8, Qc1-h1, Qg3-g8. Knight checks are the threats a bishop defender can parry (all knight checks on a dark-square king come from light squares).

With E. Bourd's engine (the threat piece guards a field square that the key's queen takes over) the threat fails in the set only through the square the threat piece vacates, and the set queen next to the king mates there: Qg3-g2 gave 1.Sb3+ Ke4 2.Qd3#, Qc7-b7 gave 1.Sc2+ Kd5 2.Qc6# (Rc8 behind) or Bc4#. Check that escape first. Cure that worked: a threat square on the set queen's own line (Qa3: 1.Sb3+ blocks the 3rd rank, so the flight e4 has no mate): claude-changed-type1-rook-bishop.

Blind evolve from a bare type-1 core (8 jobs x 5 min, about 1 solve a second) found nothing; the sound rook+bishop version came from a guard table by hand (who covers each field square in each mate, which black unit stops each check), one change per solve, from four refutations to one in three solves. evolve now has a type-1 mode (DEFSQ, TKEY, QMATE: thematic units by square, the defence read off the key phase, preferring the one whose set mate changes) and CANDS (mutate only named units on named squares). Use the search after the table, for the last layer.

"The grimshaw is useless though, although it is in the set, it is fake. It never appears, just a visual 'glitch'. If something is ready in the set but actually never fulfilled or repeated then it practically doesn't exist." A set-play effect counts only when the solution (or a try) fulfils or repeats it: a set Grimshaw whose interferences only allow the threat after the key is no content (claude-changed-type1-rook-bishop, 1...Bf5/Rf5).

"A key to the corner is always nice. And here as it sets the changes it's cool." (1.Qa8! in claude-changed-type1-rook-bishop.) The by-play 1...Rd5 2.Qxd5# is "slightly annoying, it's a flaw but not too big"; overall "nice construction".

Type 1 on two orthogonal lines (E. Bourd: each line has three mating squares): with the king in the centre only queen posts Qh5/Qh3 (ranks 5 and 3) and Qc8/Qe8 (files c and e) reach exactly the three squares of a line, and the defender pairs are always straight (c5/c3 rook on the c-file or Sa4, d5/d3 Sb4, e5/e3 rook on the e-file); no defender holds c5 and e3. The third square of each line becomes the threat after the key (2.Qd3#) and both rooks can defend on one square (Rcd1, Red1): claude-changed-type1-ranks. Cost: a rook can always step onto its own mating square on the threat line (1...Rc3 2.Qxc3#), and only units that cannot mate on a square should guard it (knights and a bishop, not Bb4/Bh6 which mated on c3/e3).

On claude-changed-type1-ranks (two mirror rooks defending on d1): "try to find something less symmetric maybe, and different pieces." Answer: claude-changed-type1-files-pawn-rook, a pawn (d6: c5/e5, its only move d5 guards the threat square e4) and a rook (h3: c3/e3, defends Rh4); a pawn's pair is horizontal, so the queen switches files (Qc8-e8).

Type 1 does not need one defender holding two squares: "instead of one piece defending 2 squares, another error happens: unguard + line close for example"; "unguard/line-close + line-opening, there are many combinations of creating two errors at once". One defence makes two errors and each phase (the queen's line) uses one: in bourd-changed-type1-pawn-errors 1...d3-d2 opens wRg3's guard of c3 (set 2.Qxc3#) and closes bBc1's guard of e3 (solution 2.Qe3#). The pairings to try: unguard+unguard, unguard+line-close (black guard cut), line-close+line-opening (white line freed), self-block+unguard, and so on; it multiplies the constructions for every queen line pair.

Type 1 on adjacent diagonals (K e5, queen b1-h7 -> a2-g8 from above): the defence for the side the queen comes from (f5/e6) cannot make two different errors. The diagram may have no flight and the threat needs f5/e4 guarded after the key, so every field square is White-guarded and each queen mate can only come from removing a Black guard; on that side every Black line to f5 or e6 also guards the other square or crosses the queen's path, and no unit that guards one of them can reach a square closing a line to the other (scratch enumerations cross2/sides; pins give nothing). A White line opened onto e6 needs e6 unguarded in the diagram: a flight. The far side (e4/d5) has three: Sf2-d3 (unguard e4 + close Rd1/Rd2-d5), Sb6-c4 (close Ra4-e4 + unguard d5), d5-d4 (unguard e4 + close Rd1-d5). E. Bourd's bench scheme has the same split: 1...d5 frees the near squares c5/e5 by a double unguard, 1...d2 the far squares c3/e3 by two errors. Result: claude-changed-type1-qg8-two-errors.

chesscomp.compose.errors FEN DEF [DEF ...] --key UCI splits a Black move into its departure (unit removed) and its arrival (a copy added, the unit kept) and says which part makes each mate, set and after the key: 'departure', 'arrival', 'either', 'both'. A two-error defence is one whose set and solution mates come from different parts (or different errors of one part, read off effects). On claude-changed-type1-unique-qg8 all four mates are 'departure'; on bourd-changed-type1-pawn-errors 1...d2 is departure (Qxc3) / arrival (Qe3).

On the two-error type-1 attempt (9+7 for one changed defence): "lets try to duplicate the closing of line maybe, and just 1 thematic move. big jump yes". One thematic move whose arrival closes two Black lines, one guarding the set mating square and one the solution mating square; each phase uses one closure. Around K e5 with the queen on b1-h7 -> a2-g8 the only crossing for e4/d5 is d4 (a rook on the 4th rank, a rook on the d-file): claude-changed-type1-double-closing, 1.Qg8! (2.Sc6#) Sd4 2.Qd5#, set Sd4 2.Qe4#.

A threat by a knight freed by the key (it held e6 or d5 until the queen took the square over) has a check-first cook: 1.Sc6+ Ke6 2.Qg8#. Leave the king on e6 an escape the queen does not cover (d7 or e7). A by-play that cuts the queen's new line (1...Se6) defends whenever the other guard of that square is a line the threat piece blocks (Bb7 behind c6): guard the square from the side the threat cannot cut (Bg2 for d5), and the by-play stops being a defence.

"maybe you can finish this - idea Qg7-f7, Sd3 Se6" (after bench sittings mv8r4h2h and mv8v9fm2: K d4, black pawns c4/e4/e5, Re8 protecting e5, Be2 protecting c4 through d3, knights b4 and g5, his queen b7 with Ba8 behind). Read as the mirrored battery: Qg7 masking Bh8; set 1...Se6 (closes Re8) 2.Qxe5#; 1.Qf7: 1...Sd3 (closes Be2/Bf1) 2.Qxc4#, 1...Se6 2.Bxe5#.

A queen standing in front of a bishop aimed at a pawn next to the king (Qg7 + Bh8 against e5, K d4) cooks by 1.Qxe5+ Rxe5 2.Bxe5# whenever the bishop's capture is one of the solution's mates: the white unit that protects e5 for the bishop in the solution protects it in the cook too, and the queen on f7 adds nothing to that mate. The one cure found: the protector is masked by the thematic knight's origin, a black Sc5 in front of a white Ra5 (Sc5 plays both Sd3 and Se6).

A threat that runs through the closure square is stopped by the very piece whose line the closure cuts: with Re8 guarding e5 through e6, 1.Qf7 (2.Qd5#) is refuted by 1...Re6, and no single added White unit gives a mate after it (enumerated). Likewise a threat that 1...Sd3 stops by cutting the third rank is also stopped by the bishop that protects c4 through d3 (1...Bd3), and Rxd3 is recaptured by the knight. Choose a threat the defences stop by a guard (both Sd3 and Se6 guard f4 and c5), never by the cut itself.

Type 1 with the set mate on the far square and the solution mate on the near square of ONE check line (K e4: set Qg2#, solution Qf3#, both through f3) cooks by 1.Qg2+ Rf3 2.Qxf3#: the black guard of the near square interposes there and the queen recaptures. It is sound only if the solution mate needs a second effect of the defence (a self-block) that the cook lacks, and the diagram still covers that square. Contact mates (both squares in the king's field) avoid it: the earlier diagonal problems used f5/e4 -> e6/d5.

Evolve on the K d4 reading (core Kd4 Sc5 Pc4 Pe5 Re8 Bf1 / Qg7 Bh8 Bg8 Ra5) moved the key to 1.Qc7 (2.Qxc5#): a Black correction S~ 2.Rd5# (Ra5 unmasked, d5 protected by Bg8), 1...Sd3 2.Qxc4# (cuts Rg3's guard of c3 and Bf1's protection of c4), 1...Se6 2.Bxe5# (cuts Bg8's protection of d5 and Re8's of e5); set 1...Se6 2.Qxe5#. Design the error table before any search: for each arrival square of the key piece, which defence it stops (it blocks the refuting line, or its new square answers the random refutation with a mate) and which mate it spoils (it takes a mating square, or cuts a White line to one). Loustau's 4th-degree correction (psis-22fa9079c1) is exactly this table on one diagonal: off the diagonal 1...Qxg1! guards b6; on it Bc5 takes the square of 2.Qc5#, Bd4 cuts Qg1 from c5, Be3 spoils nothing. evolve with WCORR found the random stage and one correction in minutes three times, and a second error never.

A white knight orthogonally next to the black king never checks by moving (the knight lands on squares of its own colour's opposite, the king's squares attacked from there are the other colour), so it can mask a queen line next to the king safely. But its landing squares sit next to the king's field and give knight checks, which become second threats in the tries and cooks in the solution (8/6rb/1N1P4/4P3/1P1kNP2/8/1K2PP2/7Q: 1.Sg5 2.Se6#/Qd5#). A masking bishop or rook has no such checks.

A black interposition on the vacated line (Rd2, Rg2) is the easy random refutation, and a correction that closes the interposer's line (Be2 on the rank, Sg3 on the file) is the easy first correction. Neither carries an error of its own, so the second correction does not come from it: the closing square must also spoil a mate, which needs a second White line through it (Loustau: the queen's g1-c5 line through d4).

For tries by the clearing piece, read its stops beyond the mating square as files: each stop can mate from its own file next to the king (Rb5, Rd5, Re5 against Kc5), and the defences choose which files still work - an arrival that blocks c4 (compensating the rook's own cut Ba6-c4 on b5) or d5, or that guards e5. 4N3/4N3/Bn6/P1k5/6P1/2P3Pp/6RQ/6K1: 1.Rd2! Sc4 Rd5#, Sd5 Rxd5#; 1.Rb2? Sd5! (Sc4 Rb5#).

A rook stopping on a file cannot cut a file pin: it takes the pin over (Rd2 between Rd1 and a pinned Sd3 still pins). Interference tries by a rook on a rank need diagonal lines through its stop squares (a1-c3 through b2, b1-d3 through c2).

Before building a 'new type' of 2x2, look for its basic form in the database first (a short scan on the key's effect: battery formed, flight given). Both the battery key (Cuppini 2003, psis-2b6418e028) and the flight-giving key with mates by the key piece (Marandyuk 2005, psis-d5310cd9be, 12 units) were published in light form; I found them after 20 search runs instead of before. chesscomp.compose.type3 counted a unit per changed defence without asking whether the mates differ: three captures on d4 all met by Qe6# scored 231 with a unique key. It now charges units that repeat a mate and needs two different mates in each phase (tested). New options: KMP (key mates by one unit, e.g. a battery's front piece), FLIGHT (the key gives a flight), TRY (compare a try with the key), MP=key.

Daily No. 12: a corner key needs a reason for the corner, not only for the line. Give every other square of the line its own error (a White line it shuts: Bg2 shuts Rh2 off d2; a black cut it allows behind it: d6-d5 between c6 and e4; a capture by the king on e4/d5) and the corner is the square without one: 8/8/K2p4/8/N2k1P1p/1P3B1R/2P4R/3Nb3, 1.Bh1!. The archive's rich corner keys (Pachl 1.Bh8!, Chepizhny 1.Ba1!, Ahues 1.Qa8!) are such line selections.

One refutation per try needs a defender with one way to do it: a black knight f1 guarding d2 could interpose on g3 and on e3, so 1.Bg2? had two refutations and both variations shared 2.Rd2#; a black bishop e1 has the same d2 guard and only one interposition (g3), which made the try pure.

Searches around a bare corner-key core (evolve KEY+TRIES, a random fill and a hill climb on python-chess) found nothing usable in 50 minutes: unique keys without diagram flights are too rare blind, and a queen in the corner takes the edge file's flights from far away. The position came from boxing the king first (pawns and knights), so the masked rook had one line, then one defender change per try table.
"lets not try zaguruiko. lets switch to a problem with batteries, we didnt try those much. no transfers, just 2 variations. and then lets try to add tries"

Battery variations by a front knight: a discharge onto a square next to the king needs a protector, and the protector also guards that square, so no defence can make such a discharge necessary by leaving its landing square open (circular every time it was tried: Se5/Sf4 from g6, Sd5/Sf5 from e7, Sd4/Sf4 from e6). Defences can only select discharges that cover a square from a distance (from g6: Se7 for d5, Sh4 for f3; from e7: Sc6 for d4, Sg6 for f4), and with every field square guarded those discharges are threats too: the result is a Fleck-like separation of a multiple threat (claude-battery-fleck-scheme). A single non-battery threat needs one more square open in the threat position that both defences close. Also: a rook or queen guarding a line next to the king drops onto it with mate in one (Rf4#, Rd4#, Qe5#); a black piece guarding the drop square is the cheapest cure.

"we have a bettery which is defended by a piece. when that black piece defends twice, it makes some kind of unguard ( we can try other errors , but lets try unguard first ). that unguard forces a specific battery move, that guards that square. it could be done via many other combinations. but need to be careful of double check mates as those are powerful". The black piece holding the battery (interposition) is the square closed before the defence that the battery variations need.

Plan after the rook-knight battery, same concept, in order: pawn battery (single/double step); bishop-knight battery (knight one square away or more); bishop-rook; rook-bishop; rook-knight with the knight two or more squares away. "in each after we have the play, we will try to add some kind of tries. and consider how to extend the probkem".

Black piece holding a front-knight battery by interposition and losing it by capturing a guard: for Kd4/Sd5/Rd8 only a queen works (battery_guards: f5 with Rc2/Sf2, b5 with Sb2/Re2; no rook or bishop). A guard on the 4th rank behind a White unit on e4 is a second battery (his exf5). Any line piece protecting the front square d5 guards c4 or e4 through d5 after the discharge. The hard part is the threat: a queen holding the line has many moves that parry a quiet threat or keep the interposition; look for a threat square her lines cannot reach before placing guards.
"try rotating, changing pieces and more..." (when the queen-held battery stalled on the threat).

Queen-held battery, what worked: rotating 180 degrees (battery from below) gave the search a one-hole post-key; changing the rear rook into a queen freed a rook for the c4 guard (both thematic squares were light, so two light bishops were the bind); a bishop masked by a black pawn next to the king turns the pawn's advance into a non-defence; extra pawns shut the queen's lines to the threat square (c2 behind c3, e2). The open problem is the key: a threat independent of the rear piece mates before the key, and a battery loaded in the diagram gives checking cooks; the key should form the battery and the threat should need the rear piece.

postsearch accepted any mate for the named defences and found Rd7#/Bg2# instead of battery discharges (577 hits in run 514). New KMP=<square> option requires each named defence to be mated by the unit on that square. Its dual count ignores moves that do not stop the threat (correct convention), and it treats e8=Q/e8=R as one move id.

A black piece holding a battery by static interposition between rear and front cuts the rear's protection of the front piece, so a threat that needs that protection fails to it. Cure that worked: let the holder reach the battery line only at the front square (then capturing the front piece pins it), here a blocked black pawn on e3 closing the queen's diagonal. Then the key can bring the rear piece and the threat can need it. Edge origins of the rear queen make the key piece out of play; an unmasking bishop from d3 has checking squares next to the king (Bc4+).

Pawn battery held by an interposer (Qb1/c2 v Ke4, black rook on the d-file): the holder interposed on d3 is pinned by the rear queen, so after 2.c3+/c4+ Rd3 every threat mate that does not need the key mates again; post-key 'other solutions' are unavoidable and only keys that bring the threat piece (1.Sg1-h3, threat Sg5#) or create it survive. Failed cures, each with its reason: a threat by the queen leaving b1 (unpins the rook, which then interposes on e3/f3) needs d2 blocked, and every blocker fails (pawn: 2.d3+ Rxd3 cxd3#; dark bishop: clashes with Ba7, or with knight guards Se6/Sb6 the recapture needs a third knight; knight: checks); a rook pinning c2 along the 2nd rank (Rg2, K a2) kills the battery checks but the only knight threats with one checking square start on the edge (Sa6-c5, Sc8-d6) and the searches kept 2-4 other solutions; a knight holder has no configuration (b4 needs a White rook on d5, which protects d3: 2.c3+ Sd3 3.Qxd3#).

Thematic tries for the pawn battery (worked out, not yet built): 1...Rxa7 refutes a try when e3 is empty and guarded only by Ba7 (through d4) and the key piece (2.c3+ Ke3); 1...Rxf7 refutes a try that blocks c4 (2.c3+ leaves d5). A knight on e3 going to d1 (key, guards e3) or c4 (guards e3, blocks c4) gives the pure Rxf7 try; the knight's other moves give Rxa7 tries. unmask_search with TRIES did not yet find it.

postsearch gained EMPTY=<squares> (squares the search may not fill): without it the search shut the holder's guard line d3-e3-f3 with black pawns in every hit. battery_guards accepts a knight holder (n); for the pawn battery against Ke4 there is none.

A holder that ATTACKS the battery's rear piece (bQb3 against wQd1 on b3-c2-d1, earlier bRb1 against Qc1) instead of interposing on the line answers the discharge by capturing the rear, is never pinned on the line, and so does not create the 2.c3+ Rd3 + threat cooks of the interposer. Its thematic moves leave the attacking line and each unguards one square by its arrival (Qb5 cuts Ra5-f5, Qxb8 takes the f4 guard). The key vacated the double-step square (Se4-d2), which also opened the threat line Bc6-f3: bourd-pawn-battery-queen-sd2.

Thematic tries by adding an error (his note: 'the thematic tries will have an additional error which will not allow the mate'): the key knight's tries land next to the king on squares protected by the very guards the thematic defences remove (Sxg5 protected along Ra5's rank, Sxg3 by Bb8). Each thematic defence then also gives a capture flight that its own battery mate does not cover: 1.Sxg5? Qb5! (Kxg5), 1.Sxg3? Qxb8! (Kxg3). Pure, distinct, and the key square (d2) adds no flight.

"btw the solution random move again is somewhat bad" (bench label 1...Q~ 2.e4#, 1...Qxb8 2.e3# for 1.Sd2! Qb5 e4#, Qxb8 e3#). A random move is a defence by departure: if the threat still mates with the piece removed, its moves defend by their arrivals and there is no random move, even when the shared mate works without the piece (the battery holder's removal frees both discharges). Both solvers now apply this (tests/test_keysel.py); the knight, bishop and knight corrections in the collection keep their random moves.

Nothing checked retro legality, so the solver, the critique and the gate all passed it and I called it sound. New chesscomp.core.illegal_position (pawn-capture assignment against the opponent's lost units, home files, promotions), fatal in the critique and the gate, applied inside every search tool's promoted() filter and in the bench (analysis.js illegalPosition). Over 5,514 orthodox Problemesis positions it flags 6 (three checked by hand: two needing one capture too many, one with eight pawns the h-pawn cannot reach, one a 20-unit parsing error).

Bishop-knight battery held by a black piece (Ke4, Bb1/Sc2 or Ba8/Sc6), what blocks it: (1) colour - a knight discharge from a light line lands on dark squares and covers light ones, so both thematic squares are light like the rear bishop and the White guards must be rooks, knights or a queen (a light bishop is a second one); (2) with the front two squares away only one non-adjacent discharge covers each square (Sb4 d5/d3, Se1 f3, Se7 f5), the adjacent ones fail to Kx; (3) rook and bishop holders have no configuration, knight holders that attack the rear need light-bishop guards, queens always reach the line; (4) a knight holder that interposes (Sf6 to d5, Sc3, Sf2/Sc5 to d3) has its guard line through the interposition square, so 1...Sd5 in advance cuts it and is a hole; (5) a queen that answers it (2.Qxd5#, from a2 with the black knight guarding d5) also mates after every discharge and interposition, so all knight checks solve (run 832: 5 other solutions).

battery_guards gained how=line|rear|both (rear: the holder attacks the rear piece, E. Bourd's fix). Bug found the same day: after a capture the holder must lose every kind of hold; checking only the rear attack let 1...Qxd7 keep the d5 interposition (runs 801-804 had no play). Full enumerations of 3 geometries x 4 holder types x 2 modes take over 10 minutes: run them one at a time under timeout 300.
