His bench sitting mvculjk2 started from the same battery (Ba8/Sc6 v Ke4) with a black knight holder on e3 whose captures (Sxc2, Sxg4) select Sb4# / Scd4#.

Thematic tries for a knight battery (his words): 'the easiest is to block the knight moves. then i had to choose 2 out of the 4 possible, and arrange a threat. so i need a threatening piece that can block those squares. i cant use a knight. i could try a rook, but then its not that easy to arrange proper play. so i used a bishop'. Recipe: plug the front knight's unwanted discharge squares with White's own pawns, keep two; pick the key piece so that its moves to the two kept squares are tries (each blocks one thematic mate, refuted by the defence that needs it) and its key move frees the threat (Bg6-h7 vacates g6 for Sh4-g6#): bourd-bishop-knight-battery-bh7, 1.Be8? Sb6!, 1.Bh5? Sxe3!, 1.Bh7!.

With the knight closer to the black king (Bh8/Sg7 v Ke5, the holder Sd5 reaching f6) the scheme was 'not that hard'. The two defences repeat his pawn-battery pair: an interference (1...Sb6 cuts Ra6-d6, so only Se8 covers d6) and a capture (1...Sxe3 takes the f4 guard, so only Sh5 covers f4).

"there is still random move notations, when there are no random moves defending" (bench: 'Solution: 1.Bh7! (2.Sg6#), 1...S~ 2.Se8#'). The bench's thematic table fell back to the set play's random group when the solution had none; the set play has no threat, so every knight move counts there. Fixed in docs/analysis.js: the summary names a random move only when the key phase has one; the change summary counts as duals only moves that stop the threat.

Bishop-knight battery with the knight next to the king (Bh8/Sf6 v Ke5), what the tools showed: (1) the thematic squares can only be d6/f4 (Se8, Sh5); the light squares d5/e4 by an occupying discharge fail by the adjacent-landing circularity; d6/f4 are dark like the rear, so the guards are rooks, knights or pawns; (2) the double checks Sd7/Sg4 mate whenever every flight is covered: plug them (a pawn on g4 also guards f5) or let them cut a guard line through d7/g4 (Rd8 guarding d6 via d7); (3) a knight holder that interposes on f6 stands on the front knight's own squares (d5, d7, e4, e8, g4, g8, h5, h7) and is captured with mate (2.Sxd5+), so the holder interposes on g7 from f5 or e6; (4) with Sf5: 1...Sd4 cuts Rd1's d-file guard of d6 (2.Se8#), 1...Sxe3 takes the f4/d4 guard (2.Sh5#), threat 2.Sc6#: claude-bishop-knight-adjacent-postkey 7B/N2Pp2K/4pN2/4kn2/4PRP1/4P3/8/3R4, no holes, no duals, but 2.Sg8+/Se8+/Sh5+ Sg7 3.Sc6# cook every key that leaves the threat knight; his bishop key (vacate the threat square, tries plugging e8/h5) needs the bishop on g6/f7, and on g6 it attacks the holder f5.

Adjacent bishop-knight battery (Bc3/Sd4 v Ke5, his bench mvcxwk0k, 151 steps): 'at first i wanted to block the cooks with the pawn defending the knight. but in the end the knight just guarding the bishop is an easy solution for the cooks.' The black holder Sd5 attacks the rear bishop c3, so after any discharge it captures the checker; that removes the checking cooks of the loaded battery without plugs. Play: threat 2.Sc4# (Sa5, the key bishop vacates c4), 1...Sxb6 (d6 loses Rb6's protection, the knight also covers c4) 2.Sb5#, 1...Sxe3 (takes the f4 guard) 2.Sxe6# (2.Se2# too unless e2 is blocked).

Finishing his Bc3/Sd4 position (3b4/3p4/1R1Ppp2/N2nkP2/2BNP3/2B1PP2/8/7K, every Bc4 move a key): unmask_search with the key fixed at e2 found a black bishop h3 whose 1...Bf1 reaches c4 through e2/d3 and refutes Ba6/Bb3/Ba2/Bf1 (8/1p4K1/1R1Pp3/N2nkP2/2BNP3/2B1PP1b/8/8), and 1.Be2 also blocks the Se2 dual. 1.Bd3 stays a second key: d3 lies on the same f1-c4 line, so any black guard of c4 along it is blocked by both; and 1.Bb5? is then refuted by Sxb6 and Bf1. 448 one-unit additions gave no unique key. Separating d3 from e2 needs a refutation that uses what only d3 does (protects e4, blocks c2-e4 and the d-file) or what only e2 does (blocks e-file/2nd rank, guards d1/f1).

He finished the adjacent bishop-knight battery by making 1.Bd3 the key and turning the old key square into a try: wPe6 plugs the e6 discharge, so 1...Sxe3 has only 2.Se2# and 1.Be2? is refuted by Sxe3 (beside 1.Bb5? Sxb6!); the bishop's other retreats are stopped one unit each (Pa6, Pb3, pg2), 1.Bxd5 by bRh4 (Rxe4 holds the line from e4), and bPb4 protects the holder when it interposes on c3. Our trim then saved two units (bPe7 idle, bPh7 only shielded Kh8; Ka7/Kb7/Kd2 work).

He removed a plug by shifting the board: with the battery one file to the left (Bb3/Sc4 v Kd5) the edge takes the knight squares that wPa6 had to block, and the 21-unit 1.Bd3! version became 17 units (1.Bc3! Sxa6 Sa5#, Sxd3 Sd2#; tries Ba5? Sxa6!, Bd2? Sxd3!). He gave the extra knight a visible role (set Se2~ Sc3#) rather than a bare cook-stopping job. His reading: the battery mechanism (which discharge guards the unguarded square) and the try mechanism (the key piece standing on a mating square) are separate, and each try's refutation goes to the side the bishop went to.

Daily No. 13: in a single-threat Novotny the unit on the crossing already closes both lines, so a mate that needs only one line closed is a second threat. A mating square guarded by BOTH black pieces waits for its own capture: one guard through the crossing, the other along the capturer's second line, given up when it goes to the crossing (Ke4, Rc6, Be7, X d6: 1...Rxd6 2.Sc5#, 1...Bxd6 2.Sf6#). chesscomp.compose.novotny_geometry lists these geometries. The same double guard makes the set Grimshaw on that square with the same mates, so this scheme cannot change them (Rice 1966 did, with a double threat).

A White pawn guarding a square on the black rook's file (Pc4 for d5) gets captured, and the mate after the capture is a recapture (1...Rxc4 2.Rxc4#). Give the square to a unit off the rook's lines (Sb6), and let the rook's arrival on the file have its own mate (1...Rc4 2.Re6#, the rook having left the sixth rank). One change also removed the White rook c1 that existed only for the recapture.

Searches with a free threat around a Novotny core (freethreat, White bishop on the crossing) returned threats that did not need the crossing unit, so the captures never defended. Fix the threat as the crossing unit's own move (postsearch THREAT=Rd6d4) and the mating unit (KMP=d7): post-key positions came in minutes.

Bishop-rook battery, rook two squares from the king (Ke5, Rc3, Bb2): every rook move discharges, and four discharges each cover one side of the field (Rc4 rank 4, Rc6 rank 6, Rd3 d-file, Rf3 f-file); the mid-side squares d5, e4, e6, f5 have one discharge each, the corners two. Rc5 and Re3 are double checks that also cover d5/f5 and e4/e6 (x-ray through the king): block them on d5 and e4 (a light black bishop on d5 cannot step onto the dark battery line; a black pawn on d5 can, d5-d4). The adjacent rook (Rd4 v Ke5) has groups of five discharges per line and is harder to select.

Bishop-rook battery: a knight holder whose two arrivals guard a shared threat square (the motive of both bishop-knight problems) does not work. Up to symmetry there is one class per rook distance (Ke5/Rc3/Bb2/Sd1, arrivals e3 and f2, threat Sg4#): e3 can only cut a guard of f4 (c1-h6), f2 only the f-file from f1, which also guards f4. The rook discharges cover whole sides, so the two cut guards overlap. Holders on the rook's file or rank are taken by a discharge (Rxc3+). A black rook holding along the second rank is cut by the discharge Rc2 itself (a second threat). setplay_search, freethreat and postsearch runs 18 Oct 2026.

When the holder's arrivals share no threat square, let the threat rely on the two guards the defences cut: each defence unguards a flight of the threat mate, and the battery discharge covering that flight mates (1...Rg6 cuts Rh6 off d6, 2.Rc6#; 1...Rg4 cuts Bh3 off f5, 2.Rf3#). The unguard is then both the defence and the selector.

A battery held by a rear-capturing unit: if the threat already works in the diagram, every checking discharge is a cook (1.R~+ Bxa2 2.threat#), so the key must create the threat. His bishop-knight solution did it by vacating the threat square (1.Bb4-c3 frees b4 for Sb4#). In the bishop-rook post-key 7K/3N4/7Q/2Pk4/7R/1Rp5/Bp6/1b6 the threat Qd6 runs along the queen's guard line (c6/d6), so masking it or occupying d6 leaves diagram flights; also note e6 and c4 are covered by every discharge (the bishop's line runs through the king), so a defence that unguards them selects nothing.

His second layer for daily No. 13: mask the threat rook (on the crossing) with a bishop that must keep protecting the threat square (Bd4 in front of Rb4, threat 2.Rd4#). Every bishop move threatens, so the bishop's squares become a white correction. The Novotny captures refute the tries on the lines where the mating knight lands (1.Bb2? Rxb4! 2.Sc3+ cuts b2-d4; 1.Ba7? Bxb4! 2.Sb6+ cuts a7-d4), black cuts refute the others (Sf6!, Re3!), and the key square c5 is next to d4, where nothing can cut. The thematic defences refute the tries through White self-interference, not by new black resources.

I called the transferred-mate Grimshaw/Novotny 'the ceiling under the gate' and stopped. He found a second layer in an hour on the bench by changing the key, not the mechanism: the crossing stays, the key becomes the unmasking of the threat piece, and the tries come from where the mating knights land. Before saying a scheme cannot grow, list what else could be the key (unmask, a correction of the masking unit), not only how the mates could change.

Rear-capturing holder, key that creates the threat (here the White king masking the threat rook, 1.Kf5-g4): the check discharges still cook when the holder's capture square is far from the king (1.Rd2+ Sxg1 2.Se6#, 1.Rc2+ Sxg1 2.Rc4#, 1.Re2+ Sxg1 2.Re4#). In a diagram with no flights every check Black cannot parry mates, and a knight on g1 parries nothing near Kd4. His bishop-knight problems escaped it because the holder's capture (Sxb3) landed next to the king's field. Remedies to try: a rear piece closer to the king (rook adjacent, holder captures on f2 and guards d3/e4), an interposing holder (allowed once the threat is not in the diagram), or a front rook whose departure gives up a field guard. Four cook-stopping pawns did not cure it (bourd-bishop-rook-battery-postkey).

He finished the bishop-rook battery by turning his Kd4/Bg1/Rf2/Sh3 scheme to Kd4/Bg7/Rf6/Se8 and taking a king key that creates the threat by guarding (1.Kf3-e2!, 2.c3#, the diagram has 1.c3+? Kd3!). The rear's square now matters: after a checking discharge the holder's capture Sxg7 lands where it guards f5 and e6, so the free rook's second checks fail (with the rear on g1 they mated). The key's departure also gave up e4, turning a five-fold set dual (1...Sxd6) into the single 2.Rf4#.

In a bishop-rook battery the rear bishop stands on the king's colour (it must attack the king along the diagonal), and so must any bishop that checks the king, near or far. A threat or mate by a second bishop therefore always means two bishops of one colour (promoted force, fatal); give the threat to a knight, a pawn or a rook line instead. His Kc5 version (1.Bb7! 2.Bb6#, thematic tries Bd5? Sxf6!, Be4? Sxe5!, each landing on the matching discharge line) fell to this; the try mechanism itself is the model for this battery.

The colour clash of a bishop threat against the battery's rear bishop has a one-unit cure he applied at once: make the rear a queen ('i just put a queen on g1 and its fine'). The queen on g1 does a bishop's job, a smaller cost than promoted force. Lesson for me: when a structural argument says 'this unit type is impossible', check whether a stronger unit of another type can take the role before restructuring.

Anticipatory closure (his Kc5 bishop-rook battery): when the key piece's tries cannot simply cover or block mating squares, let each correction close a line of a mate that does not exist yet (the discharge line that only matters after Black's capture). 'The refutations are much more unique, as you have to understand the mate in order to figure out the refutation.' He built a full white correction: B~ (off the long diagonal) Qg2+! made unique by wPh2; corrections on the diagonal Bd5!? Sxf6!, Be4!? Sxe5!, Bf3?! Sxe5!; final Bb7! closing nothing. My trim removed wPh2 because it ignored tries; a random move with one refutation is content, not the flaw 'same refutation'.

"anything that is a single phase without tries or changes is not pass for publication unless the single phase is very complicated or pretty". A second phase is a changed mate (set or try against the key) or tries refuted by the thematic defences; tries all refuted by one move the key prevents, or checking tries, do not count. Gate rule 'single phase' (fatal); the judge may except a very complicated or pretty single phase and must say why.

Airiness (his Kc5 battery, 18 Oct 2026): he replaced the black queen by a bishop for the random refutation (B~ Bg2+), dropped wPh2, and took wPc4 off so that c4 stays empty: the square at the end of the mating line f4-c4 is then 'invisible' like d6 at the end of d2-d6, and the king 'feels slightly more free'. He prefers an empty field square covered by a far line to a plug, even at a knight's cost (wSc7 for b5/d5).

A publication solution marks the thematic variations with letters [a], [b] (the same letter for the same defence in every phase, and on a try's refutation when it is a thematic defence), sets the thematic play in bold, puts by-play in brackets after it, and shows no try that captures a piece. tools/originals.py does this.

"when i meant no tries is not good for publication, i meant no thematic tries or changes. random tries dont count". A thematic try is refuted by a thematic defence (one with its own mate after the key), or is a white correction, an interference try or a self-pinning try; a set of tries with the key's threat, or key-piece tries refuted by different random moves, is not a second phase.

Rook-bishop battery (Ke5, Re1, Be3): only Bc5 covers d6 and only Bg5 covers f6 (d4/f4 have four or five discharges; Bd4/Bf4 are double checks). The targets share the bishop's colour, so their guards must be rooks, knights or pawns, and they lie on opposite sides of the battery file: knight holders near the e-file keep reaching e2/e4 and cannot free both; a rook holder reaches one side; the f3 bishop holder never releases. Idea not yet built: the king one square further (Ke6), c5 and g5 blocked, so d6 falls to Bf4 and f6 to Bd4 across the empty line square e5 (crossing discharges). setplay_search HOLDER mode, 8 runs 18 Oct: only degenerate hits.

Rook-bishop battery: a holder that captures the d6 guard on a discharge square, answered by the bishop recapturing there (1...Sxc5 2.Bxc5#), is rejected: "1...Sxc5 2.Bxc5# is bad, need a non recapturing thematic move". The mate must cover the freed square from another square.

Rook-bishop scheme with quiet mates (Ke6, Re1, Be3; 8/3N3R/2b1k3/1N3p2/2P2P2/4B3/8/K3R3, Black to move): a black LIGHT bishop c6 holds by interposing on e4 through d5; bPf5 protects e4 so 2.Rxe4 is no mate. Its other diagonal a4-e8 carries both captures in opposite directions: 1...Bxb5 (Sb5, the d6 guard; Pc4 stops b5-e2) 2.Bc5#, 1...Bxd7 (Sd7, the f6 guard, and a self-block of d7) 2.Bd4# through e5. Pf4 (or Rf4) blocks the right side. Every other bishop move stays on a8-h1 and keeps the hold. Cost: the two guards are knights next to the king, so with White to move the discharge that covers a square frees that square's knight to check after 1...Be4 (1.Bc5+ Be4 2.Sc7/Sd4#, 1.Bd4+ Be4 2.Sf8/Sc5#), and 1.Sf8+ Kf6 2.Bd4# (killed by Rf4 instead of Pf4: g5 stays free). Any key must also kill these; a third knight for the threat is promoted force.

A threat for a position whose only free units are rooks, a light bishop and pawns: a white pawn on f7 promoting 2.f8=S# (the only checking promotion, so a single threat), f7 re-guarded by Be8 which also protects Sd7, e7 self-blocked by a black pawn behind its king. Key 1.f6-f7. Cook-stoppers tried for the left discharges: bSb3 covers d4 and c5; bBd8 covers c7; the White king on f8 blocks 2.Sf8 (key 1.Kg8 clears f8) but 1.Kg7 then also works, and every black knight guarding g7 (e8, h5) reaches f6 and checks g8, while e8 is also capturable by f7. A rook on the 7th rank next to Kf8 gives 1.Rxe7#. Not solved yet.

"repeated tries should be mentioned as by play, the solution is way too verbose. keep it mostly thematic play, with the byplay at the bottom (tries and other non thematic variations)". Main solution: changed set play, each thematic try once with only its changed mates and refutation, the key thematic play, the changes; by-play last: repeated tries (as the try they repeat), random tries, other variations.

Killing the 'discharge frees the guard knight' cooks of the rook-bishop scheme (claude-rook-bishop-battery-kg8-rd8): block the knight's check squares or guard them with Black. A black dark bishop b6 covers c7 and c5 and gives a cross-check 1...Bd4+ against a White king on g7 (no check against g8), so it also refutes the rival king key; it loses d4 when the discharge goes to c5 (the bishop cuts b6-d4), so bSb3 holds d4. The White king on f8 blocks 2.Sf8 and its move is the key (clearing the promotion square of 2.f8=S#). A light bishop on c8 protecting d7 is a hidden battery with Sd7 (every knight move a discovered check); a rook on d8 does the job and frees e8 for the thematic try 1.Ke8? Bxd7+!.

Tries for a battery whose mates are fixed discharges: put a second piece of the same kind in front (a half-battery, Rd1/Bd2/Bd3, bourd-rook-bishop-halfbattery-bg5). The tries move the FRONT bishop onto the thematic mating squares, which are also the knights' check squares (1.Bb5? threatens Sc4#, 1.Bc4? threatens Sb5#); the key moves the rear bishop away, so the front one discharges. Paradox of the refutations: each captures the knight that does not threaten, because the threat needs its guard. The try moves come back crosswise as the thematic mates and the try threats come back as by-play mates (Sc6 2.Sc4#, dxe6 2.Sb5#): 'this is even better, where Nc6 and dxe6 now create the variations from the tries'.

Rook-knight battery geometry (knight two or more squares from the king). On a file (Ke6, Re1, Se4) the quiet discharge mates are Sc3 (d5) and Sg3 (f5), on opposite sides, so one holder cannot reach both guards. On a rank the pair is one-sided: Rb6/Sc6 gives Sb4 (d5) and Sb8 (d7), but the double checks Sd4/Sd8 mate whenever the holder is the only defence; Ra6/Sb6 (three away) gives Sc4 (e5) and Sc8 (e7) with no double check at all. The knight's landings next to the king (d5, d7) are rivals: occupy one with a White pawn (Pd7) and make the other cut a line (Rd2 behind the holder protects d7 only while d5 is empty; 2.Sd5 closes it). The holder knight d5 interposes on b6 and its captures on f4 and f6 take the e5 and e7 guards (claude-rook-knight-battery-d7). A pawn on the battery line (d6) masks it in the diagram: the key d6-d7 unmasks and threatens d8=S#.

setplay_search: an invalid seed (a White unit giving check) made the walk accept every candidate until the board was full and mutate crashed; mutate now returns the position when no square is free and the walk resets to the seed every 20 steps while the current position is invalid. New env NORECAP=1 (HOLDER mode) rejects a wanted mate that captures the holder on its arrival square, which the searches otherwise favour (1...Rc4 2.Sxc4#). Tests in tests/test_setplay_search.py.

Tries for a battery problem by the REAR piece leaving the battery line (bourd-queen-knight-battery-bg5): with a queen as the rear, 1.Qb6? and 1.Qb4? ruin the battery and threaten directly; in each try one thematic capture is answered by a queen mate covering the same freed square from another side (Sxf3 2.Qe3#, Sxf5 2.Qe4#) and the other capture refutes, so each defence refutes once and changes its mate once.

Daily No. 14: a black line piece used as a hinge (it interposes on d4 against both distant queen checks, Qc4+ v Ke4 and Qd3+ v Kd5, and a White unit landing on e3 cuts it) refutes the scheme by its own two moves: 1...Bxe3! takes the interferer and still reaches d4, and 1...Bd4! self-blocks in advance and closes the d-file, which carried the guard of the flight. The Le Grand stayed between two tries (7K/8/Q1N2R2/4p3/4kp2/8/6N1/2BB2b1, 1.Be3?/1.Be2?). Check a hinge's pre-emptive occupation and its capture of the cutter before building around it.

In the flight cross-geometry (Bourd, Labai) the try or the key supplies one square that the other mate covers by itself (Ke4/Qc4 v Qd3: e3 and f3), and that square is a diagram flight unless a set mate provides it. Jonsson (Springaren 1998, 3rd Prize) avoids flights altogether: one black knight opens one White file and closes another (1...Sc3: Ra1 protects a5/a6, Rc2 loses c5/c6), and the unit that left c6 or d8 decides which mate the closed file spoils.

Hill climbs (evolve, the new legrand climb) never found a Le Grand pair in 20 job-runs; the exhaustive layer of one or two added units around a hand kernel found it in 100 s. For a two-phase theme, design the kernel by hand and enumerate the last layer; do not climb from a bare core.

Royal battery (White king as the front piece), first look. On a rank or file the king's two quiet discharges cover squares on opposite sides of the line (Ra5/Kc5 vs Ke5: Kc4 covers d4, Kc6 covers d6), and no black unit can interpose on the king's square (it would attack the king now; only a pawn stepping forward can). On a diagonal (Ba1/Kc3 vs Ke5) the pair is one-sided: Kd3 covers e4, Kc4 covers d5. But a holder reaches only one side's guards (knight f3 takes Sg5 or Sd2 for e4; rook d8 takes Ba8/Bg8 for d5; rook h4 takes Bh7 for e4). A discharge square attacked by Black makes that discharge illegal: the holder searches found mechanisms where the second defence takes control of the other king square (1...Se1 attacks d3, so only 2.Kc4#) instead of unguarding.

Royal battery with an interposing holder (Ba1-Kc3 vs Ke5, holder Sf3 to d4): if the battery is loaded before the key, every legal discharge check is a cook candidate, because the interposer on d4 is pinned and White's other units (Sd2 from c4/f3, Bxd4) are free for the mate. A key that loads the battery cannot create the natural threat 2.Sd3# (a knight masking on b2 or d4 is on a dark square and cannot reach d3 in two moves; another masking unit does not change Sd3#). What worked: a black line guard of both discharge squares before the key (bBa6 on a6-f1 controls c4 and d3), cut by the key at b5 (claude-royal-battery-bb5). The cut piece is then capturable (1...Bxb5) and needs its own mate. A same-line White bishop (from d3/e2/f1) would give the try 1.Bc4? Se1! but also the cook 1.Bxa6.

Royal battery: put the holder knight next to the king on the far side (f5 against Ke5 with Ba1-Kc3, his bench sitting mvfgsr2n). Its moves can then take or cut the guards of d5 and e4 (Sxe7 2.Kc4#, Sxg3 or Se3 2.Kd3#), and each defence leaves a hole that only one discharge fills, so Kc2/Kb3/Kd2 fail without extra control. Every holder move vacates f5, so f5 needs a White guard. Searches (setplay_search, freethreat) find light schemes at once; the open problem is still the loaded battery before the key: 1.Kc4+/Kd3+ Sd4 leaves White's free units a mate (2.f4#, a knight check from e7 once Kc4 covers d5).

Royal battery with a holder next to the king (bourd-royal-battery-sd8): the cooks by discharge checks before the key (1.Kc4+/Kd3+ Sd4 and a free mate) are killed by leaving the holder's own square unguarded before the key. His knight on e6 blocks Bc8 from f5, so after a discharge and ...Sd4 the king escapes to f5; the key 1.Sd8! moves that knight to its threat square and opens the bishop's line, so f5 is guarded in every variation after the key.

Tries for a royal battery (bourd-royal-battery-rg5): a White rook masking the battery between the two kings unmasks it as the key, and its other moves block the king's thematic mating squares, so each try is refuted by the defence that needs that square (1.Re6? Rc5!, 1.Rf5? Rc2!). Only a rook can reach both squares from the masking square. Cost: from any square the rook keeps a line through the vacated masking square to one of the two guarded squares, so one defence is impure and the neutral discharge squares need blockers.

Rook-pawn battery on a rank: the pawn's step or capture attacks squares two ranks beyond its start, never in the black king's field, so the series concept (the discharge guards the square the defence unguarded) only works by occupation: a single step fills the flight next to the king. The only line a single step cuts and a double step keeps is the third rank from the rook's side, and that rook also guards the occupation square, so the occupation/line pair collides. What works is cutting a black interposer: d3 cuts a light bishop's path to e2 (b5-c4-d3), d4 a dark bishop's path to b2 (e5-d4-c3); one holder cannot have both (colours), so two holders select the discharge (claude-rook-pawn-battery-scheme).

Rook-pawn battery with two bishop interposers (Ra2/Pd2 v Kh2), what each geometry costs: (1) light bishop from b5 (path c4-d3-e2): its line runs on to f1 and cuts a first-rank rook guarding g1/h1 (hole 1...Bf1); (2) light bishop from the h7 side (path e4-d3-c2): every knight-check square on h2 (f1, f3, g4) is guarded from a square on its own path, so a staying move parries the threat (holes Bf5/Be4); (3) the dark bishop's only moves off the long diagonal run along b8-h2 and parry nothing quietly; a capture works (1...Bxf4 takes the knight guarding g2, needed in a knight mate but on the check line in the battery mates). A threat by a second battery (Rh5/Kh4, 2.Kg4+) removes the third knight but 1...Bf1 then interposes on h3 via g2. Mirrored (Ka2, Rh2/Pe2) and Kg2 versions found nothing in freethreat runs.

A battery whose mates are selected by which black interposer the front piece cuts (rook-pawn: d3 cuts the light bishop, d4 the dark one) has no key with the battery loaded: before any defence, the discharge plus the capture of the interposer (1.d3+ Bb2 2.Rxb2#, 1.d4+ Be2 2.Rxe2#) mates, and the interposition square cannot be protected by a black unit that does not itself interpose there (only a pawn can, and a pawn on rank 3 steps onto the line). So the key must load the battery (a masking unit leaves the line) and create the threat in the same move; in Ra2/Pd2 v Kh2 the only such key (1.Sf2-h3!, protecting Rg1) takes a flight. Plan the key before the interposers: it decides whether the scheme can be a problem.

Correction of Claude's lesson of the same day ('no key with the battery loaded'): it was too general. E. Bourd (bench, 1.Bh2!) kept the battery loaded in the diagram by changing what the bishops guard: the light bishop attacks the battery rook itself (e6-a2, 1.c3+? Bxa2!), so there is no interposition square to protect, and the dark bishop's interposition square b2 is protected by a black pawn that cannot step onto the line (bPa3, blocked by Ra2; 1.c4+? Bb2!). The pre-key discharges then become checking tries showing the mechanism. He also moved the bishops next to each other (e6/f6, 'more unified') and the king off the corner (h2 -> f2: 'a bit too rigid'), and both defences cut the same White line (Rg6 on the g-file), the key piece taking over g1. Before declaring a structural impossibility, list every way the discharge's refutation can be met: interposition, capture of the rear piece, protection of the interposer by a unit that cannot interpose itself.

Rook-pawn battery Ra2/Pc2 v Ke2 with two black bishops: a guard line that both bishops can cut must cross a light and a dark square of one line near the king; the f-file (f3 light, f4 dark) guarding f2 works, and the battery mate re-covers f2 along the second rank. A diagonal guard of d2 does not work: the dark bishop that cuts it stands on the same diagonal and interposes on d2 after the discharge. With the king on e2 the discharge also opens b1-c2-d3, so a queen or bishop on b1 takes over d3 by itself. Both self-blocks (f3 and e3) cannot be needed at once: the White guard that one mate needs stays in the other.

Unified try pairs for a two-discharge battery problem need an asymmetry between the two mates. In the f-file scheme (1.Sh3!, Bf4 2.c4#, Bf3 2.c3#) there are only two: 2.c4# needs a guard of f3 off the f-file (the cut at f4 removes the rook's), 2.c3# lets f3 be self-blocked; and each pawn square closes its own White lines (c3: third rank to d3, a5-e1 to d2/e1; c4: only the a6-e2 check line, usable as a protection line of a White plug on d3). A try refuted by Bf4 must lose the f3 guard; one refuted by Bf3 must leave a guard reaching its square only through c3. The units that can create the threat by moving (a masking unit on the f-file, a unit on the threat square) cannot reach those squares: a knight leaving f3 always guards f3 again and can mate on g1 itself; a queen on the f-file cannot also stand on b5/a3; static backups help only one side. Build the asymmetry into the scheme first (different self-blocks or pawn guards in the field, e.g. a bishop-pawn battery where c3/c4 guard d4/d5), then look for the try piece.

Daily No. 15: in a pawn-shell Zagoruiko (bK e5 boxed by d6/e6/f6, 1...d5 and 1...f5 opening the b8-h2 and a1-h8 diagonals) the queen alone gives two clean phases (e8: Qb8#/Qh8#; e7: Qc7#/Qg7#); every post reaching a third pair also reaches a second mate of one defence, and in a complete block every waiting move keeps the set mates (sixteen keys). Foster (The Problemist 2003, 3rd Prize) and Burda-Solarczyk (Sachove umeni 1998, 4th Prize) take the third phase from a knight key that becomes the mating piece (1.Sb5! Sc3#, 1.Se1! Sd3#/Sf3#), with the queen far away. Plan the third phase's piece first.

trychange MODE=zag (new, tested): Zagoruiko score over set play, tries and key (KP=any for phases by any White unit, THREAT='**' for blocks), mates compared by piece and square. Around bare cores it found nothing in 16 jobs (as with Le Grand): use it on a hand kernel. Its pre-filter misses the queen's capture threats (Qxf6#), so solve every hit.

Rook-knight battery with a black holder knight next to the king (Ke6, Sd5, Ra6/Sb6): put a second White line behind the holder (Rd2, whose e-file mate 2.Re2# opens when d5 empties) and threaten to capture the holder (2.cxd5#). Every knight move then parries the threat, but only by escaping the capture: no error of a defence is tied to the threat, which is the scheme's weakness (E. Bourd, 20 Oct 2026). The knight can hold only one line: from b4/c7/e7 it still stops the battery (c6 or the a6 capture) but not 2.Re2#; from c3/e3/f6 it stops 2.Re2 (e2/e4/e3) but not the battery. The key 1.Bd6-c5 creates the threat only by taking the flight Kxd6 (it guards the square it left); its unmasking of the battery is unrelated to the threat. Its other squares give tries refuted by the holding moves (1.Bb4? Sxb4!, 1.Ba3? Sb4!, 1.Bf8? Se7!). Open problems: separating the four discharges after the e-file moves and the d6 flight in the diagram. Tools: evolve CORR=d5 found it from a hand sketch in 270 s; freethreat now takes THREAT= (tested).

"lets try to do in dailies things we practiced, le-grand zaguruiko, reciproal changes is a bit rough yet" (after daily No. 14 and No. 15 were study posts on Le Grand and Zagoruiko). The rotation skips themes marked 'paused' in blog/themes.json (Le Grand, Zagoruiko, reciprocal change, and Rudenko, never practiced); unpause after practice with him.

Describe what a key really does for the threat, checked on the board, not what it does in general (E. Bourd, 20 Oct 2026, on 'the key unmasks the battery and threatens cxd5': 'how it create the threat cxd5. The whole sentence is wrong. The move has no error for the threat'). Before writing 'the key threatens X', play X in the diagram and name the Black reply that the key removes; if the key's thematic effect (unmasking) is not that reply, say so. A threat to capture the defender makes every move of it a defence by escape, with no error tied to the threat.

Rook-knight battery with the knight next to the king (Ra5/Sd5 v Ke5, no flights): the knight on d5 itself guards f4/f6, so after a discharge only Sf6 (covers e4) and Sf4 (covers e6) use their landing; Sc3/Sc7 cover the same squares and must be blocked (pawns c3, c7); no landing covers d4/d6, and a captured guard of f4/f6 cannot be followed by Sf4/Sf6 (occupation needs that guard). A black knight holder on e3 (it interposes on d5) gives 1...Sxg2 (e4 guard) 2.Sf6#, 1...Sxf5 (e6 guard) 2.Sf4# and 1...Sc4 2.Bf4# through the vacated e3; line pieces as holders found nothing. The searches first offer the threat Sxe3# (capture of the holder): exclude threats from the battery square (NOQ=d5). With the battery loaded in the post-key, discharge checks cook every key that does not create the threat.

Rook-knight battery next to the king, his small scheme (Rb4/Sd4 v Ke4, black holder Sd3 that captures the rook, 1...Sxf2 2.Sf5#, 1...Sxf4 2.Sc6#): with the battery loaded in the diagram, every key is cooked by discharge checks (1.Sb5+ Sxb4 forced, 2.Sd6#: the knight checks again from a knight-check square), and a second knight near the king mates at once (c8-d6, g8-f6). The key must load the battery: a masking unit on the line square c4 that cannot mate (a knight there reaches d6/d2): a bishop, whose move to b5 also threatens 2.Bc6# (1.Bb5!). He disliked the queen-and-far-knight scheme: 'its just all too strong, i started with something smaller'.

Daily No. 16 (study post on Manolescu): a Dombrovskis defence needs a side effect that beats the try and a main effect that parries the key's threat, and the key must be able to cancel the side effect. A pawn whose two steps only self-block and open a Black line (Kf5, e7, Bd8: 1.Qg7! (2.Qg5#) e6 2.Bc2#, e5 2.Qg6#) has no side effect a key can cancel, so no layer of one or two added units supplied a try (about 47,000 positions). Write each defence's side effect and the unit that cancels it before placing anything.

Manolescu (Buletin Problemistic 1984-85, 2nd Prize, psis-e1c54a41bb) read with the anatomy: the knight d4 is the only guard of e6; Bxd4 and Rxd4 each remove it (the flight e6 refutes 1.Sec6? and 1.c3?), the key 1.Qh3! guards e6 and threatens Qe6# protected by that knight, so both captures still defend, and the Grimshaw on d4 selects the mate: the bishop on d4 cannot reach c4 (2.c4#), the rook on d4 shuts Bf2 out of c5 (2.Ra5#). A doubled Dombrovskis from one sole guard taken by two line pieces.

Key-piece tries by white obstruction of a mating square (his rook-knight battery, 'Rf5? Rc6? R-somewhere solution'): the rook on f6 blocks the threat square; Rf5 blocks f5 (2.Sf5# after Sxf2) and Rc6 blocks c6 (2.Sc6# after Sxf4). The rook's line beyond the last try square must end: a black pawn on b6 can be taken (1.Rfxb6 cooked); a white bishop there guarded e3 through d4 after every discharge (4 keys); bRb7 protecting b6 turns 1.Rfxb6? into a third try (Rxb6! guards f6 along the rank). trypair found it in 6 s once the post-key had no holes or duals. The cost: a static key (both thematic mates set) and 21 units.

'I dont like all the clumped white pawns. Maybe can replace some with black pieces' (rook-knight battery with rook tries). Method: anatomy marks the pawns needed in no mate; one solve without each names what it stops; then trypair with SPEC units='brqp' (black only) on the kernel without that pawn, one and two units. Result: wPg3 -> bPh4 (guards g3 against the discharge checks 1.Sf5+/1.Se2+). The rest are structural: a black self-block next to the king fails when it can reach the battery line after the discharge (pawn d5-d4, bishop to c4, rook to d4); a black unit on e5 kills the flight that 1...Sxf4 opens; the white king cannot take g6 (the thematic 1...Sxf4 checks it); a black stopper on g6/h7 takes g8 or reaches f6. Pawns guarding thematic squares (f2, f4, c2) stay.

'You need to be able and recognize that pieces like b1 b7 can be changed to other pieces. Where those become available. Thats more than a single step of searching... thats the next level trimming or improving.' When trim finds nothing, write each unit's job and reassign: one piece takes two jobs, which frees a unit (or a piece type) for another job. On the rook-knight tries problem: wBe5 (free dark bishop) closed the e-file and protected d4, replacing wPe5 and wPc3; wPd5 went once a black Ba8 (through b7, c6) answered 2.Bd5+ after 1.Rd6, which needed bRb7 -> b8 (still protecting b6 through b7) and the threat knight g8 -> h7 (else 1...Rxg8). White pawns 8 -> 4 at the same unit count.

unmask_search now retypes non-core units (any piece, either colour) and takes PAWNW=<cost per white pawn>; importable (setup/main), tests/test_unmask_retype.py. From a bare seed with d5 forced empty it collapsed to small post-keys with the diagram flight Kxd5 (the flight costs only 20): the black d5 guard needed three coordinated changes (Ba8, Rb7->b8, Sg8->h7), found by reasoning about jobs, not by mutation. Seeded with the sound result it found nothing lighter in 4 x 280 s.

On bourd-rook-knight-rd6-tries (pure try pair 1.Rf5? Sxf2!, 1.Rc6? Sxf4!, key 1.Rd6!, both mates set, 20 units): 'its not the best, but i think it shows a decent clear theme with tries (i dont consider Rxb6 a real try honestly). the rook itself is somewhat just for the sake of the play... even if no changes are shown, its not bad, could be placed as recommendation in a random tourney'. Claude had said it would not be placed: a clear pure try pair earns a commendation despite a static key and support units; a try refuted by a cook-stopper's recapture is not content.

Double-check mates (his concept, 21 Oct 2026): a defence that only removes a guard can never make a double check necessary, because the double check covers its own square and is then already a mate (a threat) before the defence. A double check is needed only when a single check would be parried: a black unit that can interpose on the battery line or capture the rear piece. That unit can be static (bPc5 pushing to c4) or the defence itself (a black bishop arriving on e3 guards d4). Selection between two double checks: each mating knight lands on a white guard line (Sd2 cuts Bc1-e3, Sd6 cuts Rd8-d5) and each defence self-blocks exactly the square that line guarded (claude-double-check-two-bishops-scheme).

freethreat DOUBLE=n: post-key search without named defences, scored by the number of distinct double-check mates each the only mate of its defence (tests/test_freethreat_double.py on Bie, Springaren 2001). From bare battery cores (Ra4/Sc4, Re1/Se2, Bb1/Sd3, Bb2/Rc3) it found one double-check variation each in 270 s, never two: the second needs a designed selection, then freethreat with named defences finds it in seconds. A scan of the database (78 #2s with a double-check mate) showed them mostly incidental; Bie 2001 (six, two batteries, flight-giving key) and Vasilenko/Shanshin (half-battery, two flights) make them the theme.

Bishop-rook double checks (his request after the knight scheme). The rook's double-check landings must be separable: a landing that cuts a white guard line is spoiled unless the defence self-blocks the guarded square. Rook two squares from the king (Bb2/Rc3 v Ke5): landings c5/e3 only cut dark diagonals (b4-c5-d6, d2-e3-f4), so a second dark-square line piece would be needed besides Bb2: impossible but for the queen on one side. Rook diagonally adjacent (Bb2/Rd4 v Ke5): landings d5/e4 cut light lines (Bc6-d5-e4, Qc2-d3-e4-f5), a light bishop and the queen: three double-check mates in 11 units, including the king walking onto the battery diagonal (1...Kf6 2.Rd6#). The key is the obstacle: a loaded bishop-rook battery is armed in every diagram (the rook masks the bishop), so its discharges cook unless an interposer and flights stop them; a battery-forming bishop key leaves the front rook hanging.

On claude-bishop-rook-double-checks-scheme (three double-check mates from one bishop-rook battery, 11 units, diagram flights e6/f6, static key): 'its really nice, the fatal flaws here are kind of worth it. the force is very strong on the black side. yes there are some flaws, like the unprovided flights. but 3 double check variations is somewhat the next tier of the 2 phase. its not like is variation worth 1 flaw, its a different tier of problem you are making.' Judge by tier first: several variations each made by a hard device count like a second phase, and a flaw fatal in a light problem (a diagram flight) can be carried. CLAUDE.md and the judge checklist amended.

Masked bishop-rook battery (his idea: rook two squares from the king, a black piece in the middle causing the mates): Bb2-Rc3-bBd4-Ke5. The mask's moves open the battery and its arrival can select the double check by cutting a white guard line (1...Bb6 cuts Ra6-e6 -> 2.Re3#; 1...Bf2 cuts Qf1-f5 -> 2.Rc5#). Trap: while the mask stands, the white rook's own checks Rc5+/Re3+ are single checks and the mask cannot parry them, because the rook's departure from c3 pins it on the diagonal; and the only squares the double check covers beyond the single check are d4 (the mask) and f6 (x-ray). So the single rook checks need an interposer on d5 and e4 (a black knight on f6 or c3) or blocked paths (c4, d3) or arrival lines (d5, e4).

Daily No. 17: a black rook beside the king (Rd4 v Ke4, wBa7 behind it on a7-e3) gives an easy random move (every move opens the bishop to d4/e3) and easy corrections (Rd5 cuts the queen's 5th rank, Rc4 her b5-d3 diagonal, Rd3 pins Sf3 against Kh3). But its moves along its own lines keep guarding what it guarded: a threat against the rook or its square (2.Qxd4#) is parried by arrival, so there is no random move (E. Bourd, 17 Oct 2026; the solver reports no R~). In a block the rook is the only mobile unit and the gate fails it ('simple block'). A rook correction needs a threat parried by the rook's departure: a black line through its square (a black bishop behind it), chosen before any white guard.

Masked battery made asymmetric (his 'reduce the symmetry... rethinking the threat'): instead of fighting the rook's single check that pins the mask, make it the threat (2.Re3#: the rook leaves c3, Bb2 pins the black bishop on d4, which cannot parry). Then the mask's random moves allow the threat as a double check, and only specific mask moves defend: one that cuts a guard the threat needs (Bf2 cuts Qf1's f-file -> 2.Rc5# double check) and one that captures the front piece (Bxc3 -> 2.Bxc3#). The key forms the battery (1.Bc1-b2), so the mask's play is new after the key. freethreat found the post-key, keyfind --patch the key with one black pawn.

'we need two thematic double checks, anything less is not it' (on claude-masked-battery-bb2, one double check among three mates). For a double-check problem the floor is two thematic double-check variations; asymmetry or extra variations do not replace the second one.

Masked bishop-rook battery Bb2-Rc3-bBd4 v Ke5: the mask can select between Rc5 (needs d5 or f5 opened) and Re3 (needs e4 or e6 opened) only by its arrival square on the a7-g1 diagonal: a cut (Bb6: 6th rank -> e6; Bf2: f-file -> f5) or a capture of a white guard (Bxb6: a knight guarding d5; Bxf2: a knight guarding e4). A mixed pair (one cut, one capture) needs the same square or a white unit standing on the other mate's landing square, so the pair is cut/cut or capture/capture. Asymmetry has to come from the guards' piece types and the threat (Qa6 + Rf1, threat Sd7). Single rook checks are best stopped by black knights capturing on c5/e3; a battery-forming key (1.Bb2) makes the threat a rook check, which leaves only one double check.

Tries for two double checks selected by guard lines (masked bishop-rook battery, his 'lets think how we could add tries in theory'): Re3# leaves d5/f5 to static guards, Rc5# leaves e4/e6; d6/f4 are shared. A thematic try spoils exactly one mate: a white unit landing on the f-file guard line (f2-f4) kills f5 -> refuted only by Bb6!; a white unit landing on the 6th-rank guard line (b6-d6) kills e6 -> refuted only by Bf2!. A block of the shared bishop line (f3/e4 cutting Bg2 from e4 and d5) spoils both. b6/f2 lie on the mask's diagonal (Bxb6/Bxf2 captures). Candidate try piece: a knight on e4 (f6 key, d6 and f2 tries); tested with unmask_search TRIES (4 x 280 s): unique key 1.Se4-f6 but the diagram flight Kd5 (the knight cuts Bg2 from d5), 1.Sd6? refuted by captures on d6 and Ke6, 1.Sf2 no threat. Needed: a d5 guard not through e4 (a light bishop on the a8 side, b7/a8), d6 safe from black captures, a single threat from d6 and from f2.

Claude's claim only held for the squares between rook and king (d5/e4/e6/f5). His tries by the key bishop are the try theory in practice: 1.Bd5? blocks Rd6's check line (Bg3!), 1.Bf5? blocks the rook's path to f4 (Bxc7!).

source: Claude, theme 'Black unpins a White piece' (E. Bourd)
text: The clean engine (Ahues, Problem Forum 2001, 3rd Prize): a black bishop pins the white queen to the white king; one black knight interposes on two squares of the pin line BEYOND the queen (the pinner cannot follow there), both arrivals guarding the threat square, each guarding one of the freed queen's mating squares. Every such problem has the pinner's capture of the pinned piece with check (1...Bxc3+), which must be provided in the set too. claude-unpin-white-queen-scheme (16 units, 1.Bh3-d7!) is the bare scheme.

Keys that create the pin on White's own piece do not work in this engine: a queen moving onto an open pin line means the white king was in check in the diagram; a white unit leaving the pin line (unmasking) frees the queen in the diagram, so her unpin mates are mates in one unless the key adds a guard they all need (e4 here), and the searches found none. If the threat piece also guards the flight that the set mate after the pinner's check needs (Bb5 on c6), that check is unprovided: give the flight a permanent guard (Sb8) and bring the threat piece from a square off both its lines (Bh3-d7).

unmask_search ALLOWCHECK=1: a black check in the post-key passes when a mate answers it, and a diagram check passes only with a set mate (mated_after). Without it every unpin-of-White post-key is rejected for the pinner's capture with check.
